Uniform Title: *Mṛgendrapaddhatiṭīkā* Commentator: Vaktraśambhu Manuscript: IFP T1021 (copy of IFP manuscript RE 40086)
Description: Transcribed from IFP transcript T1021, which is itself a copy of manuscript RE 40086 of the IFP.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: April 5, 2010.
Internet Publisher: Web Publisher: Muktabodha Publication Year: 2010 Publication Country: United States
Note from the copyist of the transcript: This work entitled *Mṛgendrapaddhati*, composed by Aghoraśivācārya, has been numbered and transcribed.

This palm-leaf manuscript, which includes the root text (*mūla*) along with the commentary (*ṭīkā*) composed by Naṭeśa Śiva, measures 1" x 1". Each leaf contains six lines written in the Grantha script.
At the beginning of the work, there are omissions of words here and there due to damage caused by insects and worms. At the end of the manuscript...
Due to the lack of elegance in the characters on some palm leaves, it is inferred that there was a change in the scribe. Likewise, numerous errors are also present.
This manuscript gradually reaches completion.
The *Mṛgendrāgamapaddhati* and its commentary (*Ṭīkā*).
Śrī.
Having prostrated, I shall declare the path of the Mṛgendrāgama.
Since the division of tantras is traditionally held to be based on the distinctions of ritual action (*kriyā*) and so forth,
therefore, it should be performed exactly as prescribed in the tantras.
Or else, that which is declared by the power of the object itself should be accepted from another compendium.
Having risen at dawn and meditated upon Śiva dwelling within the lotus of the heart, one should go [to the sacred site] and perform the emission.
One should not [void urine or excrement] in rivers, ashes, pits, water, young grass, cow dung, or paths;
nor in the vicinity of a single tree, a crossroads, a cremation ground, a garden, or in public places.
Silent, with his right ear [turned toward the teacher],
standing on ground covered with grass and the like, one-pointed in mind, with his gaze fixed on the tip of his nose,
and not facing cows, Brahmins, lingas, the moon, the sun, women, or others.
One should wipe the anus with blades of grass or clods of earth, but not with wood, stones, or cow dung.
Holding the *liṅga* with the left hand and taking up earth with the other hand,
[one should apply it] fifteen times to the *liṅga*, once to the anus, and twice to the left hand.
Seven [mudrās] are to be applied to the buttocks, one to the left [buttock], and likewise to the two hands.
By removing the application of perfumes...
[having sipped water and being seated in a pure state], one should perform the cleansing of the teeth.
A tooth-stick produced from a milk-tree, pure, free from defects,
and twelve or eight finger-breadths in length, is for the attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Nor [should one use] wood from a Piśāca-dhava tree, nor from aṅguli, nor from kuśa or aśvattha, nor from any tree used for sacrificial purposes.
The Vāruṇa, Taijasa, Bhauma, Ānila, Divya,
Mānasa, Gaurava, and Māntra— these are the eight types of ablutions, among which the Vāruṇa is primary.
Having purified the earth with the Astra mantra,
one should divide it into three parts— consecrated by the Saṃhitā and encircled by the Brahma-mantra.
With one portion, one should perform the purification of the arms again and again.
Having taken [the water],
one should perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana) and, facing either east or north, partake [of the food].
Having meditated upon the Brahma-weapon, he should then perform those rites;
having divided the remaining portion into three parts, he should recite the mantra over that which is held in his left hand.
Having taken water with the first [mantra] for removing obstacles, one should make it nectar with another;
having smeared the body with yet another, one should [perform the rite] within the water according to the *saṃhitās*.
Having immersed himself up to the stars (the neck) and performed the ritual bath,
he should emerge from the water, bind his topknot, change his garment,
and perform the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules; then, withdrawing the sacred water (tīrtha) from within his mouth, he should sip water again.
The knowledge of the Self is auspicious...
[one should touch] the arms, the navel, the heart, and the head according to the prescribed rule.
One should make the supreme Āgneya station with pure ashes.
During the twilights, he should avoid contact with women and activities such as eating.
On the path, they do not maintain the fire of Śiva-vidyā near the goat;
by day, one should smear the limbs with the Tripuṇḍra and other marks.
One should touch the head and other parts with the Astra-mantra for the sake of another bath using ashes.
One should bathe [the deity] from the head, face, heart, secret place, and body, facing the northeast; this is the ritual for the secondary limbs and the hands.
Or even with water from the Ganges moistened [upon it], the earth becomes like that which has been scorched by fire.
By reciting the *māruta-saṃhitā-mantra*, one becomes the wind, free from dust;
one should then proceed to this divine, purifying mental bath,
performed constantly by mentally bathing Śakti with nectar using the root mantra.

The purification for one whose Guru has reached the summit [of the stages] is performed with the *saṃhitā* mantra; the sprinkling (*seka*) for the Varuṇa and Āgneya [initiations] is likewise appropriate.
Having first performed the salutation toward the northeast and subsequently sipped water (ācamana), one becomes consecrated through the ritual of the limbs (sakalīkṛta);
this includes the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa).
She is the sovereign of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara, the Great Goddess who is the mistress of speech.
At midnight, while his own mind is absorbed within the luster of that formless [deity],
he should perform the cleansing with the *aghamaṛṣaṇa* mantra and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the mantra.
He should sprinkle the water falling from his left hand with his other hand.
Having performed the consecration with the [mantra] joined at the crown of the head...
[the remainder] held in the right hand, having smelled it while it is white, by means of the breath.
One should pour water upon the surface of a diamond-stone (vajraśilā), which is appropriate for Kṛṣṇapiṅgala and which cuts away the impurities residing in the body; that is the *aghamarṣaṇa*.
Furthermore,
[one should worship] the deities of the mantras by their names and by their seed-syllables (bījas), preceded by the syllable Om and ending with Svāhā.
With the tips of his hands joined by darbha grass,
with a sacred thread hanging down to his ears, and with the *tīrtha* at the base of the little finger...
With mantras joined by *vaṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ*, [he should worship] Sanaka and the others in due order.
Wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), he worships the fathers and grandfathers with the ring finger and the base of the thumb.
Having meditated upon Sadāśiva and filled [the vessel], one should worship the image with the root mantra;
having recited the Saṃhitā according to one's ability, one should worship with red flowers and other offerings.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and the ritual assignment of mantras to the limbs (sakalīkaraṇa),
[he should worship] Gaṇeśa in the southern direction upon the upper udumbara post, as well as Kamalā and Vāṇī,
located on his own right branch...
With names accompanied by the fourth case ending, followed by "namaḥ" and preceded by the syllable "oṃ."
Having expelled the obstacles dwelling in the divine, atmospheric,
and terrestrial realms by means of the three [mantras], one should enter while not touching the threshold with both feet.
Having worshipped another weapon or Brahmā, [he should proceed].
Having smeared both hands, inside and out, with fragrance, one should cleanse them with a cloth.
Then, having assigned the seat and the form consisting of the pentad of Brahmā beginning with Īśa, [one should perform the assignment] with the fingers...
And one should assign the limbs, beginning with the heart and ending with the armor, to the fingers starting from the little finger.
One should envelop and purify [the two] with Śambhu ending in *vauṣaṭ*;
having meditated upon the Śakti up to the level of *samanā*, one should [place] the tuft...
Having performed inhalation and retention, one should [draw] the life-force from the heart-lotus with the heart-mantra.

One should place the *sampuṭa* residing in the subtle body in the center with the seed-syllable of the form; having placed the heart-mantra in the heart, the head-mantra on the head, the crest-mantra on the topknot, the armor-mantra between the breasts, and the weapon-mantra on the right hand.
Having displayed [the mudrā],
having performed three claps of the hands and having dispelled the obstacles with the snapping of the fingers, he spoke.
One should fashion the Sala tree from the weapon-mantra using the index finger, and the Ghana from the armor-mantra;
[one should place them] within the heart as if they were external.
One should offer oblations into the fire within the navel-cavity by means of the emission of the *bindu* through the *vāyavya* [channel];
and one should meditate upon Śiva between the eyebrows, seated amidst the throbbing *bindu*.
Having thoroughly cleansed the special arghya vessel, one should fill it with water using the *astra* mantra and the *sruva* ladle.
Having worshipped with mantras, having performed the eight-limbed prostration, and having protected it with the weapon-mantra (astra),
one should consecrate it with the root-mantra and display the cow-seal (dhenumudrā).
Having sprinkled his own head with those waters and purified the ritual substances with the Astra-mantra,
the wise practitioner, having worshipped himself with the Mūla-mantra and observed silence as desired,
should recite the mantras ending with Śiva for the purification of the mantras.
One should offer Sadyojāta and the others with the general arghya water, using the five Brahma-mantras.
Then, having removed the floral remains (nirmālya), if Caṇḍeśa is to be worshipped,
one should perform the placement (nyāsa) with the Heart mantra and [the Weapon mantra] upon the pedestal.
Having thus performed the purification of the divine signs of the mantra based upon the self,
one should worship the God with devotion by means of divine offerings according to one's own capacity.
Having worshipped Vighnanāśaka in the northwest with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should [place] Dhruva or the Hṛdaya-mantra in the center of Ādhāraśakti and Ananteśa;
then [the qualities of] dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, and aiśvarya, along with their respective powers (bala), for the Self.
One should worship Agni, Rākṣasa, and so forth, and likewise Dharma and the others in the directions starting from the east; furthermore, one should worship the covering below.
One should worship the upper covering in the southwest and the northeast;
[and] the seed, the stalk, and the sprout...
Having worshipped them in order in the directions starting from the east, located upon the filaments,
[he worships] Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and then Vikaraṇī.
Having worshipped [the goddess] Balādyā, who is preceded by Kālī,
together with Brahmā, one should place the orb of the Sun on the tips of the petals and the orb of the Moon on the tips of the filaments.
Having meditated upon the seat of Śiva, one should worship it, beginning with Earth and ending with the principle of Śakti.
One should worship the mantras of the seats (pīṭha-mantras) upon the seat, and the forms (mūrti) and so forth within the linga-image.
Having deposited the five [faces] beginning with Īśāna, one should contemplate the body of knowledge (vidyā-deha).
With hands and feet like red lotuses, reaching down to the ankles and resembling crystal in clarity.
Having the luster of snow, coral, and gold, and being exceedingly white...
holding a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), a rosary (*akṣamālā*), and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with his ten hands, he is most serene with a smiling face.
He possesses vision, action, and will;
[he has] a blue mark on his throat, beautiful limbs, and three eyes in each face.
Having meditated upon this body of knowledge (vidyādeha) and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the eyes, one should join [the breath];
having fully uttered the root mantra, [one should perform] the [rite] at the head.
Having meditated upon [the deity] arisen within the *bindu*, [one visualizes it] having emerged through the path of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Having meditated on [the deity] as contained within a handful of flowers, one should, by means of the *vāhinī* [mudrā],
restrain the harsh limbs and join them to their respective places;
and every day, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) for the sake of proximity (*sannidhya*) and for the request of permission for worship (*pūjānujñapti*).
Having displayed the Mahāmudrā, one should satisfy [the deity] with a welcome.
One should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at the lotus-feet, water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*) in the mouths, and flowers along with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) upon the heads.
In sequence, with the mantras ending in *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, *svāhā*, and *vauṣaṭ* [uttered] by Śambhu,
[he performs] anointing, rubbing with unguents, and cleansing with black mustard, salt, and other substances.
Then, O Lord of Gods, one should bathe [the deity] with the fivefold Śākta [substances],
using scented water consecrated by the root mantra starting from Īśāna;
these should be contained in jars purified by the Astra-mantra, interspersed with water and incense.
Having bathed Śiva with the waters of the Gaṅgā and other sacred fords consecrated by mantras, one should gently wipe him dry with a clean cloth.
One should adorn [the deity] with garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments;
having offered the arghya and a handful of flowers...
Having again given water for sipping and having shown him his heart's desire, he said:
Having worshipped the limbs of Brahmā within the limbs of dissolution,
[one should worship] Nara, who is stout, on the eastern petal, and Ghora, who is dark-colored, on the southern [petal].
In the north is the red left thigh, and in the west is the white [thigh].
One should place the head in the northeast with offerings of smoke-colored substances, and the crest-lock in the north with black food offerings.
In the northwest is the green armor; in the directions are the weapons with the luster of fire;
[and] by means of the Egg of Brahmā...
One should worship Śiva with offerings of food, drinks, betel-leaf, mouth-fresheners, and other such items.
One should satisfy [the deity] with a purifying offering of flowers, dūrvā grass,

and seeds; having contemplated the Lord as being fully satisfied, one should mutter the root mantra according to one's capacity and place the flower along with the arghya water into the hand of the boon-granter (varahasta), encased within the heart-mantra.
The recitation performed for the sake of the secret [mantras] and so forth—
may success be attained through your grace, while you remain present.
Oṃ! Whatever action there may be, O Lord—whether always performed well or ill—may that [be dissolved] within the heart of me who abides in the state of Śiva.
Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere; he who is Śiva is indeed myself.
Having thus performed the rite of recitation and offered himself with circumambulations,
he should worship his own guru with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while standing in the direction of the fire (the southeast).
Having performed the oblation in the fire as requested, he should present the water offering (arghya) with his face turned away.
Having given [the offerings] and worshipped the individual souls (aṇu) situated in the places of the limbs,
one should raise them with the withdrawal mudrā (saṃhāramudrā) and unite them from form to form.
Then, having worshipped Caṇḍeśa located in the northeast direction with the syllable Om (praṇava),
one should offer him the remains of the flowers (nirmālya).
In this manner, one should worship Caṇḍanāyaka upon a sacrificial mound, a painting, or similar objects.
Thus concludes this procedure for the worship of Giriśa with verses,
along with the twilight ablutions and [other rites] by the hundreds;
[this is] the path of the illustrious Mṛgendragiriśāgama.
By the wise one who bears the name Aghoraśiva, [this was written] from a mere fragment.
Thus ends the Nityārcanavidhi, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, the teacher of two hundred thousand [verses].
Having prayed to Īśāna for the sake of the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), one should proceed to the fire-sanctuary;
taking up the vessel of honorific water (*arghyapātra*), one should perform the circumambulation in the order of dissolution (*sasaṃhāra*).
The Maru [mandala] is measured by its own dimensions;
it has a height of four, three, or two finger-breadths, and is endowed with three rims of equal width.
Whether circular or square, with a navel resembling an ashvattha leaf,
it should be twelve finger-breadths [in size].
Seated in the foremost position, he should perform the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having gazed upon the pit with the Śambhu-mantra and sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra,
one should then level it, dig out [excess earth], crush [the lumps], and wipe it clean;
having smeared it [with cow dung] and conceived of it as the form of the Kalās, one should encircle it with the boundary lines (paridhi).
Three times, facing east, [and] three times facing west; or once, or even in reverse order, for the purpose of performing the vajrīkaraṇa rite.
Having performed the ritual placement at the four crossroads and the enclosure for the dice with the *varman* mantra,
and having placed thirty blades of *darbha* grass arranged in a clockwise sequence;
Having worshipped the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should place a seat within it while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
Thereafter, one should invoke the Goddess Vāgīśī, the Mother of the Universe,
from fire produced by friction, from a sun-crystal, or from [other] sources.
Having brought the fire and placed it in a worthy vessel, one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters;
then, having purified it, turned it back, worshipped it, and meditated upon the seed-syllable with the heart-mantra.

Having cooked [the offering], taken it up, and rendered it immortal, one should circumambulate the sacrificial pit three times and cast it into the womb facing forward while uttering "Vāgīśī" and "Śiva."
Having covered it with *darbha* grass, sprinkled it with water, and tied the bracelet with the *astra-mantra*,
one should offer five oblations with the *sadyojāta-mantra* on the occasion of the *garbhādhāna* rite.
Having performed [the rite] for the male [deity] with the Vāma[-mantra], one should offer drops of water;
having offered with the Bahurūpa[-mantra] at the parting of the hair, the arrangement of the faces and limbs [is completed].
Having performed [the rite] with the tip of darbha grass at the heart using the Puruṣa-sūkta during birth,
one should offer oblations and perform the opening and purification of the mouth with the sword-mantra.
Having sprinkled the sacrificial pit with the Astra-mantra to destroy the impurity of birth,
and having worshipped the Mother, one should then regard the bracelet in the directions starting from the east in due order.
One should worship Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Viṣṇu, and Ananta within the heart;
having worshipped the Weapon (astra) on the seats, one should worship the world-protectors (lokeśas) stationed at the perimeter.
In the east and other directions, one should worship Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti as the Lord,
Vāyu, Kubera, Īśāna, Ananta, and again in the southwest (Nairṛta).
On the outer side in the direction of the northeast (Īśa), one should spread kuśa grass for Brahmā;
having worshipped him with the Heart-mantra for the sake of his name, one should perform five oblations with the Īśāna-mantra.
Having meditated, "You are the auspicious fire," one should then dismiss Vāgīśa;
having offered sixteen oblations at the end, [one offers] the root-mantra soaked in ghee.
In the southeast, for the sake of nourishment, [one should construct] a sacrificial altar sixteen finger-breadths high,
thirty-six finger-breadths in length, and possessing seven or eight faces, marked with the vowels beginning with 'a'.
Its neck measures one finger-breadth; its six lotuses are broad and deep;
it has a girdle occupying half a part, adorned with various leaves and other ornaments made from the remainder.
The construction of the Kaniṣka-vessel [is made] with a fragrant base exceeding half the altar's size,
having a handle six finger-breadths long and seven finger-breadths wide.
The *sruk* ladle, made from a sacrificial tree, has a spout like a cow’s ear;
its handle is the length of a thumb, and its width is two finger-joints.
Having taken [the earth] from the sprinkled ground— measuring half a cow’s footprint in width and one karṣa in depth—
one should place the two hands, with the mouth facing downward, one after the other.
Having rotated [the vessel] repeatedly, one should touch it with darbha grass:
the root with the root-mantra, the middle with the middle-mantra, and so forth.
Having worshipped with the Hṛdaya-mantra, one should place it in protection on one's own right side, causing it to sleep upon Darbha grass.
Having taken a pavitra-cord with a central knot measuring one span, which has been protected and not sprinkled with clarified butter, one should resort to a location in the northeast.
One should take two tips of *darbha* grass fashioned together with the thumb and the ring finger.
Having turned [the vessel] toward the fire, [he should strike it] with the weapon-mantra;
having inspected it, kindled it with the darbha-fire, and performed the lustration (nīrājana), he should cast it upward again.
Having placed it into the fire, he should consecrate that extracted essence obtained through the Saṃhitā-mantras by making it immortal (amṛtīkṛtya).
One should perform the purification of the other clarified butter with the heart-mantra;
having prepared the three channels with ghee, one should take it with the *sruva* ladle and offer it as an oblation.
Having offered to Agni from the southern [part], to Soma from the northern,
and to both from the middle, one should offer into the fires presided over by Agni during the dark fortnight in reverse order.
Having offered the Soma oblation, one should again offer to the fire, and then worship Sviṣṭakṛt;
then, by offering each oblation individually, one should perform the Vaktra and Aghora rites.
Having joined Sadyojāta with Vāmadeva, and Vāmadeva with Bahurūpa;
then Aghora with Puruṣa, and Nara with Īśa, one should perform the oblation.
Then, one should perform the unification of the faces with the *Īśāna-Śiva-mantra* by offering oblations with the *sruva* ladle into the desired face.
Having filled the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter and placed it face-down,
one should grasp it with both hands, the fingers pointing toward the right, using the *śaṅkha-mudrā*.
Rising with his body erect, fixing his gaze upon its tip,
and bringing it to the region of the left breast while pronouncing the root-mantra of those two;
One should pour clarified butter with a stream measured by a single grain of barley, ending with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*;
according to the ritual rule, one should touch [the image] for the sake of each consecration from the full [oblation] down to the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*).
Every day, after first performing the purification of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the consecration of the fire should take place;
or, having protected the fire within the purified pit, one may perform the oblation elsewhere.
Then, in the heart-lotus, one should worship Śiva within the fire;
one should offer oblations with the root mantra according to one's capacity, and with portions of the Brahma-mantras in the measure of one-tenth.
One should not offer oblations when the fire has not been fully kindled, nor when its flames are agitated by smoke;
rather, the fire should be smokeless, well-established, and accompanied by the resonant sound of a conch shell and other instruments.
That which is glossy, curling to the right, and fragrant is praised;
likewise, rice, barley, mung beans, sesame seeds, and so forth, brought in sets of five stalks.
Cardamom, long pepper, licorice, milk, ghee, sugarcane, and so forth, along with a mouthful of rice,
[should be taken] by the hollowed cupped hands of the practitioner.
The edible substances should be prepared as before, marked by the lunar nodes (parvan);
the leaves and flowers should be unbroken, and the fruits should be two finger-breadths in size.

Musk, sandalwood, and other such substances that are to be offered should be the size of a chickpea; the milk-rice (*pāyasa*) should be a handful, and the parched grain (*lāja*) should be a fistful, with the root [of the plant] cut into three pieces.

Faggots of a span's length, guggulu resin, and pieces like the size of a tooth— having offered oblations with these when [other materials] are unavailable, one should offer the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Having offered water for rinsing the mouth, sandalwood paste, and betel leaf, one should ask for forgiveness;
then, having gathered the sacred ashes, one should pay homage to them and unite the deity within oneself.
Having prepared the excellence of the materials, time, and so forth, one should perform the oblation.
Having dismissed that [deity], having worshipped the fire, and having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* in due order;
Having cast the fire from the ladle onto the two mandalas at the side of the pit,
one should offer the inner and outer oblations with [mantras] ending in "svāhā."
To the western side from the Gaṇas, and then to the north from the Yakṣas.
To the planets in the northeast, to the Asuras in the southeast;
to the Nakṣatras, Rāśis, and Viśvedevas in the intermediate corners starting from the northeast in sequence; in the center, [offerings] beginning with Kṣetrapāla and ending with Varuṇa in the middle.
One should offer that [portion] in the center to the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla), and outside to the crows and other such beings.
Alternatively, one should offer the bali in brief with this mantra:
"And whoever are gentle beings, those who dwell in gentle places..."
Those dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld;
May the Mothers, those of Rudra's form, and those who are the lords of the Gaṇas—
all with minds full of great joy— accept this bali offering.
May they quickly grant us success and protect us constantly from all fears;
having offered the bali-oblation and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should pay homage to the God of gods.
Having dismissed Śiva, performed the Caṇḍeṣṭi sacrifice, and purified the ground,
one should worship the Guru and the Vidyā, and then perform the desired private recitation (svādhyāya).
Having bathed at the time of midday, one should worship Śiva as before;
or, if the deity has already been worshipped earlier, one should offer the eightfold flower-offering (aṣṭapuṣpikā).
From the Śiva-limb of the Pīṭha-mūrti, one should bring the flower-offering consisting of the limb devoid of eyes to the pure place of eating, where cooked food and other items are to be served.
Having unified the three fires— the expansive, the lunar, and the terrestrial—
and having taken them up with the fire-seed syllable, one should place them upon the hearth of the Bindu.
Having purified [the offering] that is not placed in an unsuitable vessel and has been consecrated with the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra,
one should take the *nivedya* and purify the hearth with the Astra-mantra.
Having worshipped Agni, Soma, Sūrya, and Bṛhaspati,
as well as Prajāpati, all the gods, and the Viśvedevas by their names;
One should also perform the oblation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with mantras ending in "svāhā," and briefly offer bali to all the deities of the site (vāstu).
Having washed his feet and sipped water for purification, facing either the east or as he desires,
he should worship the image prepared with cow-dung upon a ground adorned with lines.
The preceptors and others [should sit] on vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or iron, arranged in rows with lines of the same color, purified by those who sanctify the assembly (paṅktipāvana).
Or [one may offer] upon leaves of the palāśa, kadalī, cūta, padminī, and so forth—
provided they are not prohibited, are not mixed, and have their tips tied upward.
Not on bell-metal, nor on the leaves of the *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, or *piśāca* trees;
in their absence, however, it may be done on bell-metal purified with ashes and consecrated with the *ghora* mantra.
Or else, remaining silent in the *vīrāsana* posture with his hands placed between his knees,
he should place his left hand upon the vessel containing the consecrated rice as before.
Having sprinkled water and offered the *pavitra* and the *āpośāna*,
one should offer the oblations beginning with *prāṇa* into the digestive fire within the belly, which is like a lamp.
One should not spit, show contempt, yawn, or assume a crooked posture;
nor should one consume garlic, leeks, meat, *paleḍuka*, or *baka*.
Salt given by hand and fish [should not be eaten];
while eating, one should never give clarified butter or salt [to another].
One should not drink water from another person's vessel, nor with hands that have not been washed;
one should certainly not overeat, nor [drink] from those of the lowest castes.
Having removed the small amount of rice seen with flies, fingernails, hair, and so forth,
one should eat the remainder with washed hands after touching it with ashes.
Having eaten and performed the "covering with nectar" (amṛtāpidhāna), one should sip water according to the prescribed rule and sprinkle [water] on the right thumb.
Having bound the tip of the nose with the mudrā called the Parigha,
and having dried the mouth with betel and other substances, one should engage in the practice of emission.
The observer of the vow,
having received permission from his guru, should perform the *mādhūkara* rite after bathing with pure ashes.
Having taken a vessel made of copper or other such materials, purified with a sword, or one produced from a gourd,
which has been thoroughly cleansed with cloth...
Carrying a sacred filter (pavitra) and a water-pot suspended from a sling,
with his body consecrated by mantras, remaining silent, and holding an umbrella and sandals;
While reciting the mantra, one should not harbor anger or engage in dispute;
nor should one spit or touch [impure things], having followed the path of my way.
Having approached a house for the sake of alms and having uttered,
"Give alms," one should remain with the face cast downward until the cow [returns] due to her union with her calf.
That which has reached the point of emission, one should not ejaculate elsewhere than into the womb;
one should not give it away, nor should one take it up with the hand or with a bronze vessel.
One should not give cooked food or prepared alms with one's hand to a pregnant woman, a low-caste woman, or one wearing soiled garments; such an act is censured.
Even while on his way, if he is summoned from that place, he should not come;
instead, he should collect alms right there from people other than the patron of the sacrifice.
One should not accept alms from those who wander for alms but are censured;
nor from those who bear sectarian marks, nor from those who subsist on the property of Brahmins or the gods.
Neither from one who eats inferior food nor from one accused of sin, nor from the house of a playful woman,
should he return to his own hermitage at the end of the day, wishing for the welfare of the world.
Having placed his alms-bowl in a clean place and bathed with ashes,
having washed his feet and sipped water, and having changed his loincloth;
Then, having sprinkled the alms with the Astra-mantra and consecrated them with the Mṛtyuñjaya-mantra,
one should divide them into three parts and offer one portion to the Deity.
Having given the portion to the teacher, he should eat the remainder as before;
then, having bathed with water or with ash, he should perform the evening twilight devotion.
Having consecrated himself, meditated upon Śiva, and slept in his appropriate place,
he should bathe with ashes at midnight, perform the twilight rites, and worship Śiva.
If one has the capacity, having slept again and risen, one should perform in the morning what has been prescribed, using water brought from heaven (the sky) and purified by a cloth.
Now I shall explain the mudrās useful for worship and fire-offerings;
the mudrās that destroy obstacles and pacify them are called the powers of Hara.
The hands, joined together facing each other, resemble a jar and a half-moon seal;
the striking of the palms three times is known as the *parigha* (iron-bar) gesture of the index fingers.
When the two *jālās* have been brought forth, then, when [the breath] has entered the root,
the *sthāpinī* is in the thumb of the upper fist, while the *rodhinī* is in the inner thumb.
With both hands in the *mahāmudrā* gesture, touching [the head] like ghee up to the crown of the head;
in the center, the armors are joined with one another, while the *palita* [mantras] remain on their respective bases.
Having joined the tips of the ring fingers with the index fingers, one should place the tips of the thumbs upon the root joints of those [index fingers]; this is the *manoratha* [mudrā].
The two remaining little fingers should be interlocked with their palms facing each other;
the two middle fingers should be extended with their tips joined together.
The two index fingers are bent with their tips touching the backs of the middle fingers;
the two thumbs have their tips touching the sides of the middle fingers—this is declared to be the Sugī mudrā.
When the two *jyeṣṭha* [fingers] have moved behind the *sruk*, the left hand becomes the *sruc*.
When the pair of index fingers and the pair of little fingers of the two hands are bent back and merged into the three [other fingers], they are drawn forth [into union].
The two hands, moistened from within the thumbs and with fingers spread out,
are joined as "clasped hands" (vidarbhapāṇi), with the index and middle fingers interlaced with one another.
And this [mudrā] with the little finger and the ring finger is...
Thus, for the benefit of those initiated on earth, the mudrās for the fire-ritual, the offering of food, and the alms-round have been proclaimed out of compassion.
By the preceptor Aghoraśiva, who is like an elephant among teachers, [this work] has been composed in brief by means of approximately one hundred verses.
Thus ends the procedure for the fire-ritual and other rites in the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati* composed by the teacher Aghoraśiva.
By violating the conduct of their observances, Śaivas fall into the state of Piśācas;
for their avoidance of that [state], an expiation has been declared by Śiva.
When the body is in extreme pain, during fears of kings or thieves,
or for the sake of the gods, the sacred fire, or one's teacher, the omission of ritual action does not constitute a fault.
If one is incapable of performing the expiation, it should be divided and provided by kinsmen such as fathers and brothers; however, by other people, it must be provided at double the amount.
The preceptor who does not desire [to observe] vows should perform the vow as prescribed by the practitioner;
one who desires it should perform it for double that duration, while one who does not desire it should remain joined with the vow for that same period.
A son who acts according to his own will should perform double [the penance], but reduced by one-third;
for other sins, an initiate (samayin) should perform half of that.
If one fails at the time of the twilight ritual, one should recite the Śivaikādaśikā;
however, if the twilight ritual is omitted entirely, one should recite the Sadyojāta mantra one hundred times.
If one should perform [an act] unintentionally or intentionally, that very same [penance] must indeed be done with a fast;
if there is an omission of the daily worship, one should recite the Sadyojāta mantra ten thousand times.
Or, with his vital breaths restrained, he may subsist on air for a day; or, during the interruption of the fortnightly worship, he should recite the Ghorā mantra twenty thousand times.
Month by month, for a period of one year, he should increase the recitation by two hundred;
if it is omitted unintentionally, he should perform that same number of recitations three times over.
If one's own chosen *liṅga* has fallen, been lost, burnt, or even stolen,
one should recite the mantra of Maheśa one hundred thousand times and then worship another *liṅga*.
If the *liṅga* falls upon the common ground, one should recite the mantra for every single *tāla*.
Half of that, or half of its root, or a thousand, is for one who is very weak;
however, for one without support, it is double, or [one should worship] Śambhu in his manifold forms.
If [the image] is wiped, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times; if it is touched, ten times that amount;
if the linga cracks, a thousand times; and if it is overturned, double that.
Purification occurs after three or four hundred thousand [repetitions] if it has slipped from a clean place;
if it is slightly cracked, it is one hundred thousand more; but in the case of a blow from a water-jar or similar object, it is half of that if the damage is minor.
If the *liṅga* is touched with the foot or stepped over, [one should recite] twenty thousand times;
likewise, if the pedestal (*pīṭha*) attached to the foot is stepped over, one should recite twenty thousand times.
If [the mark] is on the enemy, or on a linga, or on an image and so forth,
there will be the destruction of that kingdom, and the king and the people will be oppressed by enemies.
Then, with every effort, one should give [the offering] for the purpose of installation right there;
and if it has been obtained, having placed it in a purified location...

For the sake of pacifying the fault arising from the acquisition of the *liṅga*, one should perform a thousand oblations with cow dung and clarified butter using the *ghora-mantra*, and a hundred oblations with sesame seeds and *caru*.
Having brought it to completion according to the instructions for the ritual bathing, one should establish it upon another ground.
Those who perceive the reality have abandoned the extraction of the *lakṣaṇa*, the opening of the eyes, and the entry into the water, as well as the [other] ritual acts, upon the dry land.

If one installs another new [liṅga] that has not previously been obtained, such as one without a mark (aliṅga) and so forth, it is permissible up to one month; however, if it exceeds that, it remains valid for up to three months.
A pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) should be performed for each [deity] up until the ritual bathing;
thereafter, the installation of the child-form (bāla) or the linga and so forth is proclaimed for the night.
Therefore, with every effort, in the middle of the three-month period,
having bathed the child-liṅga and so forth, perform [the rites] as before.
Whether it be a stone image, a face-liṅga, or a bāṇaliṅga and so forth, one should seek out a site facing west; otherwise, the stability of another [deity] will certainly be compromised.
Then, having either conquered [the enemy] in battle or having respectfully offered what is appropriate,
one should firmly re-install the primary linga, bera, and other images in their own proper place.
O Lord of Sages, that which is obtained with great effort within three years, or if it is obtained after three years have passed—

Having installed the primary liṅga and other objects at the root site (mūlasthāna) with the same materials and in the same proportions as before, one should worship them according to the prescribed rules of worship.
If the measurement was previously unknown, then either the architectural form or the most venerable teacher [should determine it],
in accordance with the temple and in conformity with the patron.
Having consecrated the *liṅga* according to the rite, one should install it by the prescribed path;
or else, for the sake of all accomplishments, one should install a *bāṇaliṅga* there.
One should have the pedestal or the base constructed according to this rule;
and within the temple, there shall be a courtesan who is menstruating.
Alternatively, at the time of the dance, if one performs the sweeping and sprinkling [of the site] and then dismisses that woman,
the great plagues will cease to prevail.
In whatever place the maiden resides, one should perform the purification right there;
having installed the *baliberam* (the vessel for offerings), one should perform nine *śānti-homa* oblations.
Having again completed the remainder of the ritual procession and entered within the inner sanctum,
one should perform the consecration with one hundred and eight jars.

One should not perform the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), the consecration by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), or the installation of the image (*pratimāsthāpana*) with those who are merely nominal Śaivas, lacking in essence.
If one single twilight rite is omitted, there shall be a ritual bathing, a pacifying oblation, and a recitation;
but if two twilights are omitted, one should recite the *Ghorasahasra* mantra a thousand times.
And when the three joints are missing, the wise one [should perform it];
likewise during the omission of the daily worship on festival days such as the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight.
The God of gods has prescribed a fourfold expiation specifically for failing to perform worship on a festival day.

And in the event of the neglect of vows and other observances, one should avoid the Gāyatrī. Whenever one touches any of the implements of worship, such as the pedestal (pīṭha) and so forth, [one should likewise avoid it].

One desiring [the fulfillment of] desire should recite the Aghora mantra two hundred times; however, upon seeing hair, meat, bones, songs, and so forth, or upon seeing the *naivedya* offering, one should recite it ten thousand times.
If one steps on or touches the Guru, the deity, or the Śivāgama unintentionally, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times; if intentionally, ten thousand times.
One should recite the terrible mantra ten thousand times, or sixfold if desired;
and at the end of the night, one should offer oblations into the fire for three nights or for a single night.
Having observed the fast, one should perform the recitation (japa) of the Aghora mantra ten million times;
provided that the arghya vessel has not been discarded, nor broken, nor abandoned.
From two hundred and from a thousand, one becomes pure through successive halving;
the command of Maheśa, the Guru, and Caṇḍī purifies the characteristics within the womb.
Wealth acquired for this purpose [is purified] by consumption, excluding the feet;
likewise, the rosary and the vessel are purified by washing, while the linga is purified from the feet upward.
If a hundred or a thousand threads are broken, or if the string becomes old,
or even if the rosary falls from one's hand, one should wash it with scented water.
This procedure is established for all cases by performing one hundred recitations of the Gāyatrī;
however, one should discard any water that becomes defiled by phlegm, feces, or urine, except when it is contained in a metallic vessel.
30) But when the bell strikes, purification is declared by the *liṅga* to occur at the eighth part;
one should recite [the mantra] due to contact with the *nirmālya*, and one should also recite the five Brahmans.
If one eats the remains of an offering (*nirmālya*) unintentionally, one should recite the entire collection of mantras one hundred thousand times;
if done intentionally, one is purified only through initiation.
Giving [the remains] is equal to consuming them, while neglecting them is half that [in merit].
If one steps over the *nirmālya*, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times with the *bahurūpa* formula.

The touch [of leavings] is equal to fasting; selling and eating [such food] are both equal [in gravity]. Divine property, the articles of a deity, and that which has been offered as an oblation (naivedya) are likewise [forbidden].
Caṇḍadravya and nirmālya—nirmālya is said to be of six kinds.
The property of the village lord is *devasva*, while *devadravya* refers to items such as cloths and the like.
The food offering prepared for him was presented as the remains of the deity's meal;
that substance given to Caṇḍa was cast outside as *nirmālya*.
And one should avoid consuming these [substances] as appropriate,
or anything touched by their floral remains (nirmālya), whether by a hand or by a person.
In that regard, three-quarters of what was previously stated applies to touching, stepping over, and consuming [the offerings],
as well as to the *piṇḍikā* [pedestal] and the *nirmālya* (remnants of worship), even when the deity has been dismissed.
In the case of a liṅga that has not been immediately consecrated up until the fourth day,
there is no fragrance from offerings such as food, incense, and the like, nor is there the radiance of lamps.
The flow of a river is never defiled by discarded offerings (*nirmālya*); likewise,
the Guru, sacred books, and the Nāgas are not defiled by *nirmālya*, just as Śiva is not.

For one who is pure and learned in the sacred recitation (*svādhyāya*), the fruit is tenfold when performing the ritual bath with the *liṅga*; likewise for one who restrains the breath (*prāṇasaṃyamī*) while reciting and offering oblations (*hunet*). This same rule applies to those equal [in merit], but with the addition of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Having formed a heap of boneless living beings, one should recite the Aghora mantra a hundred times.
It is declared that half [of the merit] of what was given by a sinner belongs to the recipient;
the Aghora, Vāma, and Puruṣa [mantras], along with the lords of the castes, [are applied] among the Brāhmaṇas and the other [classes].
Aghora is common to all, yet Īśa is remembered as common [to all];
one who is initiated becomes defiled by the remnants of another who is initiated and of the same caste.
If one is touched by someone who has food remnants on them, they should sip water for purification (ācamana) and recite the mantra of their own clan-lord (svajātīśa) one hundred times;
if touched by one who is uninitiated (adīkṣita), they should bathe, sip water for purification, and recite it two hundred times.
Likewise, fasting is required for one who has been initiated; for one who has not been initiated, it is the same as proximity.
Upon touching a twice-born man, a Vaiśya or a Śūdra must fast for two or three days respectively.
Having combined the lord of that caste and the lord of one's own caste, one should recite [the mantra] in sequence;
having touched those who have been initiated by a river [deity], one should perform twice the previously mentioned [penance].
Upon contact with a Śūdra, a Kṣatriya should recite [the mantra] while fasting for two days;
upon contact with one of a higher caste, it is proclaimed that the penance is reduced by one quarter.
Having reflected thus in other cases as well, a wise person should perform penance;
upon touching an outcaste, one should recite ten thousand times the mantra of one's own clan deity.
In contact with outcastes (śvapacas) and the like, [the substance] is joined with the state of its own caste;
in contact with the remnants of food from twice-born persons and the like, it possesses one of the qualities beginning with "mouth" (vaktra).
One should worship the fifth [deity] in the center of the four-petaled lotuses situated there;
one should recite the mantra a hundred thousand times while fasting for six days, or subsisting only on forest fare.
One should perform ten thousand oblations, doubled for those who have been born [into the lineage], as the cause of purification;
this applies to the followers of the Triple Veda, the Naiṣṭhika Buddhists, the Ārhats, the Kāpālikas, the Śaivas, and others.

Purity from eating that food consists in purification through contact with those of one's own caste; however, some hold that at the conclusion of the practice of the gods (devavrata), purity is attained even by eating the food of a *kāpālika*.

One should recite the mantra of Īśāna one hundred thousand times for the purification of that mixture; while practicing self-restraint, one should recite it three hundred thousand times upon a skull dedicated to Śaṅkara.

In other cases, if there is a resolve to sip water, one should recite ten thousand or more of the Vāma-mantras; likewise, twice-born men who have eaten during a period of birth or death impurity should recite one thousand of the Vāma-mantras.
For others, one should remain fasting; for those of one's own [community], one should recite the mantra facing south.
However, that does not apply to those initiated into Nirvāṇa who eat separately from the cooked food.
For those who have commissioned [the work], there is no impurity (sūtaka) for kings;
nor is there any for the consecration of deities, or on the occasions of tanks and groves.
Having eaten [at such a meal], one is purified from the fifth [period] by reciting [the mantra] five hundred times;
and having eaten at the *puṃsavana* rite, one should recite it four hundred times.
On the twelfth or eleventh day, however, three hundred [coins] are given to the Gaṇas,
to the Gaṇikās, and likewise to those who have renounced the world (saṃnyastāḥ).
Having eaten the food of a professional cook, or having eaten [at a meal] where one has consumed [forbidden food], one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
likewise after a cooked sacrifice (pākayajña), the gift of a cow, a tonsure ceremony, a marriage, or the performance of a vow.
Likewise, one who eats food from those of the same conduct and caste does not incur fault;
nor does he who, having been initiated into a particular caste, eats food without being invited by one of that same caste.
Having unified the lord of that class and the lord of its own class, one should recite [the mantra] in sequence—
once if there is one, and three times for the purification of the fire.
Having approached a woman out of negligence, one should recite ten thousand *prāṇāyāmas* and the *praṇava* twice as many times, combined with the utterance of the *praṇava* when acting out of desire.
If there is an emission of semen, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred and two times;
one should bathe and perform double [the usual penance], for on that very day, it is indeed so.
If one eats while another is eating, or if one listens to the recitation of the Vedas with a desire for food, one should perform double the penance;
having bathed and fasted for one day, one should mutter the *praṇava* (Om) one thousand times.
One should avoid bathing, worship, recitation, and fire-offerings while suffering from indigestion.
Once the food is digested, one should bathe and recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times.

Having eaten fish, thorns, or snails, or having consumed fingernails or cowrie shells, one is purified by fasting and drinking the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). One is not purified merely by drinking water.
Even when drinking water left over from others, or likewise when there is a mixture of meat and such,
a man who eats tainted food while drinking water that has fallen [into it] is defiled.

If one should drink or eat without the sacred thread, one should perform the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and a fast, and then recite the [sacred] formula a thousand times as a sacrificial fee.
Or, if one has not sipped water, one should likewise observe this very vow;
one should daily recite the Saṃhitā for the purification of all defects.
In all instances of ritual confusion, the Aghora mantra should be recited as the cause for purifying the mind, until one's wealth becomes favorable.
Having performed the *pavitraka* rite for the triad beginning with Āṣāḍha,
one should recite the Aghora mantra two hundred thousand times and then perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
Up to one thousand ten hundred [repetitions], it is proclaimed that this is merely a bath;
from there up to five hundred, one should perform both the bath and the night-rite (*nakta*).
Thereafter, for three nights, one should remain without food;
one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) consisting of a tenth part [of the recitation], and recite the Gaḍḍuka mantra half as many times.
Sleeping on the ground, practicing celibacy, abstaining from oil, pure in speech and conduct,
and eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) at night— this shall continue until the penance is completed.
Thus concludes the rule for expiation.
The *pavitraka* rite must be performed by the preceptor and others who seek the fruit of liberation, in order to fill any deficiencies in the procedures for all forms of worship.
This is declared to be a permanent limb [of the ritual], according to the prescribed rule for the specified ten-day period,
except on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in Āṣāḍha, and except in Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada.
And on those various occasions, as well as on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, [the rite] should be performed;
however, it must not be performed in the month of Āṣāḍha when Janārdana is unfavorable.
The sleep of Viṣṇu occurs during the month of Mithuna on the twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight;
it lasts for one or two months respectively during the six months beginning with Mādhava.
That should be known as a double Āṣāḍha; Viṣṇu sleeps in Karkaṭaka.
[The thread] should be spun evenly by a maiden from a single skein and the like.
A pure, white thread produced from cotton or similar materials,
having been tripled, should be wound around the central prong of the *bali* in the proper sequence.
One should calculate these for the Bāṇa, Ratna, and other types of liṅgas by reducing the count from one hundred and eight by increments of ten, using this single numerical sequence.
It should be performed with eighty-one [verses], or twenty, or sevenfold;
the purpose of the worship is the triadic nature at the crown of the head.
The pavitra should have its interior space filled with *vyantus*; ten knots should be made, or else as many as there are threads.
Beginning from the dot (bindu) and the arrow (bāṇa), up to the moon in the sky (nabhacandraka),
[these are placed] upon the liṅgas with a pair of swans (*haṃsa*), starting with the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*).
The [measures] should be twelve finger-breadths in size, or eight finger-breadths;
the unmanifest altar-ledge (vedikā) should hang down [to the knees], and the manifest one should hang down to the knees.
In that [section] on the descent of the Gaṅgā, eighteen chapters are recorded;
there are four groups of four, separated by intervals of two.
At the end, one should make two knots for the descent of the Gaṅgā;
that thread, washed by Ajāta and knotted by Guhyaka, [is thus prepared].
Having purified it with the *bahurūpa* face-mantra,
one should color it with red sandalwood, saffron, turmeric, red ochre, and so forth.
The Praṇava, the Moon, Fire, Brahmā, the Nāga, Guṇa, and the Sun—
all these deities known as Prasāda— are situated in order upon the nine threads.

One should prepare the *granthi-apavitraka* (the sacred thread with knots), which is anointed with all the ritual substances (*vidhi*), consists of a single knot, is without strands, and is free from mental measurement.
In one's own form, in Gaṇeśa, in the Guru, in the limbs, and in the book—
that single [reality] alone shall become the essence of all principles for everyone.
For Caṇḍeśvara, Viṣṇu, and Agni, there is the attainment of the thread like that of Śiva;
otherwise, one should provide a purificatory thread for each of these individually.
In the same way, for each of the doors, the guardians of the directions, the pitchers, and so forth,
one should likewise bring together nine [grains] other than those born from minerals (dhātuja) as the causal agent.
On either the seventh or the thirteenth lunar day, one should begin the consecration ceremony;
having bathed, performed the two daily rites, and adorned the sacrificial pavilion.
One should perform the special twilight rites and especially the libation (tarpaṇa),
having worshipped Śiva-Sūrya and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules.
The performer of the general *arghya* offering should worship the gatekeepers and others on the eastern boundary-line,
at the two right and left door-posts.
One should worship Nandin and Mahākāla with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order;
likewise, at the southern gate of the Vidyā-kalā, one should worship Bhṛṅgin and Vināyaka.
Next is the door of the *nivṛtti-kalā*, where the bull resides in the cave;
then the door of the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*, the goddess in the north, and Caṇḍaka.
Having worshipped the gatekeepers and others according to the prescribed rule as if they were permanent residents,
one should enter through the western door and worship Vāstunātha.

One should perform the purification of the body, the special water-offering (*arghya*), and the purification of the ritual substances. Adorned [with ornaments], one should wash the right hand and anoint it with fragrant unguents.
Having prepared a fragrant mandala, one should place Brahmāṇī with the left thumb in the center upon the branches; then, in the middle, one should worship Śiva along with his limbs (aṅgas).
Having fashioned this "Hand of Śiva," one should place it upon one's own head;
it is made of thirty-six strands of darbha grass, each sixteen finger-breadths long.
Taking up the sword of knowledge, one should contemplate, "I am Śiva.
Having brought forth the five products of the cow, one should sprinkle them with the root mantra and purify them.
Śiva is in the central square within the milk; he is to be obtained from the Īśāna-prakṛti in the square designated by the preceptor in the vessel known as Supratiṣṭhā.
In the Suśānta [cavity], the Vidyātattva is placed by Dadhivaktra;
and in the southern Koṣṭhaka, ghee is offered into the Tejovat vessel by Trivāra.
The water-mantra is [recited] over the water;
the Guru [performs this] with the Vāmadeva mantra four times from the west.
Having prepared the black vessel, one should place pure cow dung in five forms [of the deity],
with water according to the path of the primordial material cause (*prakṛti*) in the northeast.
Having made it auspicious and obtained from the *Saṃhitā*, one should protect it and wrap it;
then, in the southwest, one who is rich in water [should place] rice for the sake of following the absence of defects.
Having drawn lines upon the ground with a blade consecrated by mantras, one should fill it;
having leveled it with red powders belonging to Śakti, it should be swept, smeared, and made firm.
One should sprinkle [the area] with water for the *arghya* offering or with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) using a cloth;
then, one should carefully scatter the scattered offerings (*vikira*), such as sesame seeds, white mustard, parched rice, and so forth.
Having consecrated it with mantras and scattered [the grains], one should collect them using a bundle of *kuśa* grass;
then, having led them toward the northeast for the sake of prosperity, one should perform the *vardhana* rite.
In the southwest, one should worship Vastu and the gods at the door,
and Lakṣmī upon a vessel made of gold or other materials, placed atop a jar filled with all kinds of grain.
When it has been struck with hundreds of missiles, become solidified, covered by clouds,
filled with cool water, encircled by threads, and saturated with cloth.
In the western face, which is provided with *kuśa* grass and has a mouth of mango leaves,
one should worship Śiva, mounted upon a bull, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), seated upon a throne consisting of six [elements].
Then, one should invoke the presence of the Vardhanī vessel, situated in the southern direction and facing west,
mounted upon a lion, by means of the Śiva-weapon mantra.
Then, having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas) and given the command of Śiva for the protection of the sacrifice,
he took the *vardhanī* vessel situated at the front of the *kumbha*.
Releasing the stream from the *vardhanī* while recollecting the mantra of the weapon,
he circumambulated it clockwise and returned once more to his own place.
Having first placed the *kalaśa* vessel, one should then establish the *vardhanī*.
Thereafter, having established a firm seat for the *kumbha*, one should proceed extensively with the rite of Śiva.
Having formed the Astra-mudrā over the Vardhanī vessel of Śiva,
one should touch the Kumbha with the thumb while touching the Vardhanī with the fist.
Having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, and having performed the weapon-mantra over the *vardhanī* vessel ten times,
one should offer the *sannirodha-arghya* and present the sword of knowledge (*jñāna-khaḍga*).
One should inform Śiva until the protection of the sacrifice is secured by the nectar;
having worshipped Gaṇeśa in the quarter of Vāyu and the Guru in the direction of Īśa.
In the mandala or on the sacrificial ground, one should worship Śiva as before;
having especially bathed the deity with the five perfumes and other offerings.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and food offerings,
and having consecrated the fire in the forenoon, one should cause the fire to flourish.
Having fully worshipped Śiva, one should perform the libation with the root mantra and other rites;
one should effect the union of one's own channels and perform the sacrifice of the jar, the fire, and Śaṅkara.
On the mandala smeared with cow-dung, upon a *praṇava* [seat] of *kuśa* grass, having placed you—
who have your neck bound with a thread and the armor-mantra (*varman*)—
upon the Yoginī of purification mentioned for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), O cow-dung...
Having deposited [the substance] protected by the mantra of the hundred weapons (*astra-śata-mantra*),
one should kindle the auspicious fire (*śivāgni*) with rice grains and cook it with Śambhu.
One should move the eye with a sword-mantra and look at it with the heart-mantra; there, one should rub it with the cause of heated fire.
Having performed the *saṃhitā* with clarified butter, ending with either *svāhā* or *vauṣaṭ*,
one should perform the rite for Śītavaktra within the maṇḍala containing *darbha* grass.
Having placed [the vessel] to the west of the fire upon the seat of the *praṇava* in the mandala,
one should perform the pouring of the remnants once with the collection of mantras.
One should offer oblations into the fire with the mantra "svāhā" and "hā," using a vessel made from a dry reed as the ladle;
having announced to the deity, "This is accomplished," one should place it in the northeast.
Likewise, one should divide [the offering] with a blade of darbha grass according to the distinction between the gods, the fire, and the self;
having given a portion to Śiva and the fire, one should protect the portion for oneself.
Having brought the purifiers (pavitra) and sprinkled them near the fire,
they are placed in a pure vessel and consecrated with the Saṃhitā mantras.

Having covered himself with a black antelope skin and other garments, he should meditate upon the Supreme Lord Śiva— the Self of All, the Pervader of All, the Embodiment of the Year, and the One who possesses all aspects.
And one should encircle the case-roles (kārakas) with the *yāgayāmādi* sūtra.
Having offered scented *pavitraka* to Śiva-Sūrya with the root mantra,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should offer it to the guardians of the directions at the door, beginning with Brahmā.
To Śivakumbha, to Vardhanī, to Gaṇa, and to the lineage of Gurus—
and then to Śiva himself— one should offer these very substances.
Then, having performed the cleaning of the teeth with a mantra situated in the east,
one should consume ashes in the south and drink water from a *dhātrī* fruit in the north.
In that very auspicious vessel made of palāśa leaves, containing fragrant water and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should place the flower in the southeast and the guru [image] in sandalwood paste in the southwest.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron should be placed in the northwest; the materials for the fire-oblation, along with kuśa grass, should be in the west and then in the south.
Then, in the subsequent [section], there are the staff, the rosary, the loincloth, and the alms-bowl;
as well as collyrium, saffron, oil, a probe, and hair-cleaning rags.
One should offer betel, a mirror, and yellow pigment to Śaṅkara;
as well as a seat, sandals, a vessel, a meditation-belt, and a parasol.
One should offer rice-cakes, clarified butter, fragrant substances, and so forth, in the eastern direction;
whatever among these is incomplete, one should mentally provide that.
Having offered that [seat] to the seat of Śiva, accompanied by flowers, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice, one should say the word "pada" without a mantra: "Please accept the fragrant purifier."
(43) For every sacrifice,
through the inhalation of the self which is like a complete ritual injunction,
I empower you as the mantra that brings about the attainment of your desires.
O Lord of the sentient and the insentient, grant success to me who am performing sacrifice;
O Śambhu, in every way and at all times, salutations be unto you—be gracious to me.
Having thus addressed the deity and offered the fragrant purifier (gandhapavitraka),
the practitioner should commence the offering (bali) right there to the mantras of the objects to be accomplished.
Having sipped water, one should perform a hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra, the Mūla-mantra, or the Rūpin-mantra;
then, having performed the Pūrṇāhuti and the Vyāhṛti-homa, one leaves the fire undisturbed.
Having placed the Astra-mantra in the *pūta* vessel, and the Kavaca and Hṛdaya mantras in sequence,
one should install the purifiers— the Hṛdaya, Varma, and Āyudha.
Having performed this placement (nyāsa) by means of this [mantra] and having encircled it with threads while reciting the *varma* mantra,
one should worship it with the *saṃhitā* mantras and place it in the vicinity of the water-jar (*kumbha*).
Having offered the sacred thread (*pavitraka*) to the preceptor and placed it upon the Siddhānta manuscript,
one should perform the ritual with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances within the three outer mandalas.
Facing the east, one should cause him to consume three mouthfuls of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
except for the directions of Yama, Nirṛti, and Vāyu, it is auspicious for him from all other quarters.
For the sake of pacifying inauspiciousness, one should mentally perform a hundred oblations;
having sipped water, performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, and observed a vigil accompanied by music.
Fasting, one who desires liberation should sleep upon a bed of *darbha* grass;
for one desiring liberation, the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) is said to be performed on a bed of ashes.
Without the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), there can be no immediate consecration;
having performed the morning bath and other rites, the wise one should bring forth the sacred objects.
Having placed [the deity] in a pure vessel in the northeast and offered eight flowers,
one should bid farewell to Śambhu and perform the two daily rites on the ground in a clean place.
One should not worship [the deities] from Sūrya up to the Guru as before;
rather, having especially worshipped Īśa and performed the libation of mantras into the fire, one should proceed.
Having prepared the sacrificial porridge (caru) according to the rules, one should offer it to the gods and others;
then, for the sake of expiation, one should perform one hundred and eight oblations with *śambhu*.

One should worship [the deities] from Sūrya up to the Guru with purificatory offerings (pavitra) as before; and having offered the substances according to the measurement of the pavitra, one should proceed as previously described.
Having arranged the offerings with the exception of the *caru*, and having again presented the *caru* oblation,
one should place some water for the purifiers (*pavitra*) facing the ritual jar (*kalaśa*).
Remembering the God who is Time, one should speak this even with faltering speech:
"Oṃ, O God, whatever has been seen by you, whose nature is Time, in my ritual procedure..."
Whatever has been done that is afflicted, abandoned, taken away, guarded, or performed—
may that which was afflicted become unafflicted, and that which was taken away become nourished and honored.
Then, by your will, with this all-pervading and purifying [mantra] of Śambhu,
you should fill those two [vessels] while uttering the *praṇava*.
When the practitioner is weary from the observance of vows and restraints, he should likewise worship the Lord with mantras ending in the dative case,
consisting of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, joined with the root mantra and ending in *svāhā*.
The practitioner should offer three bracelets with the mantras beginning with Śiva;
he should then offer the descent of the limbs (aṅgāvatāraka) with the root-mantra of all the principles (tattvas).
Having given the purifiers from the limbs of Brahmā and performed the rite, one should recite:
"Whatever annual ritual of mine has been deficient in mantra, substance, or action."
"By your grace, may everything of ours be fulfilled through this purifying rite";
having thus petitioned the Lord of Gods and undertaken the desired vow, [he continued].
For four months, or three months, or two months, or even one month;
or for half a month, or seven nights, or five nights, or three days, or two days.
Or, at the conclusion of the ritual, the twice-born should satisfy the ancestors;
having offered the purifying materials to Agni and sacrificed the *caru* oblation, he should present the *bali* offering.
Having offered the expiatory oblations for the sake of the Vidyā and for the Guru as well,
and having presented the *pavitra* and performed worship, one should provide the meal and other offerings.
At the conclusion of the vow, having performed the sacrifice as before,
one should offer the expiatory oblations with sesame seeds and other materials, using the root mantra, the Śivāstra mantra, and the Rūpin mantra.
Having dismissed the fire and Śiva, one should again bring forth the purificatory items (pavitra).
One should dismiss the deities worshipped in the pavilion in reverse order.
One should worship Caṇḍa in a maṇḍala made of coins and the like, or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
having offered pure sacred threads (pavitra), one should present the remains of the previous offerings (nirmālya).
Having made the request, he should dismiss the ground after purifying it;
then, having offered the sacrificial oblation (caru), the Guru should be worshipped like Śiva with garments, wealth, and ornaments.

One should also worship with devotion the Śaivas, as well as the twice-born and the destitute. Thus is the procedure for the Pavitra rite, performed annually by those initiated into Śiva, for the purpose of pacifying the faults arising from the omission of ritual duties.
By Aghoraśivadeśika, who walks like a lion, [this work] was composed in brief by means of a hundred verses beginning with "kairava" (the night-lotus), for the sake of the elephant-like [disciples].
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the purificatory grass-blades (pavitrika).
For one who is impure, initiation consists of purification; it is both material and final.
For the seeker, initiation is twofold, while for the one whose nature is eternally Śiva, it is constant.
By destroying the portion of one's misdeeds, she bestows the enjoyment of the fruits of one's actions;
because she grants the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) after the body, she is known as Lokadharmiṇī.
The lifelong [vow] is said to be of three kinds: one devoid of conventional conduct and observances;
one independent of strength and so forth; and one endowed with those [qualities] for those who possess power.
(47) However,
that [initiation] which depends on the auspicious karma that initiates the body grants immediate liberation through the descent of the intense power.
Although the ritual action is identical, that [power] has different purposes for you, O Lord of Gods, and for the disciple; it bestows grace upon all through the forms of the gurus.
The preceptor should be a Brahmin born in a holy land, possessing all limbs in their entirety,
pure, learned in the science of words, sentences, and logic, and one who has mastered the Saṃhitās.
One should favor a disciple who is a devotee of Śiva, of virtuous conduct, tested for his integrity,
and of noble birth, when an auspicious conjunction occurs.
Having selected ground in a suitable location that conforms to the prescribed colors and is impelled by the [proper] mantras,
one should construct the sacrificial pavilion according to the ritual rules on ground where the directions have been established.
Having bathed and performed the two daily rites, the Guru, having gathered the necessary materials,
should worship the doors and the door-keepers, and then enter the inner sanctum.
Having gone to his own place on the left and sat down facing north,
he should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) specifically for the length of an arm-span.
As before, having placed the self at the dvādaśānta,
one should lead it to dissolution up to the *bindu* for the purification of the subtle body.

In the quality of darkness (tāmasa), the subtle elements consist of earth in smell, water in taste, fire in form, wind in touch, and space in sound; whereas in the quality of passion (rājasa), they are as follows:
The organs of action, as well as the mind, the intellect, and the sensory organs, dissolve into *sattva*;
these [in turn] dissolve into the qualities (*guṇas*), and those [qualities] reach dissolution in the *pradhāna*.
In Kalā reside Rāga and Vidya; Sākala resides in Niyati and Puruṣa; in Māyā resides Śuddhavidyā; and in the region of Sadāśiva resides Savartiga.
Abiding in Śiva and situated within the *bimba*, he should then purify the elements;
[he sees] the half-moon, liquid, gentle, pure, and marked with the sign of a lotus.
Having meditated upon the water-maṇḍala as having become fire, one should purify it;
the fire-maṇḍala is triangular, hollow, and marked with a svastika.
Then, one should meditate upon the water element as pure, and the black wind mandala as consisting of earth,
hexagonal in shape and joined with six dots.
One should personally meditate upon the pure vow, the ether (vyoma) conjoined with the power of the bindu;
then, having established the self within the heart, one should perform the acts of burning and flooding.
I shall meditate upon myself as the Vidyā in the form of thirty-eight Kalās;
with the letter *Na* at the end and *Śaśinī* at the head, it proceeds from the front ending with the letter *Na*.
One should place Brahmāṇī on the right, Tvaṣṭrī on the left, Svāntā and Marīcikā in the west, and Vātā and Jvālinī at the head; these are the digits (kalās) of Īśāna.

Having placed *tāra* (om) upon the head and *mūrdhan* (m) in the fire, one should know that *śānti* (peace) is in the east; *bhī* (bha) and *antā* (aḥ) are in the south, while *pratiṣṭhā* (establishment) and *dro* (dra) are in the north.
p.
49) Having given [the mantra] ending in *tti*, one should place the four *pauruṣī*-parts within the hearts and at the end of the neck.

They say that on my right shoulder is Nidrā (Sleep) consisting of two syllables, and on my left shoulder is Māyā; on my back is Śrāntā (Fatigue), within fear is Antā (End), on my chest is Jarā (Old Age) born of terror,
on my private parts is Rājarakṣā (Royal Protection), and on the linga is Ratīpālī ending with "namaḥ."
Likewise, they seize the left shoulder from the right and left thighs,
and as before, they take away the month-ending *māmonā* and the faculty of action-consciousness (*kriyābuddhi*) from the two knees.
At the end of the previous syllables on the two calves, one should place Kāryā;
on the two buttocks, Bhrāmaṇī; and at the end on the hip, Mohinī with the side-syllable.
On the left side, from the letter *bha* comes *medhā*; thus, on the left, according to the sequence of digits (*kalā*), one should place up to the letter *ma*:
*siddhi* and *ṛddhi*, with *ma* as the final letter, upon the two feet.
May she grant splendor, fortune, and intelligence to my hands and nose; may she grant me the final one [wisdom] on my head, and likewise reside in the pair of my arms.
Having deposited the *vāntā* and *antā* [mantras] and having performed the internal sacrifice (*antaryajana*),
whoever performs the purification of the site and the special *arghya* offering according to the prescribed rule;
The *arghya* for Śiva pervades up to the end of Śiva for the purpose of the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth;
the pervasion extends up to the end of Vidyā for the invocation (*āvāhana*) and dismissal (*visarjana*).
50) That [reality], which pervades the animal, the arghya-water, and the innermost essence of the self, is present during the sprinkling and other rites.
If, through negligence, these are performed in reverse order, one should offer oblations into the fire with the mantra *asi*... [etc. * * * * .
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, rice, jasmine flowers,
sesame seeds, barley, and white mustard seeds— this is declared to be the eightfold arghya offering.
Adorned and placing the hand of Śiva upon his own head,
and taking up the sword of knowledge, he should contemplate, "I am Śiva."
Having consecrated the entrance pavilion as before with the five products of the cow and other substances,
[he should offer] parched grain, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, flowers, kuśa grass, and unbroken rice.
Having scattered the *vikirāna* offerings according to the ritual manual and having withdrawn them as before,
one should then place the *vāstu-lakṣmī* (the site-deity) into the water-pot (*kumbha*), the two *vardhanī* vessels, and the movable seat (*calāsana*).
Having fully worshipped the world-protectors and commanded them to provide protection as before,
he should circumambulate the Śiva-pitcher, worship it, and sit upon a firm seat.
One should worship Śiva, whose limbs are colored by the path of purification and who is joined with the limbs of Brahmā;
one should worship the weapon of Śiva in the western face, within the Śiva-pitcher, the weapon-vessel, and the vardhanī vessel.
First, one should touch the *vardhanī* jar with the thumb after having worshipped it;
then, for the sake of enjoyment and liberation, one should subsequently touch the *ghaṭa* jar, and finally conclude with the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*).
