Having entrusted the responsibility for protecting the sacrifice to him, one should secure his presence with an *arghya* offering;
then one should worship Gaṇeśa, who has the luster of a lotus petal, as well as the lineage of gurus.
Having worshipped Śiva upon the sacrificial ground with devotion through specific sounds,
[one should worship Him] whose limbs are colored by the path of purification and who is the sole witness of all actions.
One should worship Brahmā and the limbs in the inner enclosure (garbha) as before;
in the second enclosure, Ananta, Sūkṣma, and Śivottama.
One should worship Ekanetra, Ekarudra, and Trimūrti;
and in due order starting from the east, Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin.

Having worshipped, in sequence, those which are golden, fire-colored, blue, bumblebee-black, moon-white, snow-white, red, and white, one should then worship the rivers and other groups in their proper order.
Outside of that, one should worship the world-protectors (Lokapālas) and, further out, the weapons:
the thunderbolt (vajra), the spear (śakti), the staff (daṇḍa), the sword (khaḍga), the noose (pāśa), and likewise the goad (aṅkuśa).
One should worship the mace, trident, lotus, and discus,
and satisfy the Lord with food offerings, garments, mirrors, and other such articles.
Having performed the recitation (japa) and offered it to him, the Guru goes to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
worships Śiva as before, and performs the libation of mantras into the Śiva-fire.
Having performed four hundred [recitations] for the sake of success regarding place and time,
as well as for the removal of ill omens and the production of auspicious signs.
Having offered oblations into the Śiva-fire according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should prepare the sacrificial porridge (caru) in a glowing vessel with clarified butter, measuring five handfuls (prasṛti).
52) Then, one should increase the number of disciples by adding a second and so forth.
Having offered that *saṃpāta* oblation, one should offer [oblations] for the sake of the pavilion and the colored powders (*rajas*).
One hundred threads for the water-pot and likewise a thread for the noose;
two portions mixed with honey and clarified butter for the oblation to the Devas and to Agni.
Having given a portion for his own disciples, he should set aside [the remainder] combined with clarified butter;
having performed special worship to Indra and the other deities, he should offer the bali-oblation.
To ensure there is no obstacle, one should fill two hundred [verses] of the missing portions;
having offered oblations with the sword-mantra, one receives permission from Śiva for the liberation of the bound soul (paśu).

Having placed the disciple upon a seat of *praṇava* within a sacrificial mandala made of darbha grass— with his hands on his body, facing north, and with palms joined in reverence— he should perform the *saṃpāta* rite.

Facing east, having looked [at the disciple] and sprinkled him with water while reciting the root mantra, he should strike the head of the one who has bathed and fasted with ashes using the Astra-mantra, once the bonds have been loosened.
Having scraped [the body] with the tip of a darbha grass, both above and below the navel—
one who has taken the final vows (naiṣṭhika) first [scrapes] below and then above, while one who is a householder (bhautika) does it first above and then below.
Having placed the consecrated thread upon his body and covered his eyes with a new cloth while reciting the Netra-mantra, he should lead him into the sacrificial pavilion.

Then, having placed the garland in his joined palms, he should lead it around the Deity in a clockwise circumambulation and cast the floral offering into the water, which is the supreme destroyer of darkness.
One should show the Supreme Lord, who is always unseen by bound souls (paśus),
having seen Him in the southern direction of the Lord with eyes full of bliss.
Having seated the child facing north within the mandala and performed the rites of inspection and so forth, he should purify him through meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās).
Having purified the disciple with mantras, the preceptor, by means of the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta),
should touch him from the head down to the base [of the feet] with the root mantra, for the purpose of loosening the bonds (pāśa).
Then, having caused those garlands to be placed neither upon the sacrificial mound nor in the water-pot,
he should take them to the vicinity of the fire and place them on a seat consecrated with the Praṇava to his right.
Having placed the root of a kuśa grass with its tip fixed between the teacher's shanks,
and having performed the grasping, he should effect the joining of the channels between himself and the disciple.
By means of the method of the self, one should visualize a channel resembling a lotus fiber emerging through the left [nostril] and entering the disciple, and then emerging again.
One should visualize the [deity] entering through its right side with the *dakṣiṇā* [mantra] and through the left side with the *vāmā* [mantra];
for the sake of their union, one should offer three oblations with the root mantra (*mūla*).
One should perform the union with the [deities] residing in the jar, the sacrificial ground, the day, and the lord;
having done so, one should effect the libation from the root [mantra] by means of the power of the descent upon their heads.
Having performed one hundred and eight [oblations] with a sword, one should offer them as an expiation;
one should present the full oblation according to the rule, ending with "vauṣaṭ" while uttering the name of Śambhu.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the initiation of the pledge (samayadīkṣā).
To eliminate the defects arising from eating seeds and from one's intentions,
and for the purpose of attaining the state of Rudra, one should offer three oblations.
The fitness for the womb of Vāgīśī and the state of being a portion of Rudra do not constitute the state of being Rudra himself;
rather, it is the status of being twice-born and the fitness for the womb of Vāgīśī that is required for mastery in the sciences of weaponry and sacred lore.
Since no purification is performed for the body or the caste,
one should strike [the disciple] on the head with a weapon and [then] release [the breath] into the heart through the yoga of exhalation (recaka).
Having entered his heart, having severed and then covered [the channels] with the sword,
and having extracted the life-force from the cavity of the heart, one brings it to the *dvādaśānta*.

Having brought [the deity] residing in one's own heart into a state of equal flavor by means of inhalation (pūraka), joined with the seed-syllable of the self, the salutation, and the *praṇava*, through the power of reabsorption (*saṃhāriṇī*).
Abandoning the gods by means of *kumbhaka*, one should then lead [the breath] to the station of the *dvādaśānta* via the right channel through the *brahmakara-cakra*.
Having extracted that which possesses the vitality of the heart, one should apply it to the body of the disciple;
some, however, perform the consecration by placing the bound soul (paśu) within the womb of Vāgīśvarī.
They perform the five rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* like the fire of Śiva;
and having bestowed the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), he is consecrated by his own caste.
One should offer a hundred, a thousand, or even half that number of oblations along with the final full oblation;
by this, the child becomes fit for hearing, recitation, meditation, fire-offerings, and other such practices.
p. 55) There, he should bestow upon the disciple who has taken the vow the concluding elements of the observance:
matted hair, ashes, a staff, a loincloth, and a sacred thread.
Having consecrated [the vessel] in sequence with the Saṃhitā mantras beginning with Īśa,
having offered it to the Lord of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍileśa), and having placed it beside the water-pot (kumbha);
Having bound his matted locks by the command of Śiva, he should offer those to him;
[the number of these] corresponds to the count of the Kalās, Śaktis, Pavitras, Aṇus, Tattvas, Mantras, and Īśas.
One should tie the matted locks in front of the deity while uttering "Śiva.
A Śūdra should not wear matted locks; he may, however, wear a single lock.
For one who remains with a mind fixed on the ultimate goal, the first [stage] is described as "bound by the noose" (pāśabaddha).
Having performed the satiation (tarpaṇa) of the mantras, one should perform the "kindling" (dīpana) starting from the root-mantra.
Three times, with golden seeds ending in *huṃ phaṭ* and enclosed within the *śikhā* mantra,
the previously described thread, which has been tripled and then folded threefold, [is consecrated].
Having sprinkled [the disciple] with the *prokṣaṇī* water, and having bound him with the *āveṣṭyā*, the *asivarma*, and the *śikhā* mantras,
he should then perform the *dhiṣṭhyā* [mantra], which extends down to the tips of his big toes.
In the Sūtra, the severing of bonds and so forth does not take place in the body;
rather, one should meditate on the proximity and the abiding place of the Self as being bound by those bonds consisting of its impurities and the like.
Having entered that body through the channel, uttering the name ending in the dative case along with the *tāraka*,
and grasping it while pronouncing *huṃ phaṭ* for the purpose of disjunction;
One should join the other channels to the thread of the *suṣumnā* within the cavity of the heart;
having worshipped and enveloped them with the [mantras of] presence, one should offer three oblations.
Having extracted the bonds (pāśas), such as those of Śāntyatīta and the rest, which contain within them the principles (tattvas) and worlds (lokas),
from the body of the disciple, one should join them to the thread and offer libations.
The two principles of Śiva and Śakti, the primordial syllable *praṇava* (oṃ),
and the mantras of the weapons of Śiva and Īśāna, ending with the *visarga*, as well as the gods.
One should perceive that which is beyond the worlds beginning with Śritā and ending with Nivṛtti-bhuvana,
within the Kalā known as Śāntyatītā, as being neither internal nor external.
Having separated [the deity] by means of the seed-syllable of one's own name preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ), enclosed within the heart [mantra],
and ending with *huṃ phaṭ*, one should grasp [the deity] with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*.
Having joined the *śiras-sūtra* with the word "namas" at its end, one should worship it and wrap [the thread] around [the head].
For the purpose of invoking the presence (*sannidhāna*), one should offer three oblations ending with "svāhā."
The letters *ka*, *kha*, and *ga* are for the peaceful deities; the two measures (*mātrā*) are on the coarse skin;
and [these are placed] in the principles (*tattva*) of Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā in due order.
The eleven worlds ending with Nitya and Yoginī,
as well as the worlds ending with the Lord Sadāśiva and others.
One should also join that [line] to the cord extending from the forehead to the neck;
within the Vidyā-tattva are the seven principles, beginning with Māyā and ending with Puruṣa.
The seven syllables beginning with *gha* are mantras whose nature is that of the Terrible Śiva;
furthermore, there are twenty words such as *dhyāna*, *āhāra*, *paṭa*, and so forth.
One should meditate upon the worlds, beginning with Gahaneśa and ending with Sarvendriya;
having joined them to the thread at the end of the navel as before, one should worship them and perform the fire-oblation (homa).
The twenty-four principles beginning with *prakṛti* and ending with *jala* are the letters from *ṭa* to *ma*; this is the mantra for the left head.
Then there are the worlds beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha and ending with Amareśa, which constitute the [first] steps;
starting from the first two and extending as far as the station of Mahādeva.
Having taken that [mantra] from the root-text, one should cast it into the thread at the end of the knees as before;
likewise, the syllables of the earth-element and the heart-mantra of Sadyojāta-Śambhu.
And the worlds beginning with Vīrabhadra and ending with Kālāgni,
as well as the stations beginning with Sadbhāveśvara and ending with Draviṇa.
Having meditated upon it as having entered within the *nisṛt* [mudrā] and having grasped it as before,
one should join the thread from the knee to the tip of the big toe, worship it, and perform the fire offering (*homa*).

Having observed the karmas, the power of impurity (mala-śakti), and the power of obstruction belonging to Śaṅkara, and having joined them together in the thread, one should perform the oblation for the presence of the deity.

One should perform the radiant libation with mantras ending in *svāhā*, and offer three oblations with clarified butter or sesame seeds using mantras enclosed by the *śikhā* mantra and ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
Having struck [the victim] with the *sruva* ladle or other implements using the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* for the purpose of separation,
and having offered oblations there, one should [dissolve] the principles beginning with *nivṛtti* in reverse order.
One should bind the fetters (pāśas) in their respective locations upon marks made with yellow pigment (rocanā), using the *kalā*-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

At the places of the knees, the navel, and the throat, as well as at the *alika* and the *brahmarandhra*, the bonds are severed from their knots; for these are indeed the junctions of its constituent parts.
Having placed the man’s [hair] in a pair of shallow bowls (śarāva) and the woman’s in a pair of vessels for water offerings (praṇītā),
one should place that cord of noose therein and purify it by its falling [into the fire].
Having established [the deity] upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), one should deposit [the protective implements] in the form of a water-pot for its protection;
then, having performed the svasti-rite over the sacrificial ground, the pot, and the fire, one should bestow the kuśa-grass upon the child.
Having caused [the disciples] to perform prostrations at the end of the three outer maṇḍalas,
[he should provide them with] the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), sacrificial porridge (caru), and a tooth-stick consecrated by the Śiva-mantra.
Having applied ashes as before during the casting down of the tooth-stick,
if it falls inauspiciously, one should perform a propitiatory *homa* with a sword for the sake of pacification.
In order to eliminate the defects of flaws in body, speech, and mind,
one should perform a hundred oblations each, in sequence, with the root mantra, the Aghora mantra, and the Śiva-mantra.
Having performed the libation for the mantras, one should offer a full oblation according to one's capacity;
then, having offered the *rodhārghya* to the Lord of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍileśa*) by way of the fire-passage.
Having placed that [liquid] into the pitcher, one should then [place] the two lower [ends] into the pure [vessel];
first, the heads of the serpents [are covered] with *darbha* grass obtained by reciting the Astra-mantra a hundred times.
There, having placed [the image] protected by the Astra-mantra and its crest by the Śikhā-mantra,
and having covered it with the armor (Varma) and clothed it with a garment, one should then cause it to sleep.
One should draw three lines on the outside with ashes consecrated by the recitation of the Astra-mantra;
then, having offered the external bali-oblation and consumed the pañcagavya and the caru oneself.
Having bathed, offered oblations, performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and consecrated his body with the protective syllables (sakalīkṛta-vigraha),
he should sleep upon a bed of darbha grass and recite the Svapna-māṇavaka mantra.
On the day of the consecration (adhivāsana), one should not perform the consumption of the sacrificial oblation (caru) and other such rites.
The procedure for the consecration is completed.
Regarding the procedure for auspicious and inauspicious dreams:
having performed his morning rituals and heard the dream reported by the disciple,
he should declare it auspicious if it is auspicious, and perform a rite of pacification if it is inauspicious.
Mounting an elephant, crossing through mud, bodies of water, and so forth,
obtaining royal insignia, and possessing gold, jewels, and the like.
The sight of crops, the sun, a lotus, the moon, and light is praised;
likewise, mounting a donkey or similar animals, and sinking in mud or rivers, and so forth.
(60) Wearing red garments and the like, falling from trees and so forth,
bowing down, and seeing anointing, jackals, dogs, and the like, are not commended.
In an inauspicious dream, one suffers a hundred [blows] with a sword at the beginning of the night,
a thousand at the end of the night, and five hundred at midnight.
Having performed the occasional worship, beginning with Cāra and ending with Guru,
one should then worship from east to west upon either the mandala or the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
In the center of the karaṇī, one should draw a circle using a cord joined with a water-clock;
having fashioned it into a square here according to the rule, it should then be two cubits in measure.

In the center, one should fashion a lotus measuring one cubit, with thirty-two filaments representing the eight principles (tattvas), surrounded by a line for the sky (ākāśa), and not including the peacock-feather tuft (piñchaka).
One should cause the four vows to be performed at the throat and the middle of the neck of one devoted to the Vedas;
in the first [vow], it is adorned with yellow and blue seeds upon the pericarp.
In the second [layer], the filaments have yellow, red, and white tips;
in the third, there is the junction of the petals; and in the fourth, the tips of the petals.
One should make the sky-lines, the white circles, and the petals white;
the pedestal should be one *aṅgula* in size and adorned with various lineages (*gotra*).
The red [line] has a blue peg; from the half-lotus, the white arrows [extend];
outside that, at the four gates of the same measurement, there are three lines.
The first line, characterized by the quality of sattva, is one finger-breadth in width and height and is white;
the other two are red and black, each measuring a barley-corn in thickness with a barley-corn's space between them.
Three [lines] for enjoyment, three for liberation, and one for equanimity are thus proclaimed;
[these are drawn] with flour of parched grain, white and red minerals, and turmeric.
Yellow [powder] is made from burnt barley; black-blue [powder] is produced from the leaves of the *śamī* tree and so forth.
Having sprinkled [the site], one should worship Śiva there—a place secured by the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), measured out with a hundred *śatālas*, and kept secret.
One should worship the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), the Gaṇas, the Lords of the Worlds (Lokeśas), the Weapons (Astras), and the Pīṭhas outside;
having worshipped Agni and Śiva, one should perform the libation of the mantra during the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having offered a thousand oblations with the root mantra and a tenth part with the Brahmāṃśa mantras,
he should present it to the deity for the sake of bestowing grace upon his disciples.
Having granted permission, he should not be requested [to depart]; outside the pavilion on the right, he should place the disciple as before upon the seat of the *praṇava* within the mandala.
Having gazed upon it, sprinkled it, struck it, and scratched it with darbha grass using ashes,
and having made the hand of Śiva auspicious by placing it upon the head, one should worship it.
Having led the foremost woman, whose eyes were bound, into [the temple] and performed a circumambulation of Śambhu,
he placed a garland into her joined palms while she faced northward, and then opened her eyes.
Having opened [the door], one should show the deity along with the mantra and cause the garland to fall;
the first spot where it falls, one should establish as the name of the disciple.
(62) For the best of the twice-born, [the offering] ends with Śiva; for another, it ends with the Gaṇas.
For one established in the *samaya*, [it extends further], but not for anyone else; [this applies] to the flowers, the water-jar, the fire, and the self.
Having caused [the offerings] to be given, one should place them near the fire to one's right;
then, having performed the joining of the channels (nāḍī) and so forth, one should suspend the cord of bonds (pāśasūtra).
Having visualized the path to be purified within the body of the disciple, in one's own body, in the fire, in the mandala, and also in the water-pot, as well as the pervasive worship of Aparā;
Having conceived the mutual union [of the deities], one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra;
then, having taken up the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) and worshipped it in the fire, one should satisfy it with libations.
Then, through the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra), one should perceive the pervasion of cessation (nivṛtti):
the single principle of earth (avanītattva) and the world consisting of one hundred and eight [levels].
In this world, all the worlds have names identical to those of the Rudras:
Kālāgni, Ratha, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Hāṭaka, Brahmā, and Keśava.
Thus, Rudra is the lord of these worlds within the center of the cosmic egg;
outside of it, in the directions beginning with the east, ten worlds each are situated.
Kapālīśadhvaja is the awakened one who crushes the vajra-body;
he is the inexhaustible lord of manifestations, the teacher, the wielder of the Pināka bow, and the sovereign of the thirty-three gods.
Agni, Rudra, Hutāśin, Piṅgala, Khātaka, Hara, Jvalana,
Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmāntaka, and Kṣayāntaka.
The ender of the five, the five-crested one, the one with matted locks, he whose vehicle is the clouds;
the lord of treasures, the beautiful, the fortunate one, whose body is gentle, and who wears matted hair.
The bearer of Lakṣmī, the bearer of jewels, the bearer of glory, and the temple itself;
the lord of the masters of knowledge, the omniscient one, the bearer of wisdom, and the one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
Sureśa, Śarva, Jyeṣṭha, Bhūtabāla,
Balipriya, Vṛṣa, Vṛṣadhara, Ananta, Krodhana, and Marutāśana.
Grasana, Udumbarīśa, and the lord of serpents Vajradaṃṣṭrin;
Śambhu, Vibhu, Guṇādhyakṣa, Tryakṣa, and Tridaśeśvara.
Mūrdhan, Krośa, Taru, and Rudra, and above them is Vīrabhadra.
From the final *praṇava* onwards, there are twenty-eight words:
"Namo namaḥ oṃ śivāya namo namaḥ."

O Giver of All! O Śarva, Śiva, Sūkṣma, Sūkṣma! O Sound, Knower of Sound, Knowledge, Knowledge! O Piṅga, Piṅga! O Pataṅga, Pataṅga! Turu Turu! Witness, Witness! O Thou who art well-established from of old, established from of old!
O Thou whose praise is beyond praise, whose worship is beyond worship! O Thou who bringest about the presence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and all others!
O bestower of happiness upon all beings, O source of existence, O Śarva, O Śarva, O primordial one, O primordial one, release, release!
To the Lord of Yoga, O you of great splendor, O Lord of true being, O Mahādeva!
Having contemplated the two mantras whose hearts are unarisen, the letter *kṣa*, the five paths,
and the pervasion, together with the *nivṛtti* [kalā], by means of one's own seed-syllable ending in *namaḥ*.
Having taken that [mantra] from the Sūtra, one should not employ it in the fire at the end of the ritual time;
rather, having worshipped it in its presence, one should offer three oblations ending with "svāhā."
One should simultaneously remember the actions residing therein as being of the nature of primordial matter (prakṛti);
however, for one seeking liberation, one should purify that which is distinct from the body and initiated by karma.
First, one should purify the past karma and the desire for merit of the practitioner of dharma;
having invoked and worshipped the Brahmā of the Heart, one should offer three oblations.
One should say, "Grant permission for the initiation of the animal within your own jurisdiction";
therein, Vāgīśvarī is the womb of manifold volitions.
Having invoked and worshipped that which pervades it, and having offered three oblations,
one should pray to Maheśāna regarding the initiation of the disciple.
Having sprinkled the sacrificial animal (paśu) with the Astra-mantra, one should strike it on the heart with a flower;
then, entering its body by means of the exhalation (recaka), one should separate [the soul] from it with the sword [of consciousness].

Separation should be performed by means of the *jyeṣṭhā* [power], and the joining of the animal within the wombs; then, by means of the *vāmā* Śiva-power, there is always the extraction of the *raudrī*.
Recalling the root [mantra] at the *dvādaśānta*, having led it there with the *ghṛṇimudrā*,
one should take up the heart-enclosure from the *dvādaśānta* by means of the seed-syllable.
The remainder is to be found in another treatise.
May there be auspiciousness! Salutations to the venerable gurus. Hariḥ Oṃ.
Salutation to the illustrious Sāmbaśiva.
The explanation.
I bow to Śiva, the ocean of compassion and the cause for attaining the state of Śiva-hood,
and thereafter to Gaṇeśa, who is known as the Guru and is himself Śiva.
The Śrī Kālottara-bheda, known as the Catuḥśatika,
was previously explained by the teachers according to the tradition of the Garbha [Tantra].
The scriptures beginning with the *Sarvajñānottara* have been expounded,
as well as the one known as the *Śrīmanmṛgendra*, and the manual (*paddhati*) concerning the sequence of ritual action (*kriyākrama*).
A hymn known as the *Pañcāvaraṇa* was previously composed by the Gurus;
he, too, has composed this [work] in accordance with that treatise on meditation.
Having prostrated before the supreme guru, the author of the Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati, I shall compose a commentary on this [work] according to its requirements.
Furthermore, regarding this lineage, I shall also describe those rites such as the worship of the Sun that were not previously mentioned, as well as other rituals performed within this very context.

In this regard, the first verse is as follows: "Śiva is the cause for the attainment of Śiva-hood. Śiva-hood is the state of the Self characterized by omniscience and other qualities, consisting of its own vision and action (*dṛkkriyā*).
Its "attainment" is its manifestation; the "cause" of that is Śiva, who is the instrumental means through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth.

Having prostrated before the *Mṛgendrāgama*, the manual (*paddhati*) for the venerable *Mṛgendraśāstra*— which belongs to the *Kāmika-bheda*, the first among the divisions of the Śiva-tantras— is composed according to the distinctions of the ritual action (*kriyā*) and other categories. Here, by the word "ritual action" (*kriyā*), [is meant] purification (*śauca*), sipping water (*ācamana*), and so forth.

Bathing, the twilight worship (*sandhyā-vandana*), ritual worship (*pūjā*), fire oblation (*homa*), and so forth are mentioned; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), yoga and conduct (*caryā*) are included.
It is traditionally held that the division of the *tantras* and *śāstras* arises from the differentiation of these [practices], beginning with ritual action (*kriyā*).

For it is said: "There is no division of the scripture (*śāstra*) due to a division in knowledge; rather, the division in knowledge is the cause for [the distinction between] the Pāśupata and other systems. This is because of the difference in the recipients of the Siddhānta scripture—which is divided into ten and eighteen parts and is well known through its divisions as Śiva-bheda and Rudra-bheda."
Even though there is a difference due to the lineage and the diversity of teachers, there is complete consensus regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*),
as it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
"All other differences, whether they be great or not great..."
And they serve to provide conviction regarding initiation, with the fruits being spiritual perfection and liberation.
Others have also said: "The ritual act is one and the same, recognized across all branches (śākhās), or it is not.

Therefore, for those who practice according to a specific system (tantra), only that ritual act which is prescribed in that particular tantra should be performed. Just as in the Kalpasūtras and other texts, there is a difference in systems due to the difference in the procedures (kriyā).
In the *Śrīmanmṛgendrāgnisaṃskāraprakaraṇa*:
"Having covered [the site] with *darbha* grass and having bound the *astra-kaṅkaṇa* (protective thread),
one should perform the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) by means of the mantras beginning with *Sadyojāta*, for the sake of accomplishing the *garbhādhāna* and other rites."
"One should offer five oblations for each of the five [rites], accompanied by worship with the *hṛdaya* [mantra].

Thus, according to this scripture, the worship of all five sacraments, beginning with *garbhādhāna*, is performed without distinction using the *hṛdaya-mantra* and the [mantras] beginning with *sadyojāta*.
(p. 67) Five offerings for each of the five Brahmans have been taught; thus it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should offer three oblations with the *sadyojāta* mantra and the *hṛdaya* (heart) mantra.

It is stated that once the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) has been performed, there is worship with the Brahmās beginning with *sadyojāta* according to the [mantras] such as "puṃstva" (masculinity), and for each subsequent sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*), there are three oblations with the *hṛdaya* and other [mantras]. Thus it is said.
The division of Tantras arises from the division of ritual actions; the division of Tantras arises from the division of yogas—as stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
"Withdrawal of the senses, as well as meditation, breath control, and then concentration..."
Reasoning and meditative concentration are established as the limbs of yoga.

Thus, in this [text], yoga is described as having six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), consisting of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), absorption (*samādhi*), and meditation (*dhyāna*). However, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*,
regarding the aphorism "the state of the senses being gradually rendered unassailable through the practice of breath control and so forth," [it is explained as follows:]

Commentary: By means of the statement beginning with "mastery over the senses through the practice of the seven limbs of yoga, starting with breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) whose characteristics will be described hereafter," the seven-limbed yoga has been taught. Thus, there is a division of the *tantras* based on the divisions of yoga. As for the division of conduct (*caryā*), however—

In the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*, at the end of the section on the funeral rites (*anteṣṭi*): "The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite which has been described here should be performed without the invocation (*āvāhana*)."
This Śrāddha for Śiva and other such rites has been described in brief.
By such passages as these, the ritual acts ending with the *śivaśrāddha* have been described.
In the venerable *Mṛgendra*, however, after describing the *śivaśrāddha*, the *gotraśakra* follows immediately thereafter.

"Then one should place three vessels in the maṇḍala"—thus the ritual action up to the offering of water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) and the respectful offering (*arghya*) has been stated. Thus, there is a division of tantras due to the difference in practice. In this way, why should the rituals mentioned in other tantras not be performed in every respect? It is not [forbidden] by the force of the word [itself].
Whatever is obtained through the force of the word, the force of the meaning, or the power of the thing itself,

that must indeed be performed. In this regard, "the force of the word" refers to the fact that even though the oblation (homa) along with its specific modes is enjoined, there is the requirement for a pit (kuṇḍa) as the locus for the fire.
The characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) mentioned in other *saṃhitās* are to be adopted from the ritual injunctions and so forth. Furthermore, regarding capacity:

even if not all the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the fire have been explicitly stated after mentioning one of them, those rites not mentioned here are to be taken from another *saṃhitā*. This is also due to the inherent power of the substance itself.

Although all the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and ending with the unification with the mouth (*vaktraikīkaraṇa*) have been prescribed, because the *pūrṇā*— which consists in the fulfillment of all purificatory rites—
has not been mentioned, the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) is to be taken from another *Saṃhitā*. Thus...

The definitions of the capacities of words (*śabda-sāmarthya*), the capacities of meanings (*artha-sāmarthya*), and the powers of entities (*vastu-śakti*) have been written down after being understood from the *Śrīmad-raurava-vṛtti-viveka* and other works. By the passage beginning with "Having risen in the morning," the sequence for the daily ritual practice (*nityānuṣṭhāna*) is described. A *śṛṅgāṭaka* is a crossroads; it is fame (*kīrti*).
Having meditated on the Brahma-sandhyā as the "Weapon" (astra), one should [perform] the triad beginning with Brāhmaṇa;
following the Sandhyā-vandana prescribed in the Smṛtis, there is the Pārameśvara-astra.

Meditating according to the sequence prescribed in the scriptures, one should offer three handfuls of water into the solar orb with the Astra-Gāyatrī mantra and perform the recitation (*japa*). A Śūdra, however, should perform everything except the *Brāhmī Sandhyā*. At the time of the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*), having taken up the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) with the [mantra] beginning "toyataḥ,"...

One should perform the invocation of the Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, and other sacred waters (tīrthas). However, they are not to be invoked here as external sacred sites; rather, one should invoke the currents of the Gaṅgā and others as they exist within the self, agitated by the moon of Śiva situated at the *dvādaśānta* and adorned with the *bindu*.
The sacred fords (*tīrthas*) therein are as follows: the Gāṅga, which has reached the *piṅgalā* channel; the Iḍā, which has reached the *iḍā* channel;

and the Sārasvata, which has reached the flow of the central channel (*madhyanāḍī*). These very [fords] are to be conceived here within the internal self (*adhyātman*) in accordance with the flow of all [the channels]. Thus it was stated by King Bhoja in the Tantra:

Furthermore, one should perform another rite: having dried the water with the *āgneyī-dhāraṇā* (fiery concentration) and refilled it with the *amṛta-dhāraṇā* (nectar concentration), one should encircle the water by rotating one's arms with a portion of earth consecrated by the recitation of the *śiva-mantra*, and thus conceive of it as "this is the Śiva-tīrtha. Having thus consecrated the holy site (*tīrtha*), [one should proceed] with that water.

One should perform an ablution upon one's own head with the *kumbha-mudrā*, using the root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*), the *brahmāṅga-mantras*, and the *śiva-gāyatrī*. Having bathed in this manner, immediately thereafter follows the supreme *āgneya-snāna* (fire-bath); for that, one should use ashes according to any one of the ritual procedures (*kalpa*) and so forth mentioned in the venerable *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*.
At the time of this bath,
one should also perform consecration with the mantras of the kalās, such as Nivṛtti and the rest, as well as with the root-mantra and the Brahmāṅga-mantras; this is to be done daily.
p.
70) Regarding the "pair": in the ritual bath with Varuṇa-ash, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma)—preceded by filling, retention, and exhaling—while reciting the root mantra.
At the time of the *sandhyāvandana* (the twilight worship), regarding the instruction "worship the *sandhyā*," this refers to the meditation (*adhyāna*) upon the *sandhyā*.
This is twofold, distinguished as *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (without parts). Among these, the *sakala* [form] is for the sake of the *samayin* and the *viśiṣṭasamayin*;
the *niṣkala* is for the sake of the *putraka* and others, [to be meditated upon] within the self at the locations of the heart, the *bindu*, and the *brahmarandhra*.
In that regard, the complete meditation is as follows:
one should meditate on Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Raudrī— red, white, and black respectively— at dawn, midday, and evening, in their proper sequence.
Clad in red garments and ornaments, with reddened [complexion], wearing matted hair and a sacred thread,
seated upon a swan and a lotus throne, she has four faces and four arms.
One should meditate upon Brāhmī in the eight directions at dawn, when the sky is starlit, holding a sacrificial ladle and a rosary in her right hands, and a staff and a water-pot in her left.
She wears white garments, is white in complexion, and is adorned with a forest garland and a sacred thread;
she sits upon the seat of Garuḍa and a lotus, possessing the blossoming bloom of fresh youth.
At midday, one should meditate upon the goddess Vaiṣṇavī, adorned with all ornaments, holding a conch and a discus in her left hands, and a mace and the gesture of fearlessness in her right hands.
She has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus, her youth is slightly past its peak;
she possesses four arms and three eyes, and is adorned with matted locks and the crescent moon.

One should meditate upon Raudrī, who stands at the head of the bull during the twilight when the sun has half-set and turned crimson; she holds a trident and an *akṣa* bead in her right hands, and displays the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and a spear (*śakti*) in her left hands.
All [the goddesses] wear black antelope skins and are witnesses to all ritual acts;
one should contemplate one's own body as having entered the expansive circle of their radiance.
Meditation on the Partless:
Now, the four supreme twilight-devotions (saṃdhyās) for the wise shall be declared.
The single Śiva-Śakti assumes multiplicity through limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Slender like a lotus fiber, red, white, or black;
the fourth, however, is formless or black, which is perceived at midnight.

These three, conjoined with the qualities of sattva and so forth, reside respectively in the heart, the bindu, and the brahmarandhra; while the fourth is devoid of qualities and resides eternally in the Supreme.
"The water thrown upon the surface of the vajra-stone effects the expiation of that sin";

in this regard, the throwing of water should be performed in the southwest direction (nairṛtyāṃ diśi). This is done after meditating on Sadāśiva, but prior to the offering of the handful of water (arghyāñjali) with the root mantra.
Having offered three handfuls of *arghya* with the *Śivagāyatrī*, one should perform the recitation (*japa*).

Afterwards, having offered *arghya* with the *Śiva-mantra* ending in *svāhā*, one should recite the root-mantras and the *brahmāṅga* mantras once. Then, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the deities of the mantras and others should be performed according to the sequence stated in the *Bhojarājapaddhati*.

Or it should be performed according to the sequence taught in the *Uttuṅgaśivapaddhati*. Having offered three handfuls of water preceded by meditation on the Sun with the root-mantra of the Sun, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) and worship with red flowers and so forth; by this [it is established] that the worship of the Sun [is required].

Since it has been indicated, immediately thereafter follows the worship of the Sun: having filled the *arghya* vessel— which has been purified by the *astra* mantra— with nectar-water of red color flowing from the *bindu*, along with unbroken rice (*akṣata*) and other offerings, and having worshipped the *arghya* vessel with the root mantra, one should offer the *darśana-arghya* with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*.

Thereafter, one should perform the worship. Regarding the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa during worship, having placed the heart-mantra on the thumb during the assignment of the hands (karanyāsa), one should assign the head, crest, armor, and weapon mantras to the fingers from the little finger to the index finger respectively.
This is how it is described in the Uttuṅgaśivapaddhati.

After performing the sakalīkaraṇa, having purified the vessel with the weapon-mantra (astra), and having filled it with water and other substances as before, one should worship the seat upon the yantrikā; then, having worshipped the Mūrti-mantra and the heart, head, crest, armor, and weapon-mantras within the vessel, [one should proceed] with these.

Having consecrated [the materials] with all [the mantras], performed the protective encasement (*avakuṇṭhana*), rendered them nectar-like (*amṛtīkṛta*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* using the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*), and delighted them with the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), one should sprinkle the locations of the substances with this water and,
facing east, perform the worship. Therein, of oneself—
On the right and left branches [of the door] are the gatekeepers Daṇḍa and Piṅgala, situated in the northeast and southeast corners;
one should worship Gaṇapati, Guru, Pārtha, Udumbara, and Astra according to the meditations to be described. The meditation on Daṇḍin is as follows:
To his right is Daṇḍin, who is fair-complexioned, possesses a fine beard, and has a stout belly;
he holds an ink-pot and a pen in his two hands.
"Piṅgala is on the left side, and the doorkeeper (pratīhāra) holds a staff," according to the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*.

Having meditated upon Gaṇapati— red in color, seated in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), with his left hand holding a sweetmeat ball (laḍḍuka) and a rosary (akṣamālā), and his right hand holding his own tusk as a battle-axe (kuṭhāra)— one should worship him. One should also worship the Guru,
who is adorned with a crown of matted locks (jaṭāmakuṭa), wears a sacred thread (brahmasūtra) fastened by a cloth band, and [is situated] above the region of the navel.
Having meditated upon [the deity] as being of red complexion and endowed with the *yogamudrā*, one should worship him. Immediately thereafter,
having worshipped the abundant seat (*prabhūtāsana*) in the center of the white pedestal (*śvetapīṭha*), and having propitiated Vimalasāra,
one should [worship] the footstools of the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana-pādukā*) known as Paramasukha, located in the southeast and southwest...

Having meditated upon white, red, yellow, and green lions in the corners of the east, north-west, south-east, and north-east, facing one another with their backs turned to each other, one should worship them. One should also worship the bulb, seed-syllable, sprout, stalk, lotus petals, filaments, and pericarp in the center.

One should worship the eight powers, beginning with Dīptā, in the petals starting from the east, and Sarvatomukhī in the portion consisting of the pericarp; the visualization of these [powers] is as follows: those powers are red, youthful, graceful, well-attired, resembling vermilion in hue, and of fresh youth.
The ninth [deity] is located on the tip of the petal within the pericarp; these [deities], beginning with Dīptā, have two arms and are worthy of worship.
They possess the luster of pomegranate flowers, are adorned with all ornaments, hold lotuses in their left hands, and carry chowries in their right hands.

Having meditated thus and performed worship, one should meditate upon the seat of the Sun in the form of a white lotus in the center of the pericarp, which is pervaded by the ultimate reality (*tattvānta*).
Having worshipped upon that, [one should meditate on the deity] situated in the center of a circular orb of red-colored light above that,
clad in red garments,
adorned with all ornaments, and with both hands holding a white lotus with its stalk clearly resting upon the shoulder.

Having visualized [the deity] as two-armed and endowed with all the auspicious marks (sarvalakṣaṇasaṃpanna), and having meditated on the form as pervading the interior of the Śiva-principle while holding a handful of flowers with the Khaṣotka mantra, one should worship the image. Having worshipped the two eyes with the Netra-mantra and having performed the cow-horn mudrā (goviṣāṇamudrā), [one should proceed].

Having recited the root mantra— which, as stated in the passage "of Śiva, Aśiva, and Uṣṇarociṣ," extends up to the end of the Śakti-tattva along with Māyā and Sadeśa— one should [visualize] a throbbing, reddish drop on the forehead and in the joined palms.

Having reflected, having invoked with the *āvāhinī* [mantra], having established [the deity] pervasively within that form, having caused it to be present with the *sannidhānī*, having restrained it with the *niṣṭhurā*, and having offered the *sannidhāna-arghya* and uttered "Welcome," one should place the Heart, Crest, Armor, and Weapon [mantras] in their respective locations, and the Armor in the middle of the breasts.
Having worshipped the weapon [in] the two hands with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), performed the binding of the directions (digbandha),
and enveloped [the deity] with the armor-mantra (kavaca), one should display the cow-seal (dhenumudrā) and the great seal (mahāmudrā) with the root-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
and then display the lotus-seal (padmamudrā) and the image-seal (bimbamudrā) at the feet with [the mantra] ending in *namaḥ*.

Having offered water for the feet with the root mantra ending in *svadhā*, water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) ending in *svāhā*, the respectful offering (*arghya*) ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),

Having offered incense, lamps, water for sipping (ācamanīya), and the respectful offering (arghya), and having bathed and fully worshipped [the deity], one should again offer water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping, and the respectful offering; then, having worshipped with three handfuls of flowers accompanied by the root mantra and the three principles (tattva), [one should worship] in the locations beginning with the heart.
Having worshipped the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*) with the *hṛdaya* and other mantras, and having offered the water of honor (*arghya*),
one should request permission for the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*).
Then, having invoked the *hṛdaya* and other [mantras] from the regions of the heart and the other [limbs], [one should place them] in the southeast, northeast, and north.

One should invoke the Heart-mantra and the others from the place of worship into the petals of the East, North-East, South-East, and West, as well as the Eye into the Western petal and the Weapon into the four petals starting from the East. Having offered the *arghya* to these with their respective mantras,
one should present the Bimba-mudrā and the Padma-mudrā to the Blessed One.

Having shown the *dhenumudrā* for the heart, head, crest, and armor; the *goviṣāṇamudrā* for the two eyes; and the *trāsanīmudrā* for the weapon; and having performed the act of supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*) with the root mantra and displayed the *mahāmudrā*, [one should proceed] to the four petals in the east and other directions.
One should worship the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus in the corners starting from the southeast (Agni), and likewise Mars, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu. Their visualization is as follows:
[They have] gentle faces, red-colored complexions, and lotus-like hands.
One should contemplate the two-armed limbs of the Sun as being adorned.
One should thus contemplate this weapon, terrifying the host of obstacles, with fangs formidable and possessing the brilliance of a fiercely blazing fire.

One should visualize Soma as white, Budha as fair-complexioned, Guru with the luster of gorocana, and Śukra as white, located in the directions starting from the east, and then in the corners starting from the southeast.
The son of the Earth (Mars) is red, Saturn has a dark body, Rāhu is black,
and Ketu is smoke-colored.
I bow to those six together with their left hands resting on my beautiful thighs and their right hands displaying the gesture of fearlessness.

Again, having gratified the Blessed One with water for sipping, food offerings, and so forth, and having presented the *pavitra* with the root-mantra joined with the *sarvatattva-mantra*, and having offered incense and lamps, one should recite the root-mantra and its limbs as much as possible, present the eight-flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), and recite a hymn of praise.
Having worshipped [the deity] with the mantras beginning from the weapon (astra) and ending with the heart (hṛdaya) at their respective locations while facing away,
and having offered the water of honor (arghya), and having worshipped the Blessed Lord, uttering "Forgive me" and offering the water of honor again,
[he should dismiss] the mantras residing in the places of enjoyment and those residing in the lightning-strike (vidyuccha).

Having meditated and raised [the deities] by means of the Mūrti-mantra, and having caused them to merge into the image, one should perform their dismissal while still regarding the image. In the absence of an image, however, one should cause them to go to the heart-lotus by means of the method of independent dismissal. In the northeast—
In that direction, having worshipped the form of Tejaścaṇḍeśa with the base-mantras of the seats, having offered the *arghya*,
and having presented the remains of the Sun’s offerings (*sūryanirmālya*), one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*) and then dismiss the vessel of the *āghra*.
The meditation (*dhyāna*) on Tejaścaṇḍeśvara:
One should meditate upon Caṇḍeśvara, who has matted hair and wears red garments, who is blazing with formidable fangs, and who holds a chisel, a lotus, and [the fire of] splendor.
Thus concludes the worship of the Sun.

The worship is described by the passage beginning with "having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) and the sakalīkaraṇa. Regarding that, the method of sakalīkaraṇa will be explained [later] with the words "one should purify the hands, both inside and outside, which have been smeared with fragrance, with a cloth," and so forth. As for the sequence of procedure therein: first of all, [this is done] for the purpose of dispelling their state of being composed of māyā.

Having incinerated [the impurity] with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having performed the immersion for the attainment of the Śākta-principle with the root-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should place the seat and the form upon the two palms,
and [place them] on the fingers from the thumb to the little finger.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the limb-mantras beginning with the heart and ending with the weapon, having placed the Brahmās beginning with Īśāna using the Brahma-mantras joined with the seed-syllables,
and having again performed the placement on the two palms from the Vidyā-body-mantra up to the end of the root-mantra;
Having performed the placement of the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra), beginning with the heart and ending with the weapon (astra), upon the fingers from the little finger to the thumb,

having encircled [the body] with the armor-mantra (kavaca) and consecrated it as supreme with the root-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should perform the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) with the syllable *bhyaṃ*. Therein, in the lotus of the heart, is the seat.
Having performed the placement [of the mantra] pervading the entire body from the soles of the feet upward,

one should perform the placement of that which is the collective form of the Brahmās beginning with Īśāna, characterized by five faces and so forth, pervading the entire body, using the mantras of the five Brahmās of the body.

Having placed the Netra-mantra upon the two eyes, and having performed the binding of the directions with the Astra-mantra ending in *phaṭ*— uttered three times as *tāla* and twice as *purāṇa*— one should, with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [perform] the Mahāmudrā from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
p.

78) One should show [the mantra] for the sake of the secret cause of the mantras. Thus, having performed the sakalīkaraṇa, one should sprinkle the general arghya vessel seven times with the Astra-mantra joined with the Praṇava, and [then approach] the door.

One should perform worship. Therein, although there are four doors, one should worship the gatekeepers and others as usual, enter the interior according to the ritual procedure, and then fully worship Vāstunātha at the western door;
for it has been stated that "one should open the western door and touch the other doors."
Worship at the western door alone is prescribed for movable liṅgas; however, for fixed liṅgas, worship should be performed according to the respective doors.

Regarding the meditation on the deities mentioned in the passage beginning with "In the southern [direction] of the Ūrdhvodumbara, Gaṇeśa, whose body is like a lotus," the visualization is as follows:
I take refuge in Gaṇapati, who is seated to the right of the face of the Ūrdhvodumbara and whose body is dark blue.

I bow to Sarasvatī, who possesses a white luster, holding in her pair of lotus-hands a sweetmeat and an axe on the left, a tooth and a rosary in the other, and resting upon an udumbara fruit above her left shoulder.
Holding a book in her left hand and a rosary in her right, while displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with her two hands,
she sits comfortably in the center of a lotus in their midst.
She who has performed her consecration with the water from a jar held up by both hands.
On the right [he holds] the great Lakṣmī, accompanied by the boon-granting gesture and a lotus; on the left, however, [he holds] her who bears a bilva fruit and a lotus.
He bears a trident and a rosary with his two hands— the left and the right— and has matted hair, three eyes.
Having reached the branch situated on the right of the door,
we take refuge in the red Nandin standing there; and to the north of that, we approach the form established there.
And Gaṅgā, white in color, mounted upon a crocodile.
She carries a blue lotus and a full pitcher in her two hands, positioned right and left;
on her left arm rests the dark-hued form [of Śiva], who wears a serpent as a sacred thread, has matted hair, and possesses beautiful fangs.
I take refuge in Mahākāla, whose left and right hands are equipped with a skull-cup and a trident;
I worship Yamunā, who is dark-complexioned and seated upon a tortoise, at his right side.
I worship [the deity] who holds a full water-pot and a blue lotus in his left and right hands,
and who bears a weapon resembling the fire at the end of an aeon resting upon a fig tree below.

I bow to the fair-complexioned one, who is adorned with four garlands, who possesses a beard, whose sacrificial ground is marked by a swan and a lotus, and who wards off the hosts of obstacles dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, and upon the earth.
In his two hands, he holds a water-pot and a sacrificial ladle; in the left [hand] and the other [right hand], he holds a rosary and a small spoon.

One should meditate on that Vāstuvahni as being located in the southwest corner (nir-ṛtikoṇa). Having thus visualized him, one should worship him in his respective places with their own respective mantras and offer the arghya. This is the expulsion of obstacles situated upon the ground.
In the *Pāśupatāstra* extracted from the illustrious *Śrīcatuḥśatikālottara*, it is stated: "Oṃ huṃ phaṭ.
At the time of entry, one should enter with the right foot leading, by way of the left side of the doorway.
"Sitting upon the seat, facing north, one should perform the purification of the self.

This sequence for the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) has been stated in brief because it was taught in the *Śrīmanmṛgendra* during the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*). It has likewise been stated by the Gurus for those who have not yet reached [the final state]: "For those overcome by instability..."

For those who are ill, the rite should be performed in brief; however, for those who are capable, the full detailed procedure must always be performed. Having sat facing north on the southern side of the Supreme Lord, and having propitiated Him, one should perform the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*) according to the previously described sequence.

Having first expelled the impure air residing within by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma) preceded by inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka) while reciting the Astra-mantra,
one should fill the abdomen with the external air presided over by Śiva.
From the pair of big toes up to the *mūlādhāra*, she is divided into two;
from there upwards to the *dvādaśānta*, she becomes one.

One should contemplate the *suṣumnā*, known as the abode of Śiva, shining like a streak of lightning within the interior of the body. Within it, one should contemplate the pervasive *kuṇḍalinī* power, which is eternally presided over by the Supreme Lord both internally and externally. In the center of that *suṣumnā*—

The cluster of lotuses situated with their faces downward in the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) becomes filled by the inhalation (pūraka), obstructed and held firm by the retention (kumbhaka), and then, by the exhalation (recaka), it is cast upward so that its face turns up; thereafter, at the region of the crown of the head (mūrdhāra).

Having meditated on the twilight [state] as being like the flame of a lamp, and having recited the scripture consisting of the seed-syllable of the crest (*śikhā-bīja*) ending with *phaṭ*, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) according to one's capacity— consisting of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*)— at the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*), and the twelve-finger space above the head.
Releasing the breath through the right nostril, turning back,

and again mentally reciting the seed-syllable of the crest (śikhā) in the eastern direction while preceded by meditation, one should fix the mind upon it and apply focused attention in the form of its mental activity there.
Having projected the self— which exists from the feet to the head, uninterrupted by the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*),
and having the form of a star or the flame of a lamp— upon that [object], by means of the restraint of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*);
and having meditated upon it as pure through contact with that [object], by the upward-opening of the flow of the vital breath...

By means of a single expulsion (*ekoddhāta*), having joined [the breath]— from the earth up to the point of the *bindu*— to Śiva who resides in the lotus at the end of the twelve fingers (*dvādaśānta*) through the mere separation of the rays (*raśmi*), (p. 82) ...

One should purify the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) through the process of their dissolution into their respective causes. To explain: earth is dissolved into smell, water into taste, fire into form, wind into touch, and space arises from sound; furthermore, these subtle elements (*tanmātrās*) dissolve into the *tāmasa* ego-principle (*ahaṃkṛti*). Then, the organs of action [dissolve into the *rājasa* ego].
And you shine together with the mind, intellect, and senses; that [intellect] dissolves into the quality of sattva, and that quality-group dissolves into the manifest (vyakta);
likewise, attachment and ignorance pass away into the kalā.
Masculinity, time, necessity, and limited agency; she [Māyā] [leads to] Suvidyeśa together with Sadeśa and Śakti; this [Śakti] [leads to] Śiva together with Eṣa and Bindu.

Having thus performed the purification of the subtle body, one should thereafter perform the purification of the elements that constitute the gross body. The element is the earth-element (pṛthivītattva),
yellow, solid, marked with a thunderbolt, square, and pervading the body.
Having meditated upon [the body] as conjoined with Brahmā, the Lord of Causes; presided over by Sadyojāta-Brahmā; united with the Heart-mantra; the substratum of the Nivṛtti-kalā;
and possessed of the waking state—[one should act] with the mantra of the Nivṛtti-kalā ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
Within this, five *udghātas* should be performed as a pentad consisting of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Above is the *ghāta*, which is the *mantra-ghāta*.
Regarding the impulsion up to the *dvādaśānta* by means of the movement of *nāda*, as stated in the *Trayodaśadaśatikā*:
"When the *apāna* is compressed by the *prāṇa* being uttered,
and having gone upward it returns, this is the characteristic of the *udghāta*."

One should perform these five times; thus, three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) constitute one "upward blow" (*udghāta*), which is established for the sake of the goal. In this way, by means of five upward blows, through the power presided over by the specific Śiva-śakti, which is endowed with the capacity for purification—
One should meditate on form as being overcome by air. Then, one should meditate on it as having become water— shaped like a half-moon, liquid, white, marked with a lotus,
joined with Viṣṇu as its cause, and presided over by Brahmā as Vāmadeva.
Conjoined with the head-mantra (śiromantra), it is the substratum of the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā; associated with the state of dreaming (*svapnāvasthā*),
by virtue of the four qualities contained within it, it is [attained] through four upward thrusts (*udghāta*) by means of the mantra of the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā.

One should purify while contemplating that [the object] is overwhelmed by the fire endowed with the power of purification through the presiding influence of Śiva and Śakti; [that fire] which has become the triangle, marked with a red svastika,
joined with Rudra as the causal agent, presided over by the Aghora-Brahman, and [consecrated] with the seed-syllable of the crest (śikhā).

Having meditated upon that which is joined with the state of deep sleep (suṣupti) and conjoined with the substrate of the *vidyā-kalā*, one should— by means of three *udghātas* [upward breaths] through the power of the *vidyā-kalā* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,
and by virtue of the three qualities (*guṇas*) contained therein— [perform the rite] through the power of the presiding Śiva-śakti.
One should purify [the object] while visualizing it as being overwhelmed by water endowed with the power of purification;
[then one should visualize] the hexagon as having become air.
Having meditated upon the black [syllable] marked with six dots, joined with the Lord as the cause, presided over by Brahmā as Tatpuruṣa, conjoined with the armor [mantra] and the fourth state,
and serving as the support for the Śānti-kalā, one should [proceed] with the Śānti-kalā mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

Contemplating that the circle has become the element of space— overpowered by the earth-tattva, which is endowed with the power of purification through the capacity of the presiding presence of Śiva and Śakti and by virtue of the two groups situated within it and the two upward thrusts— one should purify it.

It is presided over by the power of the Bindu; it is conjoined with the Supreme Lord known as Sadāśiva, who exists in the state of authority as the causal agent; it is further presided over by the Brahman Īśāna;
it is conjoined with the seed-syllable of Śiva’s weapon; and it is endowed with the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which is the support of the kalā beyond tranquility (śāntyatīta).

Having reflected upon this, one should purify by means of a single exhalation (*ekodghāta*) using the mantra of the *Śāntyatītakalā*, while contemplating that which resides within it as the oneness of its qualities— become the supreme point (*parabindu*) presided over by Śiva and Śakti, resembling pure crystal; such is the explanation of the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).

Having meditated upon this body— which consists of an aggregate of elements and whose power is exhausted by the destruction of its qualities— as being burnt by the Fire of Time presided over by the Power of Śiva (Śivaśakti), which has arisen from the big toe of the right foot and is accompanied by the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, [one should then purify] the ashes with the Śākta wind.
One should dispel [the mind]. Thereafter, having regarded all gross objects as "conceptualization" because they are binding,
one is not enveloped by the notion of a self in what is not-self, due to the absence of dependence on any objective support.
p. 85) Thus,
the supportless,
mere consciousness devoid of all fetters is like the solar orb of the nature of the Self.

Only tranquility remains. Then, like the departure of one's own [consciousness], everything— both gross and subtle— of the body is characterized by the total destruction of its foundational supports, because [the individual] is no longer fit for the touch of the Supreme Lord of the body except through the worship of the Supreme Lord and similar practices.

Because the bondage of impurity (malabandha), which is qualified by its association with the karma that has already begun to bear fruit (prārabdhakarman), is not removed, and because it cannot be relinquished in any way even at the time of purification due to the non-separation from the mere rays [of consciousness], all things exist in the form of being woven together as warp and woof.

Because the supreme bindu— which is the form of the eternal object of the Supreme Lord’s power, the form of supreme nectar, and the support of all— is stable, one should perform an immersion with the arisen nectar,
beginning from the *mūlādhāra* up to the end of *unmanā*, starting from the letters *pha* and *ka*.

Preceded by the contemplation of the utterance of the *mātṛkās*, one should contemplate [the self] being flooded by the supreme nectar flowing from the undisturbed moon of Śiva situated at the *dvādaśānta*— by means of the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*— according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*). Thus...

Having performed the ritual placement of the seat (*āsana-nyāsa*) with the six mantras beginning with *Ādhāraśakti* upon the pure body distinguished by the cultivation of superior meditative absorption (*dhyāna-bhāvanā*), one should perform the placement of the pervasion of the *ātmatattva*, *asaṃvit-tattva*, and *yātattva*, ending with the pervasion of the syllable *ka*.
Above that, one should contemplate the pure *puryaṣṭaka*, pervaded by the seed-syllable (*bīja*). Then,
one should contemplate oneself as Śiva, pure and consisting of Śiva, resembling a star, pervaded by the end of the *nāda*.
And by means of the *nāda*, one should likewise contemplate the sacred ford (*tīrtha*);
furthermore, because it has been established from one's own body with distinction, for that purpose—

As before, the sprinkling (āplāvana) should be performed with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Having thus performed the internal placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), one should also perform the placement of the specific Śākta form externally. The sequence therein is as follows: [the placement of] the seat of Śiva (*śivāsana*) and the manifest form of Śiva (*śivamūrti*).

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the heart with one's own two mantras according to the sequence stated in the manual (*paddhati*), [one should perform] the arrangement of the rosary, the Brahma-thread, the limbs, and the facial expressions,
again by means of those consisting of the thirty-eight *kalās*.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with the [mantras] beginning with *śaśi* and ending with *tadatva*,

and having also performed the placement of the Brahma-mantra joined with the seed-syllables (*bīja*), one should [meditate upon] the Śākta body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*), which is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the Brahman, by means of its own mantra as pervading the entire body starting from the region of the heart.

Having performed the placement of the heart and other limbs (*hṛdayādinyāsa*), and having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*) preceded by the three claps of the hands (*tālatraya*), and having established a rampart consisting of the weapon-mantra (*astramaya-prākāra*) and a barricade consisting of the armor-mantra (*kavacamaya-parigha*), [one should perform] the great mudrā with the root-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

One should demonstrate [the procedure]. Again, within the heart-lotus, having worshipped the Supreme Lord through the sequence beginning with invocation using the flowers of mental visualization as if they were external, and after offering the recitation (*japa*),
one should worship the Supreme Lord preceded by invocation in the eternally perfected fire situated in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having offered oblations with the sacrificial substance in the form of nectar drawn up by inhalation (*pūraka*), according to one's capacity, through the root-mantra, the Brahma-mantras, and the limb-mantras; having then become indifferent to that [external state] and performed the dismissal (*visarjana*); having gathered the circle of mantras (*mantracakra*) with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*);
and having united it with the Supreme Lord residing in the heart-lotus by means of the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*)—[one should perform] the eight...
Having offered the concluding flower (puṣpikā), having worshipped [the deity] with his face turned away in reverse order,
and having dismissed him with due regard as one would a Śiva-liṅga, [one should contemplate] that which resides in the center of the forehead-plate.

One should meditate upon the Supreme Lord, who resembles the orb of the autumnal moon. And although this purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) serves the purpose of purification, it does not supersede external purification such as bathing; by that [external purification], both external cleanliness and the cleansing of sin produced by touching the untouchable are accomplished.
By this [practice], the binding nature consisting of the meditation on a self and so forth within that which is non-self is removed.

Thus, through the meditation on Śiva both externally and internally, he too becomes equal to Śiva. Now, if this state of equality with Śiva is not consistent with the relationship between the worshiper and the worshipped, that [relationship] indeed exists only between the inferior and the superior, and not otherwise.

In this context, "samaya" (the state of equilibrium) refers to the state of being Śiva, which is the specific presiding presence (*viśeṣādhiṣṭhitatva*) by Śiva. This presiding presence cannot be known by the person through their own power alone, like the sun;
for thus says the Śruti: "It shines forth. As it has been said in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*:
"Having reached that which resides in the palace of the path purified by the cloth, he attains equanimity;
however, as long as he has not become equal to that [state], he is not capable of propitiation. Thus it is said.

Having thoroughly washed the vessel for the special *arghya*— that is, the special *arghya* vessel— with the *astra-mantra*, and having filled it with water in the form of nectar flowing from the *bindu* while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra* joined with the *praṇava*, he should cast into it milk, *kuśa* grass, rice grains, flowers, barley, white mustard seeds, and sesame seeds.
On the mechanical doll (yantrikā),
[one should place] the seat of Śiva; in the vessel, the form of the pentad of Brahmās beginning with Īśāna.
Having worshipped with the Vidyā, Deha, Netra, Mūla-mantra, Hṛdaya, Śiras, Śikhā, Kavaca, and Astra mantras;

having consecrated all these and performed protection and veiling (avakuṇṭhana); having rendered [the water] nectar-like with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* by means of the Dhenu-mudrā; and having sprinkled one's own head with that water using the Saṃhitā mantras.
Having brought water-pitchers for the purpose of bathing, having washed them with the *astra* mantra,

and having performed the rites of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), striking (*tāḍana*), and sprinkling from above (*abhyukṣaṇa*), one should consecrate the water-strainer (*jalapavitra*) with the *mantrasaṃhitā*; then, having filled it with the dripping water using the *hṛdaya* mantra, [one should proceed].

Having offered each flower individually, consecrated it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and conceptualized it as the sacred water of Śiva (*śivatīrtha*) by sprinkling drops from the special *arghya* water, one should perform the protective veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*) and display the *dhenumudrā* and the *mahāmudrā*.

Having first performed the four purificatory rites (saṃskāras), beginning with inspection (apara-nirīkṣaṇa) upon the collection of materials such as flowers, one should consecrate them with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra) while forming them into mere balls (piṇḍa). Then, having performed protection (rakṣā) and veiling (avakuṇṭhana), one should place a flower on one’s own head with the root-mantra (mūla-mantra) alone and perform the purification of the mantra (mantra-śuddhi). In that regard:

At the time of worship, one should employ the root mantra associated with the pervasion up to the end of the Śiva-tattva for the vessel of the special *arghya* offering; and having worshipped the *rodha-arghya* in the same manner as the special *arghya*, one should employ the root mantra associated with the pervasion up to the end of the Vidyā-tattva.

It should be performed. Purification must be effected by the utterance of the root-mantra (*mūla*), the limb-mantras (*aṅga*), the Brahmā-mantras, and the sequences ending with *nāda*, *bindu*, and *uccāra*. Then, having gazed [at the object] with the eye while reciting the *Śiva-mantra* placed upon the site of worship, [one should offer] the special water-offering (*viśeṣārghya*).
Having sprinkled [the area] with water using the Astra-mantra and having sprinkled it again with the Kavaca-mantra, preceded by three claps of the hands to expel obstacles;

With the Astra-mantra ending in *phaṭ*, one should create a moat consisting of the Astra-mantra for the purpose of removing the illusory nature (*māyeyatva*) of the place of worship and for establishing its state as the Bindu; immediately thereafter, having installed the Supreme Lord upon the altar for the ritual bathing of the Liṅga with holy waters, [one should proceed] with the Gāyatrī.
Having worshipped [the deity] with the water of the general *arghya* and offered the *arghya* with the mantra ending in *svāhā*,

one should rotate the five Brahmans, beginning with Sadyojāta, in the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) using the fingers starting from the little finger; then, having descended [the deities] from the top of the *liṅga* with the heart-mantra of worship.

Having cast the floral remains (*nirmālya*) into a pure vessel toward the northeast for Caṇḍeśa, and having performed the purification of the *liṅga* and the pedestal with the *astra* and *hṛdaya* mantras,
one should sprinkle it with the water of the general *arghya*. Immediately thereafter, in that very place...

Some say that after establishing [the deity] and worshipping with the *aṣṭapuṣpikā* offering, one should offer the *arghya* with water from the general *arghya* vessel using the root mantra, and then perform the ritual bathing (*svapana*) with the root mantra and the *brahmāṅga* mantras. However, the teachers [maintain that] one should worship the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) and [worship] the form of Ṛṣabha...

Meditating and worshipping as if it were a fixed liṅga, having performed the worship beginning with the invocation and ending with the offering of flowers accompanied by the syllable *vauṣaṭ*, they describe the bathing with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth;
the characteristics of the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) are stated in the *Vimalāvatī*. Thus it is said:
In the venerable Pūrvakrama:
"The infinite, as well as virtue, knowledge, dispassion,
and sovereignty— this sixfold lotus is the seat."
90) However, regarding the mobile liṅga, the method of bathing has been described by Lakṣārtha and others:
"But for the mobile [liṅga], there is the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), cow's milk, and so forth, for the sake of an elaborate bathing."

The wise one, having worshipped the deity seated upon the sixfold throne— consisting of the limbs of absorption (layāṅga) and joined together— and having offered perfumes, flowers, and so forth, preceded by anointing;
Having bathed [the deity] with the five products of the cow and other substances, and having wiped him with a clean cloth,
one should bathe the Lord of the World upon a pedestal covered with divine garments.

However, because this [liṅga] is mobile, they maintain that even after having performed the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites— as one would with a fixed liṅga— following the placement of the thirty-eight kalās of the complete worship of the seat (āsana-pūjā) and so forth, one must first place the mantras of the seats beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti itself upon the pedestal; yet this is not correct.

When the *liṅga* being worshipped moves slightly upon the touch of hands or other limbs, one should perform the remaining rites a hundred times with the *aghora-mantra*, as stated in the root text of the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"From the worship on the complete seat until the dismissal (*visarjana*), there should be no movement during the worship."

Furthermore, what is appropriate? Since the dismissal (visarjana) of Gaṇapati and the Guru is not prescribed between their worship [in the Vāyavya and Īśāna corners], and since an expiation is prescribed for moving before the dismissal of the deities worshipped on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), their movement is inevitable; therefore—

The worship of the complete seat (samagrāsana-pūjā) should not be performed; for in all the scriptures, it is forbidden due to the risk of moving the Śiva-kumbha and Vardhanī vessels during the process of encompassing the maṇḍala.

Since the worship of the movable seat has been taught, and furthermore the worship of the fixed seat has also been taught, one must not cause the movement of the *liṅga* that has been worshipped on both seats; moreover—

"One revolves [the vessel] twice as many times as there are thousand-fold [repetitions]; purification occurs when it has fallen from the white [vessel], provided it is joined with three or four hundred thousand revolutions. This is according to the statement of Somaśambhu. Even on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), if the rites of invocation and so forth have been performed, but before the act of worship is completed and while the Lord of Gods has not yet been dismissed, should an impairment occur through negligence...
