Because of the statement of Bhoja, "Having withdrawn the mantras from the flowers and other offerings once they have arisen," and because an expiation is prescribed for the movement of the arghya vessel— stating that "if the vessel is discarded, broken, or even moves, one becomes pure after two hundred, a thousand, or half of that [repetitions] respectively"— therefore, the vessel should not move.
Furthermore, this must indeed be done; for when the ground, which serves as the support for the throne upon which a king is seated, shakes, the king who is mounted upon it also shakes.
Thus, [it is said] regarding that throne: "The Lord, pure like clear crystal," and so forth.
Furthermore, since it is heard in scripture that even the Supreme Lord is seated upon a throne during the complete worship of His seat,

it is indeed possible for the Supreme Lord to move when the pedestal in the form of a lion-throne moves due to the shaking of the earth. Moreover, this [shaking] is improper, as [the Lord] is mounted upon a palanquin, an elephant, a horse, or the like.
Just as even the movement of a king is honored because it is preceded by intention, so too is it in the case of the *liṅga*.

It is indeed appropriate that the seat is mobile, having the form of Śiva’s water-pot (kumbha) and bull (vṛṣabha); therefore, in the case of a mobile liṅga, one should first perform worship with a mobile seat,
and then bathe it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and so forth, according to the method to be described in the ritual manual (paddhati).
Having wiped [the vessel] with a clean cloth and placed it upon an auspicious seat,

one should meditate upon and worship Gaṇapati in the northwest corner as before; then, having meditated upon and worshipped Mahālakṣmī in the northern part as before, [one should worship] [Śiva], adorned with a crown of matted hair, in the northeast corner.

Meditating upon the lineage of Gurus— white and pale-red in hue, endowed with a yogic belt, wearing a sacred thread, with two arms forming the yoga-mudrā over the region of the navel, and possessing gentle eyes— one should worship them:
Sadāśiva, Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Ambikā.
I take refuge for seven years in Guha, Viṣṇu, Dhātṛ, and my gurus.

This is the lineage of gurus. Alternatively, one should worship [the lineage] starting from below the seat (pīṭha) with the *dhruva-mantra* or the *hṛdaya-mantra*, using the respective names of Ādhāraśakti, Ananta, and the seats (āsana), each preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ). The visualization (*dhyāna*) for these is as follows:
One should worship the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti) in the center, who is the color of the Milky Ocean, whose form is like a sprout from a seed,
the support of all, and who rests upon the firm Tortoise-Stone (Kūrmaśilā).
White as a jasmine flower or the moon, bestowing boons, three-eyed, bearing a mass of matted locks, destroying fear and granting fearlessness,
holding a noose and a goad, and seated in the midst of a lotus— (p. 93).
One should contemplate the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) at the root.
I bow down to Ananta, the white mantra-leader seated upon the Brahma-stone, who has transcended all conceptual proliferation and rests upon the lotus-throne of Māyā.

Thus, one should worship the seat of Ananta, which consists of the thirty principles beginning with Earth and ending with Kalā, is endowed with the kanda-tube and other structures, is composed of Māyā because it possesses many streams, and takes the form of a thousand-petaled lotus. Above that is the third enclosure, whose characteristics will be described later.

Having meditated upon the Infinite, one should worship. One should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast corners with their respective mantras. Their visualization is as follows:
Dharma is white, Jñāna is red, Vairāgya is yellow, and Aiśvarya is black.
Regarding the reason why those whose form is infinite power (*ananta-sāmarthya*)— manifesting as lions— are established by Śambhu in the corners beginning with the southeast on the *pīṭha*,
denoted by such terms as "Dharma" and so forth, it was stated there by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha:
In the *Śrīmat-Kālottara-vṛtti*:

"Dharma and the other [qualities] are specific powers of infinite capacity by which [the Self] unites, knows, and is not colored by anything, and thus becomes the Lord of All; they are not, however, attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*)."
It must be explained due to [the reader's] ignorance, because it is not easily understood here; nor is it the case that "animals and fetters are worshipped here," since the four [principles],
beginning with Adharma, are located to the east, south, west, and north of the lion-throne.
One should worship after contemplating the forms of the limbs. Their visualization is as follows:
black, white, white-and-red for the second, red-and-yellow, and yellow-and-black, in sequence.
I take refuge in these four limbs located here on this seat, situated in the directions beginning with the east.

These too are attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*), consisting of the nature of the presiding deities of Dharma and so forth, and the form of infinite power; it was stated by him [the author] in that very same place:
"In the southwest and northeast corners are the lower covering and the upper covering."
One should worship the bulb, the seed, the sprout, the stalk, the lotus petals, the filaments, and the pericarp above that.
Thus, O Brahmins, the principles (tattvas), the entities (bhāvas), the instruments (karaṇas), and the bodies have been explained in brief according to the pure and impure paths.

In the venerable *Mṛgendra-śruta*, one should meditate on Brahmā, who consists of the principle of *śuddhavidyā* (pure knowledge), as the *kanda* (bulbous root). The fifty verbal suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) consisting of *śuddhavidyā* are to be meditated upon as the seed-syllables (*bīja*), and the intellect (*buddhi*) consisting of *śuddhavidyā* is to be meditated upon as the sprout (*aṅkura*).

That which consists of it, extending up to the *kalā*-tattva, should be meditated upon as the stalk of the lotus. This cause of the Supreme Lord, the *bindu*-tattva which is eternally presided over, should be meditated upon by the Vidyeśvaras as the lotus-tattva.

Based on the statement "encircled by petals," [it is established that] for the sake of the enjoyment (*bhoga*) of the eight Vidyeśvaras on the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*), [this occurs] primarily at every re-creation (*pratisarga*).

Since it has been stated that [the Lord] exists as the object of creation, and because of the scriptural teaching that the cities which serve as His abodes are situated in the eight directions beginning with the east, one should meditate upon eight petals conditioned by those [cities],
and pure filaments in the form of the sixty-four Vidyās.

As for the objects of meditation: the pericarp (karṇikā) should be meditated upon as the Supreme Kuṇḍalinī herself, who consists of the fifty letters that are the cause of all expressive words, and whose nature is the supreme ether. This is the meditation on these [elements].
The Gurus have said:
"I salute the eight petals of the lotus of the Lords of Knowledge, which consist of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā),
and the yellow pericarp containing the fifty seed-syllables."

The nine powers, beginning with Vāmā, are to be worshipped as residing in the filaments of the petals starting from the east; however, Manonmanī is to be worshipped in the northeast portion of the pericarp. These powers are to be worshipped because they are recipients of the grace of the Supreme Lord’s love.

The Supreme Goddess herself, whose power is differentiated by the distinctions of the presiding deities and limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of those [deities] beginning with Ananta who have been mentioned, is the very essence of these [energies].
Because she presides over these *aiśvara-rakta* [energies], they possess redness;
however, because *Manonmanī* lacks such a presiding deity, she possesses whiteness. The visualization (*dhyāna*) of these [energies] is as follows:
His left hands bear the gesture of granting boons and a cow, while his two right hands display the gestures of fearlessness and the fly-whisk;
he is red in color, adorned with a crest of matted hair marked by a crescent moon, and his entire body is decorated with ornaments.
I honor the eightfold group of powers beginning with Vāmā, who are worshipped at the filaments in the directions starting from the east; and likewise,
I honor Manonmanī, whose form is identical to theirs, seated upon the pericarp and possessing a white body.

Thus, one should worship the solar disc, the lunar disc, and the fire disc, as well as their presiding deities—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—at the tips of the petals and the tips of the filaments. These discs are not those established in the world; rather, they belong to the Bhuvarloka.

The points of light (*bindulikā*) denoted by the terms *ātmatattva*, *vidyātattva*, and *śivatattva*— which serve as the substrata for the manifestation of the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*), action (*kriyā*), and will (*icchā*)—
are established in the world; they are situated upon the divine throne (*divyasiṃhāsana*) as having entered the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
Because their approach is impossible, their presiding deities are not established in the world;
it has been stated by the Teachers that these are specific powers acting as their superintendents.
In the *Śrīmanmṛgendravṛttidīpikā*, the meditation on the lords of the maṇḍalas is described as follows:
[He visualizes] Brahmā, stout and yellow, four-armed and four-faced,
bearing a swan as his emblem, and holding a staff, a rosary, a sacrificial ladle, and a water-pot.
Viṣṇu has four arms, wears a garland, and holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
he resembles a dark blue cloud and is seated upon Garuḍa.
Īśāna is mounted upon a bull, holding a trident and a serpent;
he is as white as the autumnal moon, bears the moon upon his crest, and possesses three eyes.
97) When the nature of the pervasion of Śiva’s throne was explained by the Gurus, it was described as auspicious, consisting of the entire path beginning with Earth and ending with Kuṭilā.
One should conceive: "I take refuge in this divine Yoga-pīṭha, the seat of Śiva.
Then the pīṭha is constructed like the remaining paths (adhvan).
In the venerable Kiraṇatantra, it is stated that there is a pervasion (vyāpti) of the seat of Śiva, which is the Śruti, consisting of the levels from Earth up to the Śiva-tattva.

"Grant success to that one who sacrifices at the station of the conscious and the unconscious," according to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of this mantra; and because of the teacher’s statement that the sign (*cihna*) is the *tāra* (the syllable Om).
[This applies] to those among the selves who are divided by the distinctions of the *vijñānākala*, *pralayākala*, and *sakala*.

Of the Mantramaheshvaras and Mantreshvaras who have been graced by the Supreme Lord through the ripening of their impurities; of the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth and ending with Śiva, along with the lords of those principles; and of the worlds (bhuvanas) beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Atāśrita.
Among those lords of the worlds, such as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and others of divine origin, who have been appointed by the venerable Lord Rudra to offices among the supreme Lords of Mantras—
thus including all souls distinguished by the various divisions of mantras, whether worldly, Vedic, spiritual, and so forth.
Of all the streams of sound, whether pure or impure,
consisting of all the phonemes from *a* to *kṣa* which serve as their cause, and of the path of words (*padādhvan*) distinguished by eighty-one and other varieties of words;
[This refers] to the path of mantra which has been brought to rest by the weapon [mantra] today, as well as the path of the kalās— nivṛtti and the others— which pervades all paths,
and likewise to the entire aggregate of effects, which is differentiated by the distinctions of word and meaning.

And because its two causes, *māyā* and *bindu*, are included within the seat of Śiva in the form of the divine lion-throne, [one should contemplate her] with the seed-syllable of the self (*ātma-bīja*) in the cavity of the heart— [she who is] pervaded by the words of the double repetition, possessing the luster of a rising sun.

According to the statement, "One should place the form, whose limbs are red like those of Īśvara, within the circumference," one should [visualize] her— whose limbs are detached [from materiality] and who possesses the luster of the rising sun— by means of the heart-enclosed self-seed-syllable (*ātma-bīja*) of the Supreme Lord situated in the lotus of the *dvādaśānta*.

One should place, preceded by an offering of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), within the circumference of the *śivaliṅga* the form of Śakti as the embodiment of power— the power of the Supreme Lord regarding the task of world-creation, which consists of the nature of cause and effect and is established in the Supreme. And then:

Just as the dawn [destroys] the darkness that conceals the power of food for those situated within the interior of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), so too [does this knowledge destroy] the darkness for humans,
sages, and others who are situated within the *bindu* of the innate disposition (*prākṛta-āśaya*).

Because it dispels the great darkness of impurity and the like for all selves, from the level of the Vidyeśvaras downwards, this [state] is to be meditated upon as the manifestation of the form of the Supreme Lord;
for it is precisely through the form of the Supreme Lord— which consists of His inherent power— that He accomplishes the fivefold cosmic function.

Because they exist as cause and effect, there is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the five Brahmās beginning with Īśāna— which are differentiated by the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of their respective functions— as well as the thirty-eight *kalās* which are their intermediate subdivisions.
Thus, having formed a fist with the *bhadramudrā*, [one places them] upward upon the head.
One should place Īśāna preceded by the flower. With the syllable *oṃ* and the joining of the index finger and thumb (p.
99), there is the ear in the mouth of Tatpuruṣa; with the joining of the middle finger and thumb, *ghora* is in the heart, *oṃ*.
There is a scriptural authority stating: "With the thumb and ring finger, one should place Vāmadeva at the secret place.

Thus, by joining the little finger and the thumb, beginning from the feet, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the manifested form (*mūrti*)—which pervades the entire body and is constituted by its numerical aspects.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the unbroken *mālā-brahmāṇi* mantras in this manner upon the faces facing upward, east, south, north, and west, along with the *trābhaṅga*. Then, the placement of the *kalābhaṅga* should be performed: "Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Śaśinī, the Lord of all sciences," thus [one places it] on the upper head. Oṃ...
"Īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ gadāyai namaḥ"—thus on the eastern head;
"Brahmādhipatirbrahmaṇo'dhipatirbrahmeṣṭadāyai namaḥ"—thus on the southern head; "Oṃ śivo me astu marīcyai namaḥ"—thus on the northern head.

"Sadāśiva, salutation to Jvālinī"—thus on the western head; "Oṃ, salutation to the Unmanifest Kalā"—thus on the upper face; "Oṃ Heṃ, we know Tatpuruṣa, salutation to Śānti"—thus on the eastern face; "Oṃ, we meditate upon Mahādeva, salutation to Vidyā"—thus on the southern face.

Oṃ *tanto rudraḥ pratiṣṭhāyai namaḥ*—thus at the upper face; Oṃ *pracodayāt nivṛttyai namaḥ*—thus at the western face; Oṃ *hāṃ aghorebhyaḥ tamāyai namaḥ*—thus at the heart; Oṃ *atha ghorebhyaḥ mohāyai namaḥ*—thus at the throat; Oṃ *ghorakṣamāyai*.
*Oṃ namaḥ* on the right shoulder; *Oṃ ghoratarebhyo nihrāyai namaḥ* on the left shoulder;
*Oṃ sarvataśśarvamṛtyave namaḥ* at the navel; *Oṃ sarvebhyo māyāyai namaḥ*.

Thus, [one should apply] "Oṃ, obeisance to you, obeisance to Rudrā" on the belly; "Oṃ, obeisance to forms, obeisance to Jarā" on the back; "Oṃ, hiṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva; obeisance to Rajā" on the chest;
"Oṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā, obeisance to Rakṣā" on the private parts; and "Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra, obeisance to Ratī" on the penis.

Thus, on the right thigh: *oṃ* to Kāla, salutation; *oṃ* to Bālī, salutation. On the left thigh: *oṃ* to Kalā, salutation; *oṃ* to Kāmā, salutation. On the right knee: *oṃ* to Vikaraṇa, salutation; *oṃ* to Saṃyaminī, salutation. On the left knee:
*oṃ* to Balakriyā, salutation. On the right shank: *oṃ*...

"Oṃ, salutation to Vikaraṇā; salutation to Buddhi"—thus on the left calf. "Oṃ, salutation to Balakārī"—thus on the right buttock. "Oṃ, salutation to Pramathanā; salutation to Dhātrī"—thus on the left buttock. "Oṃ, salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana; salutation to Grāmiṇī"—thus on the waist.

Oṃ, salutation to Manonmanī—thus on the right side; Oṃ, salutation to Unmanā, salutation to Abhayā—thus on the left side; Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta, salutation to Siddhi—thus on the right foot; Oṃ, salutation indeed to Sadyojāta, salutation to Ṛddhi—thus on the left foot. Oṃ.
"Bhave dyutyai namaḥ" on the right hand; "Oṃ bhave bhakṣyai namaḥ" on the left hand;
"Oṃ anādibhave medhāyai namaḥ" on the nose; "Oṃ bhajasva mām."

"Oṃ, salutation to Kānti," [recite] on the head; "Oṃ, salutation to Bhava Svadhā," [recite] on the head; "Oṃ, salutation to Bhava Svadhā," [recite] on the right arm; "Oṃ, salutation to Udbhavā and salutation to Sthiti," [recite] on the left arm. Then...

Having performed worship upon the head, face, heart, secret place, feet, and all other parts of the body using the Brahmamantras joined with their seed-syllables, one should then [worship] the body of knowledge (vidyādeha) of the Supreme Lord, who is engaged in the act of universal grace, as being none other than the Power (śakti) residing in the lotus at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta) and fully united [with Him].

One should place upon the ascent of the Śivaliṅga that which is the cause of the body, whose nature is non-instrumentality, and which consists of a collection of powers in the form of *kalās*. As it has been said:
"Sadāśiva, endowed with the thirty-eight *kalās*, is the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*)."

"One should place [the mantra] upon the vowel 'ā' after meditating on the Śakti as radiant with its characteristic marks. This body is indeed of the nature of Śakti belonging to Sadāśiva; as it has been said:
"That stainless Śakti of Śiva which is inherent (*samavāyinī*) to him..."
That very [power], through the differentiation of form and action, is called the principle (tattva) known as Sādākhya.
Thus, because the power of this Blessed One consists of eternal, pure, and unsurpassed knowledge and action regarding all objects,
there is no dependence on other manifesting agents for the Vidyeśvaras and others, owing to the absence of various obscurations.
Precisely because it is veiled—
namely, because it is veiled by the *baindava* and other [veils]— it requires another manifestor (*vyañjaka*) such as the *baindava*. As it has been said:
In the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Because it does not originate from the root [of the body], the body of the Lord is not of such a nature as ours;
rather, it consists of five mantras, each serving its purpose five times."
"The head and so forth [are formed] from Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jyeṣṭha.
Regarding this, the meditation on the body of the Vidyā was taught by the Gurus:
"Down to the ankles it resembles crystal, with lotus-like hands and feet that are red."
The five faces are white, red, black, golden, and very white, respectively.
A sword, a shield, a bow, arrows, a trident, a skull-cup,
a water-pot, a rosary, as well as the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Holding [the weapons] with ten hands, he is serene with a smiling face;
his large eyes possess the power of vision, action, and will, and he is endowed with the digit of the moon of knowledge.
"With a blue throat, beautiful limbs, and three eyes on each face.

Regarding "blue throat": due to the power of obstruction (*rodha-śakti*), the throat is blue because of the dust (*parāga*) of that obstructive power, which—by virtue of being the substrate of the impurity that causes the concealment of one's own nature—is dark blue.

According to the scriptural statement that "it is endowed with the crescent moon of knowledge," this body of wisdom (vidyādeha) extends from his lotus feet up to the tuft of matted hair, situated at the lower part of the Tatpuruṣa face, which serves as the instrumental cause for the act of concealment (tirobhāva).
The capacity of everything— including the specific weapons held in the hands and the ornaments— is determined. Such is the *vaidavata* nature of the form of Sadāśiva.
Some others, however, maintain that the *atattva* (non-principle) resides within the animal bodies that are joined with arrows produced from the *bindu*.

Both of these positions are untenable according to the manner already described; furthermore, the first position contradicts reason, because since that body is an effect, it would require another agent, and if it were its own creation, [it would be self-contradictory].

Alternatively, if it were created by another, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). In the latter case, since the Supreme Lord is described in the scriptures as being unique and characterized by the partless *liṅga*, the superimposition of an internal consciousness (*cidantarādhyāsa*) upon Him is utterly contradictory. For this very reason, this acquisition of knowledge is *śākta*.
Thus it is well said: "Having meditated in this way upon the Śakti as luminous within the *lakṣman*— that is, within the mobile *liṅga*—
due to its being uniquely worshipped there, [it is so] because it is graced by one's own self."

One should meditate facing exactly toward the south. When this is done, indeed, that which is stated in the scriptures regarding the southern face is accomplished; as it is said in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*:
"Having entered the place, the wise one should take recourse to the Southern Form (*dakṣiṇāmūrti*). In that very same [text]:
During the initiation—
having led him inside that [shrine] of Dakṣiṇāmūrtikara—
one should cause him to cast a flower facing north and bestow upon him a name based on that [spot].
Thus,
in the venerable Parākhyatantra (p. 104):
Facing north, he should cast [the flowers] into the flower-mandala and address [the deity]:
"O Śaṅkara, the Lord of Śivā. Then, having bowed to the Lord, he should take the flowers in his joined palms while facing [the deity], as prescribed in the venerable *Mṛgendra* regarding initiation.
Endowed with faith, he should cause those prostrations to be relinquished through faith.
One should say, "O Great Lords of the limbs, look! while opening one's eyes;
[the reality] is not seen even by the immortals who are devoid of the fitness for the [divine] forms.
Beholding him with eyes full of joy,
one should raise the prostrate disciple and cast him down upon the seat of the syllable Om (praṇava) at the southern form of the Lord.

The commentary on this sūtra is as follows: Having seen him whose eyes are gladdened by the gaze of Śiva, and who is bowing again and again, one should raise him up from the ground and seat the Guru upon the right side of the Lord’s form, seated upon the syllable Om; there, having put on the consecrated garments, he should be seated.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should take [the deity] in the hand and place him upon the right side of the body of the Lord;

then, having offered a bali-oblation at that very spot at the conclusion of the rite, one should say: "O Lord, having led [him] back, what has been heard should be explained to those who seek it, and you should listen to what is to be heard from others."
In the venerable *Sarvajñānottara* it is said:
"One should bring Dakṣiṇāmūrti together with a handful of flowers;
having placed him facing Śiva, one should then scatter the flowers."
In the *Pratiṣṭhāprakaraṇa* of the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "Then, one should [orient] the summit with its peak toward the northeast, which is the region of the head."
Having prepared the auspicious ritual vessel (kumbha) for the fire-oblation (homa) or another [rite], according to the injunctions.

In the *Śrīmadrauravavṛttiviveka*, within the section on the *mudrās*, [the author] explains that "it is a specific state" (*viśiṣṭā sthitiḥ*) in order to dispel the misconception that, because the Supreme Lord is all-pervasive, the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), and withdrawal (*sannirodhana*) are impossible for Him.
The remaining aspect of presence (*sānnidhya*) is the manifestation of being oriented toward [the deity] by way of favoring it.
As stated in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*:
"In this context, invocation (*āvāhana*) is said to be the act of respectfully becoming face-to-face."
In that very same place, in another section:
"Meditating upon the god Sadāśiva, who has five faces and is facing him"; and:
"Then, having sat upon his own seat in the presence of Śambhu."
In the *Śrīmadbrahmaśambhupaddhati*:

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the bed and seat, one should gradually remove the covering cloth from the eyes and cause [the deity] Śambhu, who is present before one's eyes, to descend.
O Sahasrālokeśāna,
one should say, "Release that limb," while offering a flower toward the lotus-face of Śiva.
It is worshipped as the pollen of the supreme lotus of manifest devotion.
"Since you are the leader of the animals, and especially since this sacrifice has been initiated by you, take them into the presence of Śiva."
One should inform Lord Śiva through the vital breaths moving both internally and externally that he has been tested and is capable, having approached for the sake of liberation.
Therefore, taking [the disciple] right there, one of steady intellect should proceed with confidence according to the ancient tradition.

When the body has been visualized, one should perform the installation with the Heart mantra. Then, having meditated again upon that very place on Śiva— who possesses a form free from all limiting adjuncts— as being present before one;
He has whitened the quarters of the sky with the flow of the supreme nectar.
Having lifted up the special water for honor (arghya) and food with the left hand,
one should first present the arghya facing [the deity] with the right hand.
By such statements as these, since the practitioner (sādhaka) is also prescribed to sit facing north,

it is established that the Lord faces southward in the case of the mobile liṅga and in the maṇḍala; this is demonstrated by the cited texts through the repeated application of the rule for the Lord of the Maṇḍala.
Even when the indicative mark is moving, the state of facing south is perceived. Furthermore, on the northeast side of the pavilion, one should place a water-pot facing west.

Because it is stated that [the deity] stands upon all grains, and because the facing westward of the Supreme Lord— who is worshipped for the purpose of protecting the pavilion— is heard of in all the *saṃhitās* and all the *paddhatis*, his presence is established for the sake of protecting those who are to be protected.
Regarding the object of one's own chosen *liṅga*, because it is unique to oneself, its status as Dakṣiṇāmūrti— as the protector of oneself— is most appropriately established; and in the verses cited,
the meaning of the word *mūrti* used in the term "Dakṣiṇāmūrti" is as follows:

In the *Śrīmatsārdhatriṃśatikālottara*, a commentary was composed by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha, which has been determined [as follows]: "Thereafter, for the sake of the disciples, there should be the reception of the form of the Guru.
This is the aphorism (*sūtra*). Its commentary (*vṛtti*) is as follows: "Thus, even after the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)," and so forth.

Of that body— the physical form consisting of the head, face, and so forth— which belongs to the teacher (guru) and preceptor (ācārya), the supreme and inferior excellence for practitioners, who is known as the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold subtle body) that manifests cognition and action, and who has approached [the disciple] by way of being the primordial point (*pūrvabindu*).
"Appropriation" (grahaṇa) means acceptance by way of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā); the meaning is that one should perform it with the syllable *oṃ*.

As it was stated here in this manual (*paddhati*) by the True Gurus: "Having first meditated upon the form according to its divisions, such as the head and so forth, with the *praṇava*, one should then perform the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the *tāra* [syllable *oṃ*] alone. Thus...
In the case of accomplishment facing south, [the visualization involves] the head, face, belly, heart, hands, feet, and other limbs.
The fact that even the names [of the faces] face southward is stated in the illustrious *Catuḥśatikālottara*:
"In the upper face, Mahāsena is remembered; in that [face], the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) is prescribed.
One should cause the oblation to be offered in the Brahma-face, which extends down to the feet. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, for the practitioner seated facing north, at the time of performing the deposition of the thirty-eight kalās upon his own body, and specifically during the deposition of Brahman through the bodily postures,
the face of Tatpuruṣa must necessarily face north; otherwise, [the ritual would be invalid].

The assignment of the limbs (*aṅgabhaṅginyāsa*) is indeed untenable; likewise, for the Supreme Lord as well, when facing south, the assignment of the limbs must be performed while facing south. Furthermore, this applies to the face of Īśāna, which abides as the bestower of grace within the group of five faces (*vaktrapañcaka*).

Because it faces south for the sake of being oriented toward protection (*rakṣā*), even the head and other limbs face southward. Now, one might ask: since Īśāna and Tatpuruṣa are situated [in the north and east], how can it be said that [Aghora] is situated above the Aghora face? True; this refers to the portions (*kalā*) of Tatpuruṣa.

Since those three [faces] exist and Tatpuruṣa is situated on the right, it is not at all logical for Īśāna to be above him. However, some, accepting the scriptural statements found in the *Bṛhatkālottara* and other texts, maintain that the Supreme Lord should be meditated upon as facing exactly eastward.

"In the midst of such statements as, 'One should fashion the five-faced [Lord], endowed with fifteen eyes, the God of gods, Sadāśiva, adorned with the powers beginning with Vāmā' (p. 109), they believe [this]."
The constant duty of the Lord is to look toward the main entrance;
since it has been stated that "one should always remain facing east, or else face west," these statements refer to being oriented toward the eastern door.
Regarding the locations of the installed *liṅgas*,
it is stated in previous scriptural passages such as "named Puruṣa, measured within the heart," and so forth:
"Dakṣa is situated upon the neck, connected to the right shoulder."
This statement has been asserted by some as establishing that a movable liṅga should face the east;
for within the body of this statement, there is the perception that it concerns a movable liṅga.
[However,] it concerns a liṅga installed at the eastern door which is situated to the west.

The statement, "having resorted to some portion of the northeastern direction," and so forth, as well as the statement, "that very [deity] facing westward with the eastern support," refers to the case of a permanent *liṅga*, because of the scriptural injunction regarding its perpetual eastward orientation; the same applies to the *śivakumbha* and other such objects.
In the case of *prāpti*, facing westward is prescribed. Regarding the statement that it consists of a mass of knowledge (*jñāna*) and realization (*vijñāna*),
the heart of the written [mantra] is situated near the right knee and directed toward the southeast.
(110) Since the statement regarding the "vajra-body" has as its object only the eastern door,
there is the perception of facing east (prāṅmukhatva) in all ritual contexts, such as the obligatory and occasional rites; [this is not the case] by facing west (pratyaṅmukhatvena).
Since the rule that the installed *liṅga* and the *śivakumbha* must face east would contradict all the scriptures, this specific statement— "one should stand before the Lord"—
is intended to apply even to a *liṅga* installed with a western entrance.
The state of facing east has been established; however, this is indeed contradictory, and for that very reason, it must also refer specifically to the case of a *liṅga* installed facing east.
Furthermore, even regarding a fixed *liṅga*, the necessity of facing east is observed in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*.
"The most excellent linga faces west; in the absence [of such], it is traditionally held to face east.
Furthermore:
"In the case of a mobile linga, one should worship the deity facing east; for them as well, this applies to the domain of daily rites."
Primarily, one should first observe the main entrance of the desired northeast direction; then,
by the specific strength of the fixed [planetary] positions as prescribed in the scriptures,
those skilled in the composition of ritual acts should ensure that the face of the deity faces westward.

Some, by their own arbitrary reasoning, have concluded that even in the case of a movable liṅga installed like a fixed liṅga at the eastern door, worship through the eastern door is the primary rule; therefore— (p.
Even for them, the insistence on worshipping the eastern door is merely based on hope;
moreover, in the *Kriyāgrantha*, worship of the southern door is prescribed for these [temples] just as it is for those with eastern and western doors.
Therefore, the insistence on the eastern door is indeed contradicted even by their own school regarding these cases.

Since no movement of gender (*calaliṅga*) is observed even in all the words mentioned in every instance, it is understood that in the case of a moving gender (*calaliṅga*), the composition is "well-fashioned according to one's own preference" based on facing the east. Furthermore,
this has been explained by great teachers such as Sadyojyotis and others.
In the illustrious *Raurava*, *Svāyambhuva*, *Mṛgendra*, *Kiraṇa*, *Parākhya*, *Mataṅga*, *Sūkṣma*, *Svāyambhuva*, *Viṃśati*, *Sārdhatriśatika*, *Catuḥśatika*,
*Sarvajñānottara*, *Mohaśūrottara*, and other [scriptures] that have been explained;

In the *Śrīmat-trayodaśaśatika-niśvāsa* and other such scriptures, as well as in the ritual manuals (*paddhati*) composed by the venerable Somaśambhu, Brahmaśambhu, King Bhoja, Vāruṇaśiva, and others, and in their respective commentaries concerning the mobile liṅga (*calaliṅga*).
Because, unlike the various requirements for consecrations (*pratiṣṭhā*), no injunction regarding facing east is observed [in the case of moving lingas],
and because the rules for worship— stated as indicating that one should face east in the case of moving lingas—
are already fulfilled by referring to the case of fixed lingas (*sthiraliṅga*).
Because it has been practiced by distinguished scholars, householders, ascetics, and teachers from Kashmir, Āryāvarta, Gauḍa, and the Deccan,
the worship of the mobile liṅga— which is the embodiment of one’s chosen deity— is performed facing southward alone.

112) Furthermore, something must be performed with the mantra "to the Aghora-heart," because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra; thus, by way of a structural arrangement of the limbs, the heart [is addressed] with the Aghora-Brahman.

Because the Aghora [face] is to be conceptualized as being situated in the southern direction, and because the heart is the primary among the limbs of the body, the limbs such as the head and so forth—both above and below it—must be conceptualized as being precisely to the south. Now, one might object: "But for the sake of the mouth of Tatpuruṣa..."

Because the Tatpuruṣa is situated to the east according to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, why is it not postulated that the [other] faces and so forth are imagined in relation to him? True; however, because there exist four parts (*kalā*) of the Tatpuruṣa, there is also a part of the Tatpuruṣa to the south.

Because of the origin of the Heart and that of the Puruṣa, and because of the origin of those two which are primary, it is logical to conceive of the other limbs as being on the right side in relation to both of them. [Objection: But [what about the mantra] "to Vāmadeva and the Secret"?

Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, it follows from the perspective of that ritual manual (*kalpa*) that the arrangement of other limbs (*aṅga*) would also apply to the north; however,
the facing toward the north is not established by the statement beginning with "the southern and northern faces" (*yāmyakauberavaktra*).
That is not tenable. But is it not the case that the same applies to the Yāmya [mantra] as well?
Now, having worshipped the Great Lords, one should sacrifice to the *sādhya-mantra* for the sake of prosperity;
it must be kept secret at all times and in every way by the practitioner, as will be described hereafter.
Or else, on the southern petal of the lotus, one should place the recipient of the portion (bhāgadheya) in the form of a woman;
[this should be done] in the midst of the light of the Aghora-eye, and nowhere else.

Since the purpose of the Veda is established as the practice of mantra-sādhana in the presence of the face of Aghora, adjacent to the glorious face of Mṛgendra, even those desiring supernatural powers (siddhi) perform the propitiation of mantras to the south; therefore, facing southward is prescribed for those seeking excellence.
For those desiring spiritual success (*siddhi*), facing south is even more effective than merely hearing of it;

this is as stated in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*. There exists an *Upaniṣad*, and there are also the words of the *Purāṇas*; in these, the ten incarnations (*prādurbhāva*) and so forth are heard. Therefore...
"O you who are yellow, protect my right [face] which is directed to the south, facing me as I sit for the sake of protection—that face known as Īśāna—protect it constantly with your mouth.
This means that he, being engaged in bestowing grace during the fivefold rites, should protect [me]. Furthermore:
In the four directions beginning with the east, the northern direction alone is heard of as being characterized by Rudra with great effort;
there is a scriptural authority for this. On the summit of that mountain of sunrise, his own attendants face westward, and in that very direction, the Supreme Lord has been established.
Facing south alone is appropriate. Thus it is stated in the Śaiva Purāṇa:
"Those who are afraid of birth take refuge in this unborn sovereignty of Rudra through their intellect, seeking protection at his southern face."
In the *Mahāstotra* as well:
"Indeed, those [portions] of the Veda which exist in the branches extending from the north to the east..."
One should look at you from behind while you are seated; then, facing toward the south, [the teacher says]:

"I am unborn"—because you have taken refuge in me, I fear death for you who are born. You ought to look at me facing toward the south; such is the purpose. Indeed, there is a mantra for that: "I am unborn. Because you have taken refuge in me, I fear death for you who are born. You ought to look at me facing toward the south; such is the purpose. Indeed, there is a mantra for that.

Thus, by the passage beginning with "Not in front of Śambhu," it is stated that it is not proper to perform worship and so forth while standing in the immediate presence of the Lord. As it has been said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
Having bathed up to the head and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),
facing either north or east, one should perform the Sandhyā worship— beginning with the verse "vedasiddhāñchirāśramī" and so forth—
until the conclusion of the Sandhyā-vandana; then, having meditated upon the Lord, who is sharp, pure, and seated within the [solar] orb.
One should cast [the offering] toward Sadāśiva,
while mentally recollecting Him at the conclusion of the mantra that purifies with water.
The commentary on this sūtra is as follows: having meditated upon Lord Sadāśiva residing in the *bimba*, at the conclusion of the recitation of the mantra...

Meditating upon Him alone with the mind, one should offer a handful of water; having thus performed that divine and complete worship as it has been described, preceded by the offering of *arghya*, and then having recited the mantra and informed Śiva along with His limbs (*sāṅga*), one should commence the subsequent rite.
The commentary on this is as follows: "The worship of the God which is to be described—that [worship] should be performed together with the *arghya* offering at the beginning, in a divine manner.
Having thus prepared it, complete with its constituent parts such as incense, unguents, flowers, and so forth.

Having performed the recitation (japa) of the Śiva-mantra together with its ancillaries (aṅgas) and having offered that to the Blessed One, one should begin the subsequent rite, the Āgneya bath. Thus, by this concise worship,
[the practitioner] has been made to face the Lord.
In the venerable Kiraṇatantra as well:

"Having performed the duties at the junction of the twilight (saṃdhyā), and having formed a heart-añjali, one should fill the añjali with water three times; then, having offered it richly with flowers to the Sun, one should subsequently mutter the Śiva-mantra."
One should recite [the mantra] until a hundred is complete, or according to one's own capacity.
In the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati* as well:
"One should perform the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) for the form of the Sun with the six-limbed [mantra]."
The offering of the recitation (*japanivedana*) is stated by the verse beginning with "śatamūrdham" and so forth.
It is also found in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*:

Having sipped water according to the rule, one should offer the *arghya* with three handfuls of water containing red flowers and other ingredients, using the root mantra "bhānave" (to the Sun), as stated in that very same [text] regarding the worship of the Sun. Then,
having performed the placement of the hands and limbs (*karāṅgavinyāsa*) with those mantras for the heart and so forth, [one should proceed].
Having meditated upon oneself in the form of the sun, one should offer the arghya water.
One should fill [the space] with the color red and a black dot on the forehead;
having worshipped that with the limbs of the Sun and performed the protective veiling (avakuṇṭhana), [one should proceed].
Having sprinkled [the materials] with that water, facing the east, one should worship the Sun.
Thus it is also stated in the *Śrīmat-kriyākāṇḍa-śekhara*:
"The substances [should be purified] with those waters" in the section on worship.
O blameless ones, this is indeed the form of the Supreme Being sporting in another realm;
it is radiant with rays emanating from its own limbs, resembling upward-pointing crystals.
He meditated upon Maheśvara, the God of gods, who has five heads, fifteen eyes, a serene countenance, five faces, and beautiful eyes.
Ten-armed and large-eyed, with a serpent as his sacred thread,
he holds a blue lotus, a sword, a rosary, a bracelet, and displays the gesture of fearlessness.
The trident with the secret [weapon] is mentioned; on the right are five arms:
a citron, a bow, a shield, the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), and a staff with a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
Those which are proclaimed as the five arms of the God of Gods are to be given.
Īśāna is like pure jasmine, while Nara is the color of saffron;
to the south is Aghora, who is terrible like a common man, and Vāmadeva is always in the north.
Sadāśiva has five faces; he resembles the pomegranate flower when fresh and situated in the western direction, yet he has the appearance of a mass of piled-up snow.
One should meditate upon that [deity], the size of a thumb-joint, above the pericarp;
having thus fashioned the body of the mantra, one should then cause the radiant light to enter.

Thus, regarding the worship of the *niṣkala-liṅga*, it has been stated in common with all the *saṃhitās* such as the venerable *Mṛgendra* that the mantra-body (*mantramaya-śarīra*) is to be fashioned by means of the thirty-eight *kalās*. In this very [text]:

In the *Saṃhitā*, within the section on the characteristics of images (*pratimā-lakṣaṇa-prakaraṇa*), regarding the dimensions of the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*) in terms of width and height, it is stated that a five-faced [lion] should be fashioned;
this is indicated by such statements as "endowed with three or five eyes," and so forth.

Since it is not contradicted by the context of the cognition of facing eastward, the rule of facing eastward does not serve as a restrictive factor regarding the object of worship when the sign (liṅga) is mobile; this is because [the rule applies] through the coloring of the consecrated Sadāśiva, just as in the case of the worship colored by the Vidyeśvaras and others.
For practitioners who have attained the world of Sadāśiva, such characteristics are prescribed for the purpose of worship and consecration in order to attain that world.
As it has been said:
"Sadāśiva is the lord of both knowledge and ignorance, preceded by the bound soul (paśu).
O you whose limbs are born from these principles, he is the source of the splendor of the city, enjoyments, and so forth."
Presiding over Sadāśiva, they too are consecrated by the name "Sadāśiva," and thus the true nature of Sadāśiva has been declared. Twenty-four lords of mantras have been described.
"Because of the statement: 'The Āṇava, Śāmbhava, and Śākta [mantras], as well as other millions of mantras,
are indeed the sustainers of the Egg (aṇḍa), with Vīrabhadra at their head,' it is heard that the Supreme Lord and His Power are colored by the coloring of the Lord of the World."

Thus, for those desiring to attain the world of Sadāśiva, the worship of the Supreme Lord through the consecrated object (saṃskārya) colored by the nature of Sadāśiva is appropriate; therefore, because there is no instruction regarding a formless liṅga (niṣkalaliṅga) within the body of such statements as "one should fashion [the liṅga] with five faces," [the liṅga must have form].
Some maintain that because of the scriptural injunction to "construct," it is appropriate to state that this refers specifically to the characteristics of an image.
One should designate as the east that direction in which the door is located.
By such statements as these, both [points] are established: that the liṅga installed by way of the western door faces eastward, and that the Tatpuruṣa form alone is situated above the Heart.
119) This is illogical because it contradicts the treatises; for example, [it would be like] having a face on one's back, positioned directly upward, facing toward the front door.
"And the right and left [hands] on the two sides"—by this statement also it is meant:
"The right [hand] rests upon the neck connected to the right shoulder;
the left [hand] rests upon the neck connected to the left shoulder."
This statement was also spoken for the sake of establishing that it refers specifically to the eastern door.

Regarding the Śiva-kumbha, its constant orientation toward the pavilion (maṇḍapa) is stated in the Vimalāvatī: "In the case of the Mūrti-kumbha used for daily worship, [it faces] eastward; in the case of the [Śiva-]kumbha, [it faces] westward."

It is argued that this contradicts the statement, "One should worship Śambhu; likewise, his Kriyā-śakti is [denoted] by the syllable *vu*. However, according to such statements as, "The water-pot (*kumbha*), situated upon all kinds of grain, [should face] westward," and so forth, because of the circumambulation, [the pot] faces west first and then faces east afterwards.

Because there is no mention of a specific subject and because it would contradict all established ritual manuals (*saṃhitā*), it is improper to interpret this statement as being intended to enjoin facing east; for that very reason, it is more appropriate that the sentence "again, [place] the jar with its face toward the east" means facing the sacrificial pavilion itself.
Since the word *para* has the meaning of "maṇḍapa," *purānanam* means "facing the maṇḍapa";
that is, facing toward the maṇḍapa. For the purpose of protecting the maṇḍapa, there is the worship of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) in the *devaśivakumbha*.
In the maṇḍala, he is the witness of ritual acts; in the water-jar, the protector of the sacrifice;
in the fire, the locus of the oblation; and in the disciple, the liberator from bondage.

According to that statement, in all the ritual bases— the moving liṅga, the maṇḍala, the Śiva-pitcher, and the fire— at the eastern door, one should [worship] all four faces— Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta— in the sequence prescribed in the venerable Parākhya and other scriptures.

Because the colors yellow, black, white, and red are established in Śakra, Yama, Kubera, and Varuṇa respectively, these four [deities] occupy their respective directions. However, in the case of a fixed liṅga, Īśāna faces the door; in the case of a mobile one, he faces the worshipper.

In the case of the Śiva-pitcher (śivakumbha), [the orientation] is toward the pavilion; in the case of the mandala, it is toward the south; in the case of the fire, it is toward the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

Thus, the manner of facing has been illustrated for Sadāśiva’s mantra, for the form that serves as the cause of movement, and regarding mobile liṅgas and the like. This applies to the practitioner (sādhaka) as well.

However, this form is traditionally taught for the sake of the practitioner's ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*); thus, it is to be worshipped according to its appearance, as there is no fixed rule, since the intellect does not attain the form of the actual object.
This is the deposition of the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha-nyāsa*), preceded by an offering of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and performed with the root mantra joined with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).

It should be performed. Regarding the requirement of how the recitation is to be carried out when it says "having uttered the root mantra," [the text states] "uttering the mantra ending with Śiva," meaning "Paraśiva at the end of Unmanā" (p.
Regarding the invocation at the beginning of the discourse, it has been stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu:
"In this [system], the Supreme Lord is the ultimate cause, free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi),
endowed with qualities such as omniscience, and without beginning."
One should honor the partless [deity] within the embodied self through ritual arrangements,
with devotion, while reciting the mantra of the temple-self (*prāsādātmāna*) beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*).

Having filled his joined palms with flowers, he should recite [the mantra] directed toward Śiva, who resides at the forefront of the heart, until he attains the realization of the partless (niṣkala) sphere.
Pervaded by the contemplation of that state, one should meditate upon [the deity] arisen within the drop amidst a shimmering circle of rays, for the purpose of the rite of invocation.
"Therefore, having taken [the deity] with confidence while the firm-minded one stands before him,
he should perform the installation (sthāpana) by means of the heart-mantra upon the body that has been made the locus (lakṣmīkṛta).
Thus it is said.

As it is stated in the *Vimalāvatī*: "Then, having performed the ritual of the six limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with mantras, one should recite [the mantra] up to its dissolution (*layānta*), while abandoning the five causal deities, Brahmā and the others, who reside in the locations beginning with the heart."

While reciting the root mantra, one should perform the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), and absorption (*nirodhana*) upon the heart— which resembles the orb of the setting sun— using their respective mudrās; then, while reciting the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*) ending in *phaṭ*, one should employ the Kālakarṇī mudrā.
Having dispelled the obstacles, displayed the *liṅgamudrā* and the *namaskāramudrā*, and said "Welcome," [he should offer] the vessel for the *nirodhārghya*.

Lifting up the vessel with its lid with the left hand, one should offer the *arghya* facing the five [faces] beginning with Īśāna, which are enriched [with the syllables], using the root mantra ending in *svāhā* and pervaded by the end of the *vidyā*, with the right hand.

"Daily, there is no invocation for the sake of bringing [the deity] into presence, but rather for the sake of requesting permission for worship. Now, one might object: "In this case, the invocation of the Supreme Lord—who, being omnipresent and omniscient, exists as the pervader of all other entities—is not appropriate, for he cannot be brought near by virtue of his omnipresence. [Response: He is not... [omnipresent].

The invocation (*āvāhana*) is the formal request for the Lord’s specific presence for the sake of the recipient [of grace], within His iconic form (*liṅgamūrti*), which— according to the scriptures on installation— is of the nature of pure power of knowledge (*kevalajñānaśakti*) and has been cleared away of its substrate-nature (*ādheyasvarūpa*).
Regarding the Supreme Lord who has established His eternal presence within both the *svayambhu* and *bāṇa* liṅgas:

because of the scriptural injunction that "the ritual for practitioners consists of the rites beginning with worship and ending with the dismissal (*visarga*) due to the necessity of not interrupting the worship," and because it is ordained that worship must be performed every day, this is the method for its commencement.

This one! Indeed, by means of the daily distinction, having uttered the root mantra ending with the *unmanā*, starting from the *dvādaśānta*—consisting of the two *a*s, the *ū*, the *m*, the *bindu*, the half-moon, the *nirodhinī*, the *nāda*, the end of the *nāda*, the *śakti*, the *vyāpinī*, the *samana*, and the *unmanā*— [The text continues: ...this one! Is it not so? Having uttered the root mantra ending with the *unmanā*, starting from the *dvādaśānta*—consisting of the two *a*s, the *ū*, the *m*, the *bindu*, the half-moon, the *nirodhinī*, the *nāda*, the end of the *nāda*, the *śakti*, the *vyāpinī*, the *samana*, and the *unmanā*—[one proceeds].

It is not appropriate to perform the installation by meditating on [the deity] as being contained within a handful of flowers; for the recitation of mantras is not enjoined for the sake of worship itself, but rather because of the necessity of the mantra-recitation.
Because it is to be contemplated as extending from the root (mūla) up to the limit of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta),
[it includes] everything situated within that interval, beginning from the world of Kālāgni— the originator of the body— up to the world of Anāśrita.
Because it is heard in the scripture as the "path of power" (*śaktimārga*) by virtue of being the object of contemplation, it serves as the means for realizing the paths situated within it; thus,
for this pure-souled one who is detached due to the desire for liberation, the Supreme Lord exists as the impeller of that path.

Because it is independent, it has transcended [all else]. Even for the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord, its contemplation must necessarily be performed; for even when that has been so contemplated, there is stability of the intellect through the worship of one's own nature as taught in the scriptures.

Because it is impossible for the Supreme Lord, the ocean of compassion, to act otherwise, by His own word and through the power of the recitation of mantras distinguished by the sequence of creation, the invocation and installation are indeed performed even in a Linga already established previously,
so as to establish the firm conviction that "this is that very same one."
Having considered all this, our Gurus have stated in their manual:

"There is no invocation (āvāhana) when [the deity] is already present, because [invocation] is for the purpose of requesting permission to worship every day. Thus it has also been said by the Teachers:
"[One should worship] the All-knowing, the All-doer, the All-pervading Lord, who consists of consciousness and bliss."
Having meditated upon the supreme Śiva as partless and self-luminous.
Having led the mantra to the abode of Śiva by abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā,
one should then [visualize] that which resides in the middle of the forehead, possessing the radiance of the shimmering moon.

Having meditated upon the supreme Śiva in the form of a drop (bindu), endowed with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and resting within the handful of flowers, one should cause him to enter the image of the deity.
Having invoked Śaṅkara with the Āvāhinī [mudrā], established him with the Sthāpinī,
brought him into proximity with the Sannidhānī, one should cause him to be firmly fixed with the Niṣṭhurā.
Having expelled the obstacles with the *kālakaṇṭhī* mantra ending in *phaṭ*, which destroys misfortune,
one should perform the salutation with the *liṅgamudrā* and, having formed it with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), perform the ritual sprinkling (*avakuṇṭhana*).
Here, "invocation" (āvāhana) is said to be the act of respectfully bringing [the deity] into presence;
the wise have stated that "establishment" (sthāpana) therein is the making [the deity] permanently reside.
The act of prostrating before Jagannātha while declaring, "I am yours," does not obstruct the Lord's presence, even though He is all-pervading.
Up to the limit of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), [the deity] is to be examined as being present;
even though Śambhu is all-pervasive, his "restraint" (nirodha) is proclaimed.
The non-manifestation of Śiva— the seed of bliss, consisting of the bliss of awakening—
to those who are not devotees, that is what constitutes *avakuṇṭhana*.
Then one should assign the limbs to their respective places;
the heart, head, crest, armor, and weapon are the protective limbs.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Heart, Head, Crest, the [Heart-]Seat, the Armor at the center of the breasts, and the Weapon upon the hands,
one should perform the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*) with the Armor-mantra using the mantra for the binding of the directions. Now,
it is indeed stated in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati* that the veiling occurs immediately after the confinement (*sannirodha*).
For example:
having invoked Śaṅkara into the heart with the *āvāhinī* [mudrā], having established him with the *sthāpinī*,
having brought him into proximity with the *sannidhānī*, one should cause him to remain fixed with the *niṣṭhurā*.
"Having expelled the obstacles with the *kālakaṇṭhī* mantra ending in *phaṭ*,
and having performed the *liṅgamudrā* and salutation with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should perform the *avakuṇṭhana*.
Immediately thereafter, having performed the *sakalīkaraṇa* with the six mantras, [one should effect] oneness."
"One should effect the immortalization of the limbs together with the possessor of the limbs.
Thus, the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) for the heart and other parts is stated here as occurring after the *avakuṇṭhana* (concealment); as it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
Having offered the edge of the three mandalas as a seat for the Heart of the Lord,
one should perform the invocation into the form by means of the mantra through the path of its emanation.

Thus the invocation has been described. Then, having performed the placement of the limbs of the fresh fire with the *āvāhana-mudrā*, one should perform the installation with the *sthāpinī* [mudrā] while taking refuge in the peaceful form.
Having prostrated and brought [the object] into proximity, one should restrain it by means of the *ārodha-mudrā*.
This is its function. (p. 126)

One should arrange the limbs upon the body of the Blessed One, first spoken of, according to their respective places starting from the heart. To the question of by which [mantra] the invocation and the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) are to be performed, he says: "Having invoked with the āvāhinī [mantra], one should perform salutation with the namaskāra."
And by means of Śaśikaṇṭhī there is establishment; in cessation, those who have resorted to harshness [are present].
One should effect the removal of obstacles situated above that form by contemplating the identity of the embodied [deity] with the [obstacles], like the rays of the sun.
One should place the [deity] called Liṅga by means of proximity; then one should place the heart and the other [limbs].
Having placed the weapon (astra) with both hands, the state of being "attained through speech" (vāgata) of the Lord is to be performed; thus it is stated in the venerable Mataṅgapārameśvara.
One should cause [the deity] to enter by means of one not yet born; one should settle [the deity] by means of a Guhyaka;
and one should restrain [the deity] by means of the very word of repeated practice from the previous state.
Having established the presence [of the deity] through the Puruṣa mantra itself, one should then assign the limbs:
having placed the Heart in the heart, one should place the Head in the head.
Having placed the *śikhā* [mantra] on the crest-lock (*śikhā*), one should place the armor (*kavaca*) on all the limbs;
having placed the *śivāstra* [mantra] on the two garments, one should offer the water for honor (*arghya*) and so forth to the Lord with the mouth.
Thus it is also stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*:
"One should [visualize] the form with the syllable of Brahman, and the body as consisting of the subtle parts (*kalā*).
One should invoke the deity with the *sadyojāta* [face], establish him with the *guhyaka* [face],
ensure his presence (*sānnidhya*) with the *aghora* face, and perform the offering of water (*arghya*) and other rites with the [same] face.
As it is stated in the *Sūkṣmasvāyambhuva*: "One should worship the Lord with the Īśāna mantra, and then the limbs in their proper order. Furthermore:
"Having made the *añjali* gesture with the *āvāhinī* [mantra], one should effect the confinement [of the deity] with the *aghora* [mantra]."
And having bound Niṣṭhurā once, the limbs of the Lord should indeed be offered.
One should place the *netra* (eye) in the region of the eyes, or else one should assign *gāyatrī* and *sāvitrī*; this is declared for all ritual actions.
"The binding of the directions with the divine weapon-mantra and the veiling with the armor-mantra.
In the *Śrīmad-Brahmaśambhu-paddhati*:
"One should invoke Śiva into the *bindu* [central point] with palms full of flowers."
Resembling the orb of the sun as it descends, its radiance was reflected upon her face.
Then, under the pretext of flowers, one should place them upon her; the *pūrṇā* offering consists of a closed fist with the thumb pressing down on the flowers, with the fingers slightly extended.
The wise practitioner should meditate upon the Saṃsthāpanāñjali mudrā:
a fist with the thumbs raised, well-joined and containing flowers.
By means of this Liṅga-mudrā, the presence of Śambhu occurs through the heart-mantra.
One should form the fist with both hands containing the firm thumbs;
likewise, one should maintain this complete restraint until the dismissal of the Lord.

Having first performed these four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)— namely, invocation (*āvāhana*), stabilization (*sthiti*), presence (*sannidhi*), and [firm] proximity (*sannirodha*)— according to their qualities, one should perform [them] from the west.

"Having performed the *avakuṇṭhana* (sealing) with the limbs beginning with the heart and ending with the weapon— each qualified by the word 'Śiva'— for the sake of dispelling obstacles like those of Indra's enemies," as it is said in the *Vimalāvatī*:

Having offered *kālaṇa* flowers and performed the salutation ending with the *liṅgamudrā*, one should effect the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) by means of the *hṛdaya* and other mantras. As stated by the teachers in the *Yadukta*, which contains twenty-two and a half verses: "The knower of mantras should perform the installation, the water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), as well as the bathing (*snapana*), by means of the very same method of worship."

"One should cause [it] to be performed"—this is the sūtra; its commentary is as follows: because these [terms] are indicative (upalakṣaṇa), there is the invocation (āvāhana), the bringing near (sannidhāna), the confinement (sannirodha), the veiling (avakuṇṭhana), the immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa), and the offering of water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), the guest-offering (arghya), dūrvā grass, flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth. Thus [is it].
In the statement of the root scripture,

it is said that after the four purificatory rites (saṃskāras) of invocation, installation, presence, and confinement, along with the offerings of water (arghya), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantras of the heart, head, crest, armor, and weapon upon their respective [limbs] by means of the ritual applications (vṛtti).
However, according to the venerable Brahmaśambhu, the *avakuṇṭhana* (veiling) is stated to occur immediately after the placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart and other limbs;
whereas in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*, it occurs after the *sakalīkaraṇa*.

The statement regarding *sakalīkaraṇa* (the rite of making [the deity] possessed of all parts) is understood as being established by all scriptures; however, just as there are various scriptural injunctions for different mantras in certain variations of the *saṃhitās*, the rite of *avakuṇṭhana* (veiling) might also optionally occur prior to *sakalīkaraṇa*. Now, with respect to Śiva:
Since there is no scriptural authority for binding the eastern direction prior to the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), how can the binding of the directions be performed as a binding of the directions?
It is said in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*:
Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa with the six mantras,
one should then effect the state of immortality by means of oneness with the half-moon at the tip of the nose.

Thus is the sakalīkaraṇa enjoined. As for the sakalīkaraṇa regarding the self, it is taught immediately after the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi): "Having bathed [the self] with divine nectar, one should perform the sakalīkṛti."
From the heart and so forth, up to the ends of the hands, and upon the fingers beginning with the little finger.
The ritual placement of mantras on the heart and other limbs is considered the act of sakalīkaraṇa;
one should cast [the mantra] in all directions, preceded by the three claps of the hand.
With *coṭikās*, one should protect Śiva’s weapon from obstacles for the sake of protection;
then, having extended the network of *śaktis* below and above, one should lead [the disciple] forward.

Having displayed the Mahāmudrā from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of complete integration) is said to be accompanied by the binding of the directions (*digbandha*). [This is performed] through worship.

By prescribing the sakalīkaraṇa (the ritual of bestowing the limbs), the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) is also explicitly stated by his own mouth, as it is said in the *Antaḥkaraṇanyāsapaṭala* of the *Sārdhatriśatikālottara*:
"Just as in worship, so too in the fire-oblation (*homa*), in meditation, and likewise in the [selection of] location."

"Just as in the body, so one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) in the deity. Thus it is said in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*: "One should always perform the ritual placement of mantras upon oneself, just as one does for Śiva."
Its function is "always" (sada), meaning it also occurs during other rites such as the twilight rituals (*saṃdhyā*) and so forth.
As stated in the *Śrīkaṇṭhaśivapaddhati*:
"Having led [the breath] to the station of the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*), which is radiant like a mass of lightning..."
Having meditated upon Śiva as being present within the handful of flowers, one should invoke him through his form.

Having performed the invocation (āvāhana), installation (sthāpana), presence (sannidhāna), and confinement (nirodhana) with their respective mudrās, and having performed the veiling (avakuṇṭhana) and protection (rakṣaṇa),
one should perform the rite of nectarization (amṛtīkaraṇa) by means of the armor (kavaca) and sword (khaḍga) mudrās.
Thus it was stated by the venerable teacher, the younger brother of the incomparable [Abhinavagupta], in his *Nityapaddhati*:

"Having filled the hollow of one's hands with flowers, and having uttered the root mantra up to the *pluta* vowel by means of the sequence of discarding the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, [one should offer them] from the *dvādaśānta* according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*)."
Having meditated upon [the deity] resembling the autumnal moon, situated between the eyebrows and reached via the path of the *brahmarandhra*,
and having then emerged through the right nostril,
one should invoke the partless (*niṣkala*), self-luminous Śiva into the form [of the flower-offering] by means of the *āvāhinī* [mudrā], and establish him there by means of the *sthāpinī* [mudrā].

Having restrained [the breath] with the *niṣṭhurā* [mudrā], having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs of one's own body, such as the heart and so forth, upon the locations of the heart and so forth; having protected it with the *astra* mantra and enveloped it with the *kavaca* mantra—furthermore, having protected it with the *saṃrakṣya-bha* mantra, one should envelop it with the *kavaca* mantra; then, having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, one should not [proceed] in haste.

Having consecrated with the heart-mantra the armor (*varman*) that protects the sword and is characterized by a slow recitation, and having placed it along with the weapon (*astra*) and the mail (*kaṅkaṭa*) into a purified vessel such as one made of *vaśa* wood, [one should proceed].
Then, one should place the purifiers there upon the presiding deity;
one should apply the Heart, the Armor, and the Weapon mantras over them.
With joyful minds, they should all proceed to the bathing pavilion;
[the deity] upon a lotus-seat marked with a lotus, flanked on both sides by two seats of the syllable Om.
Having placed the Lord of Gods there, one should strike [the vessel] and cover it;
then, touching the base of the liṅga, they should mutter [mantras] as many times as the number of oblations.
"One should perform the *sannidhāna* with the heart-mantra and the sealing (*avakuṇṭhana*) with the armor-mantra"—

through such statements, the sealing of the journey (*yātrāvakuṇṭhana*) is enjoined because it is understood as being inseparable [from the ritual]. In that context, the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) is also necessarily required.

"What more need be said? This is what has been practiced even by the gurus. Therefore, because of the statement, 'Even though there are many scriptures, one should [act] according to one's own gurus,' [the practice follows] from approaching the guru."

From that point onward, everything is carried out solely by the word of the Guru; thus, according to the teacher’s instruction, one should perform the four purificatory rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana), followed by the placement of the heart-mantra and others (hṛdayādinyāsa), and then effect the binding of the directions and the veiling (digbandhana-avakuṇṭhana) with the Astra and Kavaca mantras. Then, with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*—

Facing the ten fingers of his hands, he should display the *dhenumudrā*— which consists of the supreme nectar (*paramāmṛta*) emitted through the openings of the ten channels— and then the *mahāmudrā*. Thereafter, he should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at [the deity's] feet using the special *arghya* water.

One should offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) into the mouths and the respectful offering (*arghya*) upon the heads with the root mantra ending in *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, and *svāhā*. Then, having offered *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) upon the five heads with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

Having consecrated [the deity] with these ten purificatory rites— namely, invocation (āvāhana), installation (sthāpana), presence (sannidhāna), firm presence (sannirodha), unification (sakalīkaraṇa), nectarization (amṛtīkaraṇa), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (arghya), and the offering of flowers ending with the syllable vauṣaṭ— one should subsequently worship according to the method that will be described hereafter.

Having performed the bathing with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and so forth, and having finally consecrated [the deity] with scented water, wiped it with a pure cloth, and offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*),
one should offer camphor, sandalwood, and other substances. In the case of a fixed linga (*sthiraliṅga*), this is preceded by the complete worship of the seat (*āsana*).
One should perform the ceremonial bath (*snapana*). Having worshipped with handfuls of flowers accompanied by the root mantra and the *ātmatattva* and *śivatattva*,
and having offered incense and lamps, as well as water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) and the respectful offering (*arghya*), one should proceed.

Thereafter, one should perform the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*). In that regard, on the northeast petal of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should worship Īśāna starting from the northeast; on the eastern [petal], Tatpuruṣa starting from the east; on the southern petal, Aghora starting from the south; on the northern petal, Vāmadeva starting from the north; and on the western petal—
From Sadyojāta to Sadyojāta again on the petal of Īśāna; from the eyes to the eye on the petal of Agni;
from the heart to the heart again at the tip of the petal of Īśāna; from the heads to the head on the petal of Nairṛti;
from the crest (śikhā) to the crest on the petal of Vāyu; and [from] all the limbs to the armor (kavaca) on the [remaining] petal.

Having invoked the weapons from the hands [of the deities] onto the tips of the petals in the four directions, one should worship them. Regarding these Brahma-aṅgas, the visualization (dhyāna) as described by the Gurus is as follows:
[Īśāna], whose hair is like the stalks of a bowing lotus...
Seated in the *bhoga* posture, with a crown of matted locks marked by the spotless moon;
with two hands joined in the gestures of the trident and fearlessness; single-faced, with a serene countenance; his body as pure as crystal, and possessing three eyes.
Holding a rosary in his right hand and a citron in the other, adorned with all ornaments, and possessing three eyes.

I take refuge in that Person who wears a crown of matted hair and the yellow moon, who possesses the splendor of ten thousand suns, and who is anointed with yellow unguents and clad in yellow garments.

With his left hands holding a skull-topped staff and a severed head, and with others a shield, a noose, a terrifying trident, an axe, a sword, and a hand-drum; and with yet another, a fang placed upon the vessel of Yama;
he has tawny eyebrows, beard, and eyes, with matted locks of deep brownish-yellow hair, and scorpions wound around his ears.
I bow to Aghora, who bears the beautiful crescent moon and whose limbs are adorned by serpents.
Red with unguents, flowers, garments, and eyes; his entire body beautiful and endowed with all ornaments;
having one face, bearing the moon, and possessing three eyes.
I pay homage to the one rich in fresh youth, whose hands grant boons and fearlessness.
I worship the three eyes at the tip of a petal of the Lord of the Lotus—
the reality consisting of vision, action, and will, the abode of my bowing head like a cloud.
I worship the fire-leaf in the heart of Śambhu, which consists of the power of knowledge;
it is the self of all, white or blazing, and possesses three eyes.
O Śiva, the white or smoky [form] situated upon the leaf of Īśa is the most auspicious Śiva;
it is the secret sovereignty consisting of the nature of the Lord of All, blazing with radiant ornaments.
On the southwestern petal, one should place the crest (śikhā), which is red or black; and the Lord’s armor (kavaca), which is independent of Śiva,
of the form to be described,
and is tawny, black, or green, located in the northwest.
I bow to the splendor of the All-pervading Lord, which protects the universe and transcends all things.
I bow to the crest-tip of the Lord, which resembles the sun at the time of universal dissolution, worshipped in the four directions, possessing fangs and a terrifying roar— his very majesty.

I bow to the limbs of Śiva, which hold the boon-granting gesture (*vara-mudrā*), the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*), the spear (*śakti*), and the trident (*śūla*), seated upon lotuses and facing forward;
or alternatively, I bow to his four faces, which likewise display the boon-granting and fearlessness gestures.
And some had single faces, adorned with matted hair and the moon.
Among the limbs, the meditation on the eye begins from the feet up to the heart as red; above that, up to the nose, it is blue; and above that, up to the crown of the head, it is white.
The faces display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and they are adorned with matted hair and the crescent moon. Among the limbs...

One should meditate upon [the deity] holding the tridents of power (śakti-śūla) in his eyes, as described as resting within the three mandalas. Having thus first performed meditation and worshipped the Brahma-aṅgas with their respective mantras ending in *svāhā*, one should offer the arghya; by which [offering], the lotus, trident, and crocodile...
Having given the *sruca* mudrā to the Brāhmaṇa and having given the *namaskāra* mudrā to the limbs,
immediately thereafter, for the sake of attaining the state of being beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Having uttered the *paramāntika*, one should place the temple as before.
And having thus inspired [the disciple] according to rule with the previously taken mudrā,
as stated in the words of Brahmaśambhu:
"Worship performed without the *pavitra* is proclaimed to be *rājasī*."
And worship would be of the nature of darkness (tāmasī) if it were devoid of the process of supreme unification (paramīkaraṇa).
Thus it is said in the *Mohaśūrottara*.

And after the utterance of the blood-mantra (*raktavacana*), the act of supreme unification (*paramīkaraṇa*) must be performed.
