The method for supreme unification is as follows: first, with a handful of flowers in hand, one should recite the root mantra up to the *dvādaśānta* (the twelve-finger space above the head);
then, having worshipped for the sake of filling the power (*śakti*) brought forth for the purpose of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*), one should present the water offering (*arghya*).

One should display the Mahāmudrā. Then, having first performed meditation, one should worship the eight [deities] beginning with Ananta in the second enclosure, the eight beginning with Nandi in the third enclosure, the ten world-protectors beginning with Indra in the fourth enclosure, and the ten weapons beginning with the Vajra in the fifth enclosure.

Having offered the *arghya* with the general *arghya*, one should display the *namaskāra-mudrā*. Here, by way of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), the hundred Rudras themselves are to be worshipped; by way of the weapons such as the *vajra*, [the same applies].
Having thus worshipped the Pāśupata weapon, the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha stated this in his commentary on the Sārdhatriśatikālottara. Their visualization is as follows:
In the second enclosure, in the east, I salute Ananta, who resembles gold, who is subtle, who abides in the fire-quarter, and who possesses a luster equal to fire.
I bow to Śivottama, who resembles the tamāla tree in the southern quarter,
and who stands in the southwest like a six-legged bee, possessing but a single eye.
In the western quarter, one should take refuge in Ekarudra, whose form is as white as a jasmine flower or the moon;
and in the northern portion, one should take refuge in Trimūrti, who resembles the color of frost.
I take refuge in Śrīkaṇṭha, who is red in color and situated in the northern direction,
and in Śikhaṇḍin, who has a white form and resides in the northeast.
With our right hands we hold a sword, an arrow, a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and a lotus; with our left hands we hold a shield, a bow, a water-pot, and tridents.
We bear these along with four-faced deities seated upon lotuses, each endowed with three eyes on every face.
I worship the Lords of Knowledge, whose faces are radiant, who bear matted locks of hair and crescents of the moon.
In the third enclosure, in the east, is a four-armed celestial chariot (vimānaka),
red in color, holding a boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, a trident, and a rosary, and accompanied by a bard.
His left hand is endowed with a skull and a sword,
and his right hand holds a shield and a trident.
I bow to Mahākāla, who has stout limbs, tawny matted hair, and is most formidable, located in the south-eastern quarter.

I worship the attendant named Mṛgīśa, who stands upon the path, possesses limbs born of youth, has a white complexion, resides in the southern quarter, dwells in a celestial chariot, and is three-eyed.
I worship Gaṇeśa in the form of Vāmana, possessing the aforementioned appearance and weapons,
stationed in the direction of the Rākṣasas, three-eyed, with ears like winnowing baskets, and an elephant face.
I salute the bull, who has the form of a bull and rests upon the western quarter—
the white, three-eyed Dharma personified, the vehicle of the Supreme Lord.
Yellow in color, holding in his hands a spear, a skull-necklace, a banner, a lotus, a cock, a sword, and a staff;
or else, in the quarter of Vāyu, he bears a boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, a bow, and an arrow, as well as a chisel;
having six faces and twelve eyes, he is born from fire and the Śara tree, possessing four hands.
With a single face, he holds two śaktis and a cock adorned with gold, silver, and excellent jewels.
I salute her who is mounted upon a lion, adorned, appearing for two days in a mirror,
the goddess situated on the gentle side, possessing two arms and a fair-complexioned form.
Salutations to the one seated in the celestial chariot of Caṇḍeśvara, whose form will be described below;
he is dark-hued and stands within the enclosure of Gaṇeśa, facing the hundred directions of the Lord.
I pay homage to the one of golden complexion, thousand-eyed, holding a thunderbolt in hand, seated upon an elephant,
who follows the eastern direction and resides in the fourth enclosure.
I salute the bearer of oblations, who is mounted upon a ram, blazing with radiant flames,
holding a staff, terrifying, fanged, and possessed of beautiful eyes.
I worship Nirṛti, who stands in his own quarter, mounted upon a corpse, known as Karāla, holding a sword in hand, a night-stalker who is smoke-colored and fierce of gaze.
I bow to Varuṇa, the lord of the western quarter, who holds a noose, whose vehicle is a crocodile, who has a white complexion, and whose feet are my refuge.
With stout limbs, seated upon a deer, holding a goad, he is the ever-moving wind;
dark-bodied with arched eyebrows, he dwells within his own quarter.
And [he saw] Kubera, the lord of the northern quarter, with mace in hand, fair-limbed, seated upon a treasure,
surrounded by women whose feet and hands were short.
I praise Īśāna, who is white, seated upon a bull, three-eyed, clothed in a tiger skin,
bearing a trident, with matted hair, wearing the crescent moon, and established in his own quarter.
Therein, I worship the Lord of the upward direction, who has the previously described form, four faces, and holds a water-pot, a rosary, a goad, and a staff.
Viṣṇu has a conch, discus, mace, and lotus in his hands; he rides upon Garuḍa, is dark-complexioned, has one face, and is adorned with a choice garland.
I worship the beloved lord of the downward direction, who is endowed with splendor, wears yellow garments,
possesses four faces or three faces, and reclines upon a bed of enjoyments.
The Vajra, however, is a person who is stout, with a firm and harsh body, powerful,
with a face and head [at the top], radiant, and located in the first enclosure to the east.
And I take refuge in Śakti, who has the form of a woman, red in color and situated in the south-eastern direction,
bearing a trident upon her head and stationed within a triangle.
And on the right side, one should worship Daṇḍa, who has a black human form,
possesses a head shaped like a staff, and has red eyes.
Homage to the deity of the Nairṛta direction, who has the form of a man, is endowed with a sword and dark radiance,
whose head is adorned with a sword, and who is wrathful with cruel eyes.
Below the navel, it is shaped like a serpent, and above that, it has the form of a man;
I worship the noose in the west, which is endowed with a stiff hood as its head.
I take refuge in the one who has a yellowish luster, a human form, a covered face, and great arms; he stands in the direction of the wind, adorned with a banner atop a raised flagpole.
I bow down to her in the northern direction, who has assumed the form of a maiden, who is yellowish in hue, whose hips are full and fleshy,
and whose head is shaped like a mace.
I perpetually bow to the divine trident in the form of a person, with a dark-complexioned body and the head of a trident,
situated in the direction of Ishana (the northeast).
I praise the divine Viriñci, who has the luster of a conch shell, whose head is marked by a lotus bud, who possesses a human form, whose limbs are white, and whose eyes are auspicious.
I worship [the deity] located in the southwest corner, who has a head marked with a hundred-spoked wheel, possesses a human form, has a dark-blue body, and holds the Mukunda weapon.

Having meditated thus, one should perform worship. Then, having offered incense and a lamp to the Supreme Lord, having offered water for sipping (ācamanīya) and the respectful offering (arghya), and having again offered water for sipping, one should offer the food offering (naivedya), drinking water, betel leaf, mouth-freshener, and so forth, saying "Śiva" over the food offering and other items.
All ritual services (upacāra) should be performed specifically at the face of Īśāna, as it is stated in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Food, edibles, drinks, and the like— whether licked, sucked, or eaten in various ways—
whatever is enjoined by the ritual rule should be offered to the upper face."
"Furthermore, one should offer the oblation consecrated by mantra upon the covering.
Thus it is said in the *Bṛhatkālottara*:
"In the Īśāna [face] is the liberated yogin; in the Tatpuruṣa [face] are the powers such as *aṇimā*."
Likewise, in a terrible situation, there may be expiatory rites and even cruel deeds.
"And for the purpose of subjugation and attraction, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the Vāmadeva [face].
Also, in the venerable *Catuḥśatika*: "O Mahāsena, in that upward-facing [mouth], the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) is prescribed."
One should cause the oblation to be offered upon the back of the hand with the palm facing upward.

In the illustrious *Dvādaśatikālottara*: "O Six-faced One, food that is chewed, eaten, drunk, licked, and sucked— these five kinds should be offered into the upward-facing [aperture] with the heart-mantra."
By such statements as these, the ritual service (upacāra) consisting of food offerings (naivedya) and so forth should be presented to Īśāna alone; indeed,
the cleansing of the teeth with the *varman* mantra should first be performed from the east.
O man, in the east, [place] sacrificial porridge with clarified butter and rice, along with perfumes and other offerings.

[The opponent argues: "By such statements as 'In the east, one should offer the tooth-stick with the Tatpuruṣa [mantra],' the offering of the tooth-stick and other items should be made to Tatpuruṣa and the others. This is not so; for these statements serve the purpose of offering [the items] as auxiliary parts of the vow (*vrata*).
[Furthermore, offerings are to be made] in the south-eastern direction with Rocanā and Agaru, and in the south-western and north-western directions.

Just as in the case of the rule "equal parts of the four" (*catuḥsama*) and so forth, the statement "in the east, the sacrificial porridge with clarified butter" (*sājya-caruka*) is merely a specification of the components of the vow (*vrata-aṅga*); it does not serve as a restrictive rule for that which is being offered as an oblation (*naivedya*). This is because no specific distinction is stated regarding the time of offering the oblation; therefore, the upward-facing [vessel] holds primacy.

And because of the demonstration of its preeminence: "All that was previously spoken by the Lord in the foremost stream [was taught] by Dakṣa through the upward-facing mouth; therefore, one should comprehend that. Since the streams of Tatpuruṣa and the others are the causes for the activity of that [stream], the upward-facing mouth [is established] without any intervening gap.
Furthermore, because it is the cause for the manifestation of the stream of the Siddhānta,
the offerings of food (naivedya) and other services should be presented specifically to the face of Īśāna by those who practice according to the teachings of the Siddhānta scriptures.

Then, having again offered water for rinsing the mouth (ācamanīya) and the respectful offering (arghya), [one should worship] with a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) joined with dūrvā grass and unbroken grains (akṣata).

Reciting the *sarvatattva* mantra up to the end of the dissolution (*layānta*), one should offer that which is eternally pure (*nityapavitra*). Then, having offered the *arghya* with the root mantra once more, the subsequent rite should be performed by the practitioner.

According to the scriptural injunction, after the invocation, the water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamanīya*) and the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*)— which are distinct from the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamana*) that have already been provided—

should be offered only once to Īśāna. Regarding the *marthayāma* [offering], it is established that while reciting the mantra, one should slowly draw out each syllable using the thumb and the index finger.

A wise person should perform the recitation (japa) neither too slowly, nor indistinctly, nor with the sound suppressed, nor too hurriedly; it should not be innumerable, nor with the lips closed, nor confused.

According to this statement, one should resolve that it is the site of manifestation by means of handfuls of flowers held in the left hand; then, having sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra, embraced it with the Hṛdaya-mantra,
and protected it by encircling it with the Kavaca-mantra, one should recite the verse beginning with "guhyātiguhyam."
Having grasped the Rudrākṣa rosary consecrated by the hand of the Supreme Lord with his right hand— using the two Śiva-mantras ending in *svāhā* along with the *udbhava-mudrā* of the particular Śiva—
and having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times in the manner described, [he should worship] the Brahma-mantras and the limbs (*aṅga*).

Having recited the mantra ten times, one should resolve that the place where the flower held in the left hand manifests the recitation is the site of the *japa*; then, having sprinkled it with the *astra-mantra*, embraced it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and protected it by encircling it with the *kavaca-mantra*, one should recite the verse beginning with "guhyātiguhyam."
One should offer [the oblation] as before. This is the meaning of the verse beginning with *guhyātiguhyam*:
"The secret and the ultra-secret" refers to the initial words of address (*mantraṇapada*); that which is secret and that which is ultra-secret are "the secret and the ultra-secret. (p. 144)

In this context, by the word "sound" (*śabda*), those cloth-like forms of the Person (*puruṣākṛti*) established in the scriptures—such as the passage beginning "this twenty-fifth is the Person"—are meant within the synonymy of the secret doctrine. These exist transcending [the previous levels] and are established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*); they are the most secret. By the term "most secret," the principles of the *bindu* and the *bindava* are indicated.

The forms of sound beginning with *nāda* and ending with *vaiparya*, as well as those consisting of *māyā* and its effects (*māyeya*), all the *vidyeśvaras* residing in the respective *tattvas* starting from *kalā* up to *rāga*, and all the *ātman*s are said to be yours. He who is the one to be presided over by all these is the secret beyond secrets; you are that protector, the Self of all.
You alone are the protector; there is no other.
The meaning is this:
O Śiva, the most secret of secrets, the protector of all, please accept the recitation performed by us;
for while you, as the cause, remain present as our guardian, [may there be success] for us through the grace of that recitation.

"Success is attained"—here, by the word "success," the sovereign powers (aiśvaryas) such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth, which reside in their respective stages, are referred to in relation to the practitioner. These are offered by one who has dedicated himself to seeking liberation, and they are performed for the sake of removing obstacles for those seeking liberation. "Whatever [is offered]," and so forth.
Whatever action, whether good or evil, is performed by us—O God, O Śaṅkara, both kinds of such action [belong to one] who stands upon the state of Śiva. (p.

For one who has been joined to the quarters in the state of Śiva, which is the very nature of Śiva, the meaning of the mantra-form *huṃ kṣuṃ* is expressed by the word *kṣapayet* (he should destroy). This mantra’s expression of the meaning "destruction" is due to the first syllable being connected with the *śikhā* (the crest-lock) and the second syllable [being connected with the *kavaca*].

Because it is the primary mantra taught in the venerable *Kiraṇa*, it is indeed prescribed for the purpose of severing the knots and so forth through the application of the *śikhā*. Now, by means of this [mantra], the period following initiation is for the purpose of expiation;
intentional sinful karma and unintentional meritorious karma acquired [in the past] shall be exhausted.

Since expiation (*prāyaścitta*) has been prescribed in both general and specific scriptures for sins committed intentionally, and since intentional action is forbidden for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), such an act would lead to misfortune; this is the meaning. By the phrase "Śiva is the giver," [it is implied that He grants the fruit of action].

The offering of oneself (*ātmanivedana*) is performed by means of this verse. By the first half of it, Śiva, who is the recipient of this self-offering, is described. Śiva is the giver; by the word "Śiva," he is signified as one who is eternally pure, unsurpassed, and endowed with the state of *śivatva*, which consists of the knowledge and action of all objects.

The Supreme Lord is so called. He alone is the giver and the purifier of those possessed of beginningless impurity. Because he is the one from whom the accomplishment [of purification] proceeds, Śiva is the enjoyer and the protector of all. Regarding the term "enjoyer" (*bhoktṛ*), the root *bhuji* is used here in the sense of protection (*pālana*), because it has been stated that in the case of Śiva, it refers specifically to protection.
It proceeds; because it is impossible for Śiva to be stolen away, there is a scriptural authority (śruti) on this point: "Śiva is all this world—consisting of the pure, the impure, and the mixed."
This entire world, in its pure form, is pervaded by Him who abides as both its protector and its purifier;

there exists no other purifier or protector than He. By the second half of the verse, the nature of the agent and the instrument is expressed: having cast off the ordinary state [by thinking] "Śiva conquers," one realizes "I am Śiva."

One should meditate; having become Śiva, one should worship Śiva. According to such statements as "As long as one has not become equal to Him, one is not competent for Nārāyaṇa," one who is purified by the previously mentioned methods such as the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is [qualified] for those things enjoined in the Sarvārthaśāstra.

In all ritual proceedings (*adhikaraṇa*), whether through the purification of one's own actions or the destruction of impurity, he who sacrifices, worships, and honors with the word "I am Śiva" [is the agent]. Here, the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is Śiva, while the self (*ātman*)—which is the object to be given—is said to be his essential nature as delimited by the eightfold primordial matter (*pūrvaṣṭaka*). Of this...
After offering self-surrender with the mantra and performing three circumambulations, one should pay homage to the Lord of the Gods, who has the moon as his crest-jewel and wears a garland of skulls,
and say: "I bow forever to the god Sadāśiva."
I bow to Sadāśiva, the doer of all, the giver of all, the omniscient, the unconquered,
who dwells as the self within all beings.
I bow always to that Sadāśiva, the knower of the worlds, who created all beings, including Brahmā and the other gods and asuras.
I bow always to Sadāśiva, the God who is the boon, the most worthy of choice, the giver of boons, the most excellent, whose vehicle is the best, and who wears the garland of boons.
I bow forever to Sadāśiva, the beloved of Umā and the eternal lover,
whom the high-souled sages devoted to their vows constantly meditate upon.
I bow always to that supreme, subtle Aṅkāra, who is Sadāśiva,
the object of the mind, intellect, ego, the subtle elements, and the senses.
I bow forever to Sadāśiva, the Pradhāna, the Lord of Puruṣa;
[He who is] earth, water, fire, wind, ether, the self, the moon, and the sun.
The mind, the intellect, the ego, and even the supreme primordial nature—
all these follow the will of that which undergoes transformation through existence and non-existence.
To that supreme deity, the highest, the Supreme Self,
who is greater than the great, the possessor of the great illusion and the master of supreme illusion.
Having paid homage to the infinite Self, who is subtler than the subtlest,
to Śarva, the God of gods, together with the lords of knowledge and the lords of ignorance;
I shall proclaim the knowledge of Śiva; listen to it with concentrated minds—[the knowledge] which is expert in the piercing of the knots at Jayā, Antaka, Pṛthu-skanda, and Vandha.
Victory to you, O supreme lord of heroes, who restrained the consumer of cities!
Victory to you, O terrifying one, the shatterer of the heads of all the lords of the gods!
Victory to you, whose power is renowned, O Manmatha, destroyer of the world's stability!
Victory to you, who cause the dissolution of even the expanded body [of Brahmā], and who bear the Kālakūṭa poison!
Victory to you, O Great God, who dispel all distress! Victory to you, who infatuated the wives of the sages in the Dāruvana grove!
Victory to you, terrible with the agitation caused by the great onset of your dance!
Victory to you, who have terrified the gods and asuras with the fury of your fierce form!
O you who have shown yourself to Jayakrūra and Jayendra, O ageless one;
O destroyer of the sacrifice through the vigorous exertion of the hero Jaya!
Victory to you, O wondrous Great Liṅga, who are proud of the power of your manifestation! Victory to you, the fierce white omen that brings down the body of Death!
Victory to you, O Daughter of the Mountain, who delude those desiring a dwelling in all happiness;
victory to you, who remove the darkness of the web of delusion born from the suffering of Upamanyu!
Victory to the one who burns the worlds from the base of the netherworld (pātāla) up to the heavens!
Seated there, resembling crystal, with glorious limbs reaching down to the ankles, he is Brahman endowed with the eight [qualities], his form composed of thirty-six subtle portions (anukalās).
It bears a white canopy in front, a red one at the rear, a golden and beautiful one on the right, and a white one above.
O Lord, he has red hands and feet, with three eyes on each face;
the all-pervading one has his lotus seat bound by the water-moisture of the moon of gnosis upon his crest.
(149) I shall describe [the deity] as being exceedingly serene, endowed with a smile, wearing a crown of matted locks, sixteen years of age, and possessed of the thirty-two major marks.
I salute her who holds in her left hands a shield, a skull-bowl, a water-pot, and the gesture of fearlessness,
as well as a sword, an arrow, and a khaṭvāṅga staff.
With other hands, [he holds] a rosary and a boon-granting gesture.
In his right hands, he holds a snake-noose, a rosary of *nāgakeśara* seeds, a *ḍamaru*, an *utpala* lotus, and a *bījapūra* fruit; and in his left hands,
he is endowed with a *khaṭvāṅga*, a trident, an excellent spear, and the gesture of fearlessness.
We pay homage to the one of beautiful form, who is the essential nature of all.
He is omniscient, the creator of all, the supreme benefactor of all,
free from beginningless bonds, partless, and immutable.
Having thoroughly ripened the impurity of the bound soul (paśu) through the functions known as creation, maintenance, dissolution, and protection,
[the Lord grants] liberation by means of the instrument consisting of initiation, which is like water of compassion.
O Paśupati, by your grace, you release [us] from the three bonds.
O Jayantī, those initiated men who have performed their ablutions with water and ashes, their twilight prayers and prostrations,
and their worship of the Sun, and who have duly accomplished the five purifications—
those men [worship] you here.
O Śiva, you bestow upon them that which is free from obstacles and liberated.
And those here who, desiring the enjoyments arising from the pure worlds, worship you with various modes of sacrifice;
Having offered [the self] to those practitioners of the Supreme Lord,
immediately thereafter, liberation is granted.
Śaiva knowledge, as well as initiation accompanied by consecration, bestows liberation;
it is worshiped by others, and its instruments of worship destroy the disease of the heart.
And when one is established [in this], one obtains devotion and incomparable grace toward devotees.
O ocean of compassion, what is there that would not be easily attained by one who serves Your feet?

Whatever action was previously unperformed that you now prescribe as subsequent to initiation would otherwise be contrary to what has been ordained; all of that is indeed restrained by your mere remembrance [of the tradition].
Let there be no pretext for attaining birth from a womb of flesh-eaters.
Until the fall of my body, may there be for me here the accomplishment of my desired aims, and the destruction of the three [afflictions] through the churning of the heart of Maheśa.
With the destruction of the obstacles caused by the cooperation of the body resulting from past karma (*prārabdhadeha*), there is finally the attainment of supreme liberation without impediment.

O Lord, for those who constantly worship you— whether in the unmanifest known as the manifest, or in the linga which is both manifest and unmanifest, or on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila)— for them there shall certainly be [attainment].
Liberation from the recitations and the sacrificial oblations.
Worshipped by the hosts of all the Ātman-s, beginning with the Vidyeśvaras, through the head, the chest, the pair of hands, the two feet, speech, the stainless gaze, the mind, and the intellect;
To you, the Great One, I bow with devotion through these words of praise.
O ocean of compassion, you who are endowed with infinite distinctions— primarily knowledge, action, and will— through the application of metaphorical designation in the acts of creation and so forth.
I take refuge in the power of the All-pervading Lord, who possesses that power.
That which, abiding in the limbs of the Guide, has the form of a division between the fire and the hand of activity,
cuts through all the bonds of bound souls.
I go for refuge to that primordial Śakti.
p.
152) Some say that you here are the Daughter of the Mountain; others, the lords of sages, consider your speech to be Kamalā.
Some, however, [identify] primordial nature as the illusion of others; some consider the *bindu* to be the primal Lord.
Having performed all these limbs of worship here for Śambhu, which have been brought forth by my power,
may the fruit of my entire worship be free from obstacles.
O Supreme Goddess, fulfill [my desire] and protect me!

Having praised [the deity] with hymns and prostrated, one should perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) either according to the sequence stated in the *Paddhati* or according to the sequence stated in the *Līlāvallī*. However, in the case of an occasional rite (*naimittika*), one should perform it only according to the sequence stated in the *Paddhati*.
Immediately thereafter, having performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should perform the worship of the gateway and the worship of Gaṇapati and the other deities.

"Accept the rites of worship, fire-offerings, and so forth; this is the fruit of merit"— having said this, and having meditated upon [the deity] as endowed with that very form according to the method taught in the *Śrīmatkiraṇa*, preceded by the offering water (*arghyodaka*) with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, and including the offering of food (*naivedya*) and so forth, up to the dedication of the recitation (*japanivedana*).

The ritual action must be performed; and the worship must be performed with the root-mantra and the Brahmā-aṅgas, while the worship of Vidyā in the northeast corner is performed with the eightfold flower offering (aṣṭapuṣpikā).

Having performed [the rites] from the weapon-mantra (astra) to Īśāna, having worshipped with their respective mantras starting from the north, and having offered the arghya-water for the enclosure, one should perform the worship upon the form of Śiva using the mantras of Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna corresponding to the head and the other parts.
One should offer [the water] with the root mantra ending in *svāhā* and preceded by *nirodha*.
As it has been said:
"Then the *arghya* is offered facing away, from Sadyojāta up to Śiva."
"Up to the heart of the weapon [mudrā], with perfumes, incense, and so forth.

Then, having raised the mantras situated in the place of enjoyment by means of the *nārāca* mudrā, and having meditated upon them as arising like lightning, one should contemplate that they have dissolved into the form of Śiva from the eastern direction by means of the *mūrti-mantra*. Then...

Having performed the protective veiling (*rakṣāvakuṇṭha*) and worshipped with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should display the *liṅgamudrā* and the *dhenumudrā*. Immediately thereafter, one should internalize the Guru, Mahālakṣmī, Gaṇapati, and the door-mantras (*dvāramantra*) within oneself. Then, on the pedestal (*pīṭha*) covered by the image (*bera*) in the northeastern direction (*īśānadigbhāga*), [one should proceed].
Or, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), having worshipped Caṇḍeśvara with the primary mantras of the seat-forms and the limbs of Brahmā,
and having offered the special arghya-water, one should worship him with food offerings, incense, and so forth; then,
having presented the recitation (japa) and the remains of the offering (nirmālya), as well as foods to be licked, sucked, and drunk, along with betel leaf.
O you who wear garlands and apply unguents, this offering of withered flowers has been given to you by the command of Śiva.

"Having made this request: 'All this section on ritual action has been performed by me, O Caṇḍa, at your command; whatever was done deficiently or in excess through delusion, may it always be complete for me.'"

Saying "Forgive me," he should offer the *arghya* water, withdraw it with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, and establish it within himself using the heart-mantra. Having dismissed the mantras of the *arghya* locations and performed the purification of the remains (*nirmālya*), he should sprinkle everything with the common *arghya* and then dismiss that as well.

Having washed his hands, feet, and mouth, he should perform the sakalīkaraṇa. Regarding the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), it is stated in the *Vimalāvatī*: "Having meditated on [the goddess] arisen like lightning, one should lead her to dissolution in her own place.
One should cause the mantras residing in the place of dissolution to dissolve by means of the root mantra."
Then one should meditate on the root mantra as it moves toward the point of dissolution within the throbbing bindu.
"When Bindu is dissolved into Deva, and Nāda possesses the power of the cognition of Nāda;

when [the soul] is merged into the supreme Power of Knowledge (jñānaśakti), it abides in the space of the heart (hṛdvyoman). From that, mantra is produced, and by mantra alone it is dissolved. Thus it is said.
One should not employ mantras upon a male person, nor upon another reality, nor upon a [mere] power.
Thus,
the Supreme Goddess, endowed with the aforementioned modes,
[performs] worship according to what is established in both general and specific scriptures.

The unsurpassed means for achieving liberation is that which arises from knowledge, yoga, breath-control, meditative absorption, wisdom, recitation, austerity, and so forth; as it has been stated in the *Śrīmat-somaśambhupaddhati* (p.
Through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), austerity, meditation, retention, cultivation, and recitation,
[one should worship] in one's own form, in the form of the Cow (Gaurī), in a book, in water, and in fire.

"Whether on a painted image, a sacrificial mound, or even a *liṅga*, the worship is most excellent. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*: "The seat, the form, and that which is to be invoked—these three constitute the path of the principles (*tattva*)."
Having understood [the relationship] through the nature of the pervaded and the pervader, one should begin the sacrifice.

Thus, because concentration (*samādhi*) and the other factors are described as being of the nature of worship (*pūjā*), worship holds primacy; for among the limbs of yoga, the primary limb is the most important. This applies even to men who possess knowledge, meditation, union, and concentration.

Furthermore, because an expiation is prescribed for the failure to perform the worship of the Śiva-liṅga, one should perform the worship of Śiva even in the absence of knowledge and other such qualities; this is also because an expiation is prescribed. As it was said by the teacher Avadhūta:
Even those who are self-controlled, though they are deluded and possess defiled intellects, their minds colored by attachment to worldly conventions,
[become pure] by adopting the outward signs prescribed in your teaching.
"They are liberated"—this is your exceedingly great lion's roar.
O Blessed One, the power of your unimpeded teaching is like that of a great wish-fulfilling gem; for,
having obtained initiation bestowed during the period of transition, [one attains this].
Indeed, when knowledge is veiled, it attains the state of being absolute. Thus [it is said].
In the *Śivasaptati*:
"At the very moment [he] was bound with joined palms by [her] whose fingers are dark like the interior of a blue lotus..."
It has the blossoms of the *strambaka* tree within its core;
thus, the very bonds of cyclic existence— the bonds of karma— dissolve.

It has also been stated by Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha in the *Śrīmanmṛgendravṛtti*: "For those whose souls are devoted and whose instruments [of action] possess the form of Śiva, service to the lotus-feet [of the Guru] arises from companionship."
Look up! I am certain that those who desire the immediate creation of new bodies must be destined for liberation.
As it is stated in the venerable *Mohaśūrottara*:
"Gods, asuras, humans, yakṣas, and sages free from envy have attained perfection and eternal liberation through the worship of the *liṅga*."
Thus, by relying upon the *liṅga* endowed with ritual action,
the practitioner who is intent on liberation attains his desired perfection and liberation.
Just as water on a lotus leaf is flickering when stirred by the wind,
even so is the life of those who hold the rank of Śakra, unstable upon this earth.
Youth is unstable, and the wealth of Indra is likewise unstable;
sons, grandsons, and so forth are unstable, comparable to the essence of a plantain tree.
"Therefore, having abandoned the nets of delusion— such as sons, wives, and so forth, as well as friends, companions, and wealth— one should undertake the adoption of the ascetic mark (liṅga)."

In the venerable *Mṛgendra* as well: "Thus, your worship consists of a mere fraction of the splendor that serves as the cause for the manifestation of light existing within the limits of the fire of dissolution."
Let alone its other incomparable fruit that has been described; for now, it is sufficient that it attains the excellence of being "good" (sādhu) through its equality with the word *pad*.
Thus concludes the rule for the daily rites.
The Ritual Procedure for the Fire Sacrifice (Agnikārya)

"For the sake of the fire-ritual (agnikārya)," [referring to] "Īśāna," "the arghya-vessel," and "the ritual materials" (saṃbhārāḥ)— such as the sacrificial pap (caru), clarified butter (ājya), and fuel-sticks (samidh) placed within; and "endowed with three rims (nemi) of four, three, and two finger-breadths in height and width"—
the sequence begins from the top.

The three girdles (mekhalās) should be made with heights of four, three, and two finger-breadths (aṅgulas), respectively, and provided with widths. They should be four finger-breadths long, six finger-breadths wide, and one finger-breadth thick. It should be understood that there are three types of finger-breadths; according to the statement "by the distinction of six barley-corns," the smallest is six barley-corns.
The middle [measure] is seven barley grains; the superior is eight barley grains. Thus, by means of any one of these types of finger-breadths (aṅgula), there are twenty-four.
It becomes a *hasta*. Alternatively,

having made the length nine finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) according to the measurement of the width of the middle joint of the middle finger of the sacrificer’s right hand, twenty-four of those [nine-finger units] should be made into a *hasta*.

The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be made one cubit (hasta) in size, either in consideration of the oblation (āhuti) or according to the measure of a handful (muṣṭi) and so forth. For obligatory rites (nitya), for initiation (dīkṣā), and for other ritual acts, the pit should indeed be made one cubit in measure. In optional rites (kāmya), it should be made according to the specific requirements, such as the distinctions in size and form. This applies to all types of sacrificial pits.

Since it is stated that "the twenty-fourth part of the pit (kuṇḍa), known as an *aṅgula*, having been divided by this [measure], the girdle (mekhalā), the neck (kaṇṭha), and the navel (nābhi) are to be made," one should divide any one of the cubits (hasta) possessing the aforementioned characteristics into twenty-four parts, and the constituent members [of the altar] are to be formed with those *aṅgulas*.
Standing upon the *khābhūmi*, one should perform the visualization of the *śānti*, *vidyā*, *pratiṣṭhā*, and *nivṛtti* kalās within the girdles (*mekhalā*),
and having performed the visualization of the *śāntyatīta* kalā in the space between the girdles, [one should recite]: *oṃ kalāmayāya*.

Having purified [the vessel] with the four purificatory rites (catuḥ-saṃskāra), one should worship it with "Obeisance to the Vessel" (kuṇḍāya namaḥ). Having encircled it with the Armour-mantra (kavaca) and having touched it with the Lotus-gesture (padmāñjali), one should face it toward oneself at the root and the navel.
Here, some also worship Vāgīśvara, just as they worship Vāgīśvarī. This is stated in other Saṃhitās.

Those who practice according to what has been stated should act accordingly; however, regarding that which is not mentioned in the venerable *Mṛgendra*, it should be performed as [prescribed] therein.

In the case of a male, however, at birth, during the *jātakarman*, and likewise during other rites such as the *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, and so forth, five oblations each must be performed. One should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara—known as Brāhmaṇa-Śaṅkara—in the east, west, south, and north respectively. Then...
This is because it has been stated: "In Sureśa, Varuṇa, Preta, and Nakṣatrabhartṛ. By the word *ananta*, Īśvara is meant.
In the passage beginning with "Indra and Agni in Parva and so forth," here too, by way of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), the Śatarudras themselves are to be worshipped.
In the phrase "Ananta and Nairṛta again," by the word *ananta*, Viṣṇu is meant.

"Seven or eight-faced pedestal" means that the face is seven *aṅgulas* and its lower part is eight *aṅgulas*, showing a square shape. By the term "neck" (*galāṅgula*), the intermediate space between the face and the pedestal is denoted as one *aṅgula*. "A lotus-pool six times as wide and deep" means...

By the word *puṣkara*, the primary base is indicated. It should be made six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width. Its excavation should be three finger-breadths deep, and the rim (*mekhalā*) should be half a part;
by the word "part" (*bhāga*), a finger-breadth is meant. Thus, the meaning is that the rim should be made half a finger-breadth thick.
"With the two little fingers [one takes] the essence of the clarified butter" means that the support for the flow of the clarified butter is the size of the little finger.

"For the sake of the altar, [it is] scented with the fragrance of the scriptures" means that since the altar is stated to be eight finger-breadths in measure, the tip of the *kuśa* grass is four finger-breadths.

The *caturaśra* is a specific type of *yava* situated in the lower portion of the *gaṇḍikā-vedi*. The term "seven-finger-widths in circumference" refers to a specific part located at the base of the horn (*śṛṅga*). It is shaped like a water-pot (*kumbha*).

The circumference should be made seven finger-breadths. Regarding the phrase "six-fold," the circumference of the skin-like portion situated between the *khaṭā* and the *upavedī* should be made six finger-breadths. Therein, regarding the two—the *sruk* and *sruva*—one should place [the markings] at their tips, middles, and bases according to the sequence of the Śiva-tattvas.

The ritual placement (nyāsa) should be performed. Regarding the phrase "having extracted from the three channels" (nāḍitrayād dhṛte tu), for the purpose of accomplishing the consecration as nectar (amṛtīkaraṇa) through the *dhenumudrā* upon the clarified butter (*ghṛta*), one should contemplate that [the butter] has entered the three channels, which are the locus and site for the manifestation of one's own power (*śakti*).

"From the southern portion, [the oblations go] to the fires. For the purpose of plucking out the eye of Agni, these three oblations and the fourth, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, should be performed into the mouth [of the fire] by the offering of each individual oblation.
Thus, with the *sadya* and other mantras—specifically reciting the seeds of *sadyojāta* and *vāmadeva* according to the rule "one should join with the left"—[the ritual proceeds].
Alternatively, a conjunction-oblation (*sandhānāhuti*) should be performed using both words ending in the dative case.

In this way, for the others as well, a conjunction-oblation occurs through their mutual union with their respective mantras, ending with the unification of the faces (*vaktraikīkaraṇa*). [This applies to] the words denoting Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna.

Having recited [the mantra] in sequence, one should [sweep] the entire space of the sacrificial pit with a stream of ghee from a *sruva* ladle, starting from the southeast direction of the fire within the pit and reaching the northwest, then again starting from the southwest and reaching the northeast.
Having contemplated [the deity] as the face of Īśāna, one should perform unification.
As it was stated by Somaśambhu:

"By [the oblation] gone from the fire, by that which blows toward the south-western direction, one should effect the unification of the faces with a stream of clarified butter using the *sruva* ladle.
Thus, the statement "the face is praised by the fire" pertains to the domain of optional rites (*kāmya*). In this manner, [it refers] to the face of such a distinguished fire.
And the body of the tongue is also heard of; as it is stated in the venerable *Somaśambhupaddhati*:
"Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, and after that Suprabhā; Atiraktā is the tongue of fire, and Bahurūpā is the seventh."
In the spheres of Rudra, Indra, Vahni, Māṃsāda, Varuṇa, and Anila,
the tongue named Hiraṇyā is designated in heaven according to the sequence of six.
In the center, however, is the Bahurūpā river, flowing toward the south and north;
the Hiraṇyā has the luster of refined gold, while the Kanakā possesses the brilliance of a diamond.
Raktā, Atidāruṇā, Prakhyā, Kṛṣṇā, Anilagocarā, and Hiraṇyā are designated as the six tongues (rasanās) in successive order within the domain of the wind.
In the middle is the Bahurūpā, flowing toward the south and north;
the Hiraṇyā has the luster of molten gold, and the Kanakā has the brilliance of a diamond.
The red [light] is known as exceedingly terrible; the black has the luster of a sapphire;
the "Excellent Radiance" (Suprabhā) has the brilliance of a pearl; and the "Exceedingly Red" is like a ruby.
Like the moonlight of the autumnal moon, she possesses many forms;
she is the foremost in the rites of subjugation and attraction, and in the paralyzing of enemies with hailstones.
(162) Vidya is considered [appropriate] for the red and black rites of killing;
Esham for prosperity; Suprabha for power; and Surakta for the rite of eradication.
She is indeed one, yet multiform, the bestower of the fruits of all desires;
for it is said that she is the "Fire-Tongued" (Agnijihvā) among the desired deities, thus she is indeed the mouth of one's own longing.
In the positions of Rudra, Indra, and the others, the seven tongues are to be contemplated. Daily...
"The consecration [of the fire] should be preceded by the consecration of the *kuraṇḍa*; otherwise, one should offer oblations into the consecrated fire.

Regarding the phrase "one should offer oblations into the consecrated [fire] otherwise": when the oblation is performed in a single *kuṇḍa*, since the worship of Caṇḍa necessarily occurs at the conclusion of the oblation, [the text refers to] the performance of the rites for Caṇḍa and so forth for Śiva.

It is said that worship, fire-offerings (homa), and so forth are not appropriate [in the external fire]. For when the fire is maintained elsewhere, the accomplishment of incense, lamps, and other offerings would become easily available without effort. Therefore, "of the fire in the heart-lotus" means that one should enter the heart-lotus of the fire by means of the connection of the channels and perform worship there.

Regarding the phrase "mṛgī, tila, etc.," one should worship the ashes with the *mṛgamudrā*. Prior to [meeting] a virtuous Śiva-devotee, one should apply the ashes— which have been purified by the *darbha* grass used for the fire-ritual and which manifest the very nature of Śiva— as a support (*ālambana*) upon the forehead and other parts of the body, provided that the necessary materials such as time and place are available.

The worship of Caṇḍa must not be performed at all if the materials, time, and other requirements are incomplete; even when they are complete and the worship is being performed, the ritual seat, the worship of Caṇḍa, and the fire-oblation must be carried out only after completing the worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
As before, having performed the worship of Caṇḍa in the maṇḍala and other locations, one should subsequently perform it in the fire as well;
[one should worship] the Lord named Caṇḍa, the wielder of the discus, within his own domain.
"All [the deities] face toward the east, with the exception of the one in the middle line. Thus,
in the *Śrīmanmohaśūrottara*,
having heard this, one should worship [the deity] facing south in the northeast corner.
Having sipped water repeatedly, [the officiant offers oblations] to Rudra and the others, who reside within the *antarbali* and *bāhyabali*.

Since it is not mentioned that those residing on the path of impurity (*aśuddhādhvan*) are to be worshipped, [one should worship] those residing in the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyātattva*).
One should announce, "The [rite] has been performed," and thus report the fruit of the *homa* according to the previously described method.

The statement "having worshipped the Guru and the Vidyā" was spoken with the intention of addressing cases where there is a lack of space or materials for the preliminary worship and the worship of the Vidyā; now, it is stated that one should perform them with the intention of having all the necessary materials available. Regarding the phrase "the desired private recitation," *īpsitaṃ* means "desired."
The meaning is that one has studied one of the compendia of the Śiva scriptures (*śivaśāstrasamhitā*).
The mention of the term "self-study" (*svādhyāya*) is intended as an elliptical indication of [the stages of] hearing, reflection, and so forth.
Having taken food out from a vessel such as a *viśodhya* or *nāda*, the meaning is that one should offer it to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
As before, having consecrated the boiled rice with the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra, by offering oblations of breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth,

and prior even to the *āpośana* rite, [one offers] to Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya in the southeast, southwest, northwest, northeast, and center corners respectively, ending with *svāhā*, using their respective mantras for the external activity.

164) Because they cause [the practitioner] to act externally, an external offering (*bali*) should be given. Furthermore, as for their causing engagement with the external world, when they manifest, those of one's own caste and those of low caste (*avarṇa*) would beg from him. Thus it has been said:
Regarding conduct, seats, food, drink, and so forth, their mantra is "separate abiding.

Because it is stated "in [the case of] power" (*śaktau*) as "brought by the gods," it is indicated that there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) in failing to perform the midnight rite or the two twilight worships (*sandhyārcana*). However, regarding the failure to perform the three other twilights:
Because of the scriptural mention of transgression [for failing to perform it]. Thus ends the section concerning the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) and so forth.
Now follows the expiation.
Regarding the phrase "due to the violation of the conduct of the *samaya*": by violating the conduct prescribed in the scriptures, one attains the state of a *piśāca*.

Here, within the principle of the *piśāca* (*piśācatattva*), the state of being a *piśāca* situated among the eight classes of divine beings residing in the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*) is meant.
Having attained that state of a *piśāca* and having dwelt there for some time, one subsequently attains liberation (*apavarga*).
Therefore, even one who has not performed the rite wanders for some time as the king of the excellent Piśācas;

then, with a purified soul, he indeed attains equality through entry. This is stated by Sadyojyotis in his verses: "by kinsmen such as fathers and brothers," and it is spoken by the practitioner using refined [Sanskrit] words.
"One should perform the vow"—this [injunction] from the science of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) refers to the practitioner, taking into account the period beginning at sunrise and ending at sunset.

The expiation is now stated: a householder who is not desirous [of higher attainment] and has not taken vows, having incurred an expiation through negligence, should perform the supreme expiation prescribed for an *ācārya* or a *sādhaka*. He alone, however, if he is desirous, should perform double the vow prescribed for a *sādhaka*.

"One who does not desire [the result], being bound by the vow, should perform it"— thus the *vratyācārya* (the teacher of the vow) and the householder teacher (*gṛhasthācārya*) should perform the penance when [the act] was unintentional;
"one who desires it, double that"— this refers to the same person, the student-teacher (*brahmacāryācārya*), in the case of intentional [action].
One who has unintentionally incurred [an offense] should perform double the prescribed penance.
A *putraka*—one initiated for liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣita*)—should perform three-quarters of that;
thus, having intentionally incurred what was stated for a *sādhaka*, he should perform [the penance] reduced by one-third.

One should make it double and then reduce it by one-third. However, a *samayin* should perform half of the expiation prescribed for a *sādhaka*. But if [the transgression] was intentional, he should perform double the expiation for what was intentional. This applies to both a *samayin* and a distinguished *samayin*.

Regarding the matter of expiation (prāyaścitta), however, there is no distinction; because of the absence of purification of the path (adhvaśuddhi), one should recite [the mantra] joined with the *tāla* and *tālei*. Here, *tāla* is two thousand [recitations], and for animals it is eight.

It is not only by means of those who have not been initiated, such as through the reverse order (*pratiloma*) or the single-turn (*ekavarta*), but rather by those who possess merely the [initiated] caste-status (*varṇamātra*). Their...
Since even in the case of contact, a generally lighter penance is heard [in the scriptures], [the phrase] "touched by one looked upon by a *śvapaca* and others" means:

*śvapacas* are *caṇḍālas*; those for whom they are the first (*ādi*) are the *pacas* and so forth; the "looked upon" (*īkṣita*) refers to their looking, and "touched" (*spṛṣṭa*) refers to their touching.

When these [obstacles] arise, one who desires enjoyment and possesses compassion should perform worship and give gifts at night during the full moon and other festival days, such as the fourteenth day, in conjunction with the five weapons in their proper order.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*), the festival days (*parvan*), the solstices (*ayana*), and so forth are included. Here, the word *parvan* denotes time.
For the omission of obligatory rites (*nitya*), the penalty is fourfold; for the omission of a vow (*vrata*), it is likewise fourfold.

By the term "known" (*vedya*), that which has been prescribed for the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days—such as eating only at night (*nakta*) or eating only once a day (*ekabhukta*)—is intended.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), ritual action (*kriyā*) and observance (*niyama*) are included. Recitations, circumambulations, and so forth are performed according to one's own resolve;

one revolves with the *gāyatrī*. Regarding the word "that" (*yat*), one should recite the *gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times. Violation of the command of Maheśa, the Guru, and Caṇḍa constitutes a violation of the command of Maheśa.

Transgressing the knowledge, ritual action, and so forth prescribed in the Śiva-śāstras is a violation because the scripture is heard to be of the nature of consciousness; likewise is the transgression of what has been taught by the Guru and the like, which is the transgression of Caṇḍa’s command.
Regarding contact with *nirmālya*, it is not as if one has directly eaten food that has been touched by someone who was touched [by the *nirmālya*].

Regarding prohibitions such as "one should not look at those of the lowest castes with food remaining from one's own meal," where no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is heard, one should consult the *Prāyaścittasamuccaya* in other manuals. Even there, if [the specific expiation] is not seen, it should be sought in the Smṛtis.
Thus concludes the section on expiatory rites.
Now follows the procedure for the *pavitra* (purification).

"Except for the eighth day of the bright fortnight, [the month] Āṣāḍha"—here, by the word "Āṣāḍha," the zodiac sign of Gemini (Mithuna) is intended. As stated by our supreme venerable [preceptor]: "When the sun is in Gemini on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, it brings about the sleep of Hari; when the sun is in Cancer, [it brings about his awakening], starting from Aries."
In the six zodiac signs,

if there is an intercalary month even in one of them while Hari is asleep, then the purification rite (*pavitrikriyā*) and the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) are prescribed; otherwise, it is stated in the venerable *Mohaśūrottara*.

Thus, regarding the commentary on this verse, it has been determined in the *Siddhāntasamuccaya* that the zodiac sign of Gemini (*mithuna-rāśi*) alone is Āṣāḍha, because it was so stated by the Gurus; furthermore, it is said therein that time is defined because specific rites such as initiation (*dīkṣā*), consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), and the purification thread (*pavitra*) must be performed at particular times. That [time]...
And [time] is twofold: internal and external.
Time is defined as internal by means of the movement of the living soul (jīva), which consists of the breath (prāṇa) and the *haṃsa* within the body; now, the definition of external time begins.
As it is stated in the venerable *Niśvāsakārikā*:
"The muhūrtas, the durations, and the lengths of days and nights.
The seasons, months, fortnights, planets, constellations, and zodiac signs.
All this, O Great Goddess, proceeds from the Sun:
the Aṃśas, the Sandhyās, as well as Rāhu, Ādreka, and Kāṇaka.
And when the sun has risen, all this proceeds;
this, O Supreme Goddess, is declared to be the worldly time.
Is it not heard that the calculation of months and so forth is based on the motion of the moon?
As it has been stated by those who analyze the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*): "A lunar month is desired as ending with the new moon (*darśa*)."
Likewise, [a day] from the movement of the sun through a zodiacal sign is solar; they say that thirty days is called a *sāvana* [day],
and a [lunar] day is from the moon’s movement through a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).

True; nevertheless, just as in the case of internal [astronomy], in the Siddhāntas of the Sun and others, rites such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) are prescribed according to the movement of the months and so forth, without depending on the movement of the wind. Furthermore, the movement of the moon is required for the calculation of intercalary months, lunar days (*tithi*), and so on. As it has been said:

By those skilled in the science of astrology (jyotiṣa), starting with Yugānarta and others, it has been established that the increase and decrease of the two months of intercalation, as well as the intercalary month (adhimāsa) and the solar festivals, do not occur apart from the solar measure; likewise, even the [lunar] days and so forth do not exceed [the solar],
and thus Capricorn and the other signs occur within the solar year.
It is established that the six signs ending with Gemini constitute the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), while those beginning with Cancer constitute the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*).
Furthermore, it is heard in the scriptures that these [signs] beginning with Capricorn are designated by the names of the months starting with Māgha.
As it is stated in the venerable *Niśvāsakārikā*:
"Having begun from the month of Māgha and ending with Āṣāḍha, O auspicious one,
the worldly time known as the supreme *uttarāyaṇa* (northern course) should be understood."
Starting from the month of Śrāvaṇa and ending with Puṣya, but not including the month of Śobhana,
the worldly time known as the supreme Dakṣiṇāyana is to be understood.
In that very place, in another recension:
In whichever zodiac sign the soul is situated when one performs the rites beginning with Māgha, those six signs—
Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces, Aries, Taurus, and Gemini,
with Cancer as the sixth— are proclaimed as the six months.
In Cancer, Leo, Virgo, and also in Libra and Scorpio;
And the bow is indeed declared to have its locus in the Sun on the southern side;

furthermore, we shall demonstrate that in the *Śrīmanmohaśūrottara* and other texts concerning the rules for the time of installation (*pratiṣṭhākālavidhāna*), it is heard everywhere that the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) begins with the month of Māgha.

Even by those proficient in the science of astrology (jyotiṣa): "From the Sun's transit through two zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn, there are six seasons: the cold season (suśiśira), spring, summer, the rainy season, and autumn."
Likewise, that which is called Hemanta is said to be the sixth;
thus it is stated in Vāhaṭa (p. 170).
The six seasons are traditionally reckoned starting from Māgha in pairs, beginning with Māgha;
however, the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) is known to begin with the three seasons starting from Śiśira.
And so forth.
In the treatise of Āyurveda:
"By means of the two months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa..."
In succession, there are the six seasons—Hemanta, Śiśira, Vasanta, Grīṣma, Varṣā, and Sudāruṇa (Śarad)—which are very extensive.

Among them, the three beginning with Śiśira constitute the northern course (*udagayana*) of the Sun; and specifically, the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) consists of Ādāna (the period of withdrawal) and Visarjana (the period of release). And in the *Amarakośa*: "Two by two..."

Two months beginning with Māgha constitute a season (ṛtu); three such seasons make a solstice (ayana). The movement of the sun toward the north and the south constitutes two solstices, which together form a year (vatsara).

Thus it is said. Therefore, it is established that the month beginning the northern transit (uttarāyaṇa), which is the sign of Capricorn (makara), is indeed Māgha. Now, [it may be argued]: "The full moon joined with the Puṣya constellation is Pauṣī; the month in which that occurs is named Pauṣa. Likewise, the others, beginning with Māgha, are determined in this same manner. [The answer follows: The other eleven months are likewise determined by the full moon conjunctions. However, the first month of the year is specifically designated as Māgha because the sun enters Capricorn during that month. Thus, the sequence of months from Māgha onwards is established according to the solar ingress into the zodiacal signs.

Because of this statement from the *Amarakośa*, and because designations such as "Māgha" and so forth are worldly conventions, those months in which the full moon is conjoined with the Puṣya asterism are therefore appropriately designated as "Pauṣa" and so on. True; [this applies] to the lunar months.

This is based on conventional designation (*saṃjñānibandhana*), because the designations for solar months— such as Māgha and so forth— are established in connection with the moon, the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), and the solar months themselves.

This is because, with respect to etymological derivation (*nirvacana*), the [years] in the zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn (*makara*) are caused by the movement of the sun; and if that were not accepted, there would be a contradiction with all the previously cited statements.
For this very reason, even in the *Amarakośa*, it is stated in the earlier verse: "the year of the sun" (*arkasya vatsara*). And therefore:
Since the signs beginning with Capricorn (makara) are designated by names such as Māgha and so forth due to their being solar months— as stated everywhere—
and since the seasons associated with the northern solstice are heard of as beginning with the cool season (śiśira),
[the months] Madhu and Mādhava constitute the spring (vāsantika), and Tapa and Tapasya [constitute the summer].
However, the hearing and seeing of the *śrutis* ending with the group of winter clouds (*śaiśirābhrakula*) occurs in the middle [of the year],

because of the statement by Nikhaṇḍu that "the two months beginning with Caitra are the two months of spring (*madhu*)," and because even for the signs starting with Capricorn (*makara*), the sequence beginning with Māgha is appropriate due to the occurrence of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*).

Because the practice [of naming] is observed on the full moon day conjoined with the Puṣya asterism, and because it is established that words which are proper names (saṃjñā-śabda) are conventional (rūḍhi), and because the names such as Māgha are well-known for the years as well,
in all regions extending as far as Hr̥drama, the [asterisms] beginning with Kṛttikā are indeed associated with the zodiac signs beginning with Libra (tulā).

And because we observe the performance of the *pādya* [observance], it is well said that the month beginning with the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*), when the sun is in the sign of Capricorn (*makara*), is indeed Māgha. (p.
In the Draviḍa country, however, the signs beginning with Capricorn (makara) have the names of Pauṣa and so forth;

for these are established because they are generally observed in conjunction with the full moon that constitutes the connection with the lunar month, and because there is no contradiction in their being proven [by usage]. And thus:

All statements are valid; otherwise, due to mutual contradiction, they would all be non-authoritative. For this very reason, [the Buddha], being omniscient, [is the one who] asserts the authority of all scriptures.
In this regard, the Supreme Lord, relying precisely upon the internal analogy of the calf and the cow,
taught that in the *Śrīmat-Svāyambhuva* and other scriptures, the conjunction of autumn and spring is the best for the performance of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and related rites.
However, even in the general scriptures, it is stated that because those two seasons may not be available, [initiation] is recommended elsewhere as well, even without them, during the rainy season.

In the same way, [mantras] are generally prescribed for specific times; for instance, "one should mutter [the mantra] with which one goes to battle" in the autumn, and so forth—thus has time been defined. Now, the time for the *pavitraka* rite, which is an obligatory constituent part [of the ritual], is recorded.
Furthermore, a threefold rule is indicated regarding its performance. As they say:
During the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha, while Janārdana is indeed asleep, one should certainly perform the Pavitraka rite; regarding the thread, there is this threefold rule.

By the restrictive phrase "and indeed in the triad beginning with Āṣāḍha," it is stated that one prohibits the commencement of the *pavitra* rite after the zodiac sign of Leo, which is designated as the month of Bhādrapada. This is stated in the venerable *Mohaśūrottara*:
One should not perform [the rite] beyond the Bhadra [stage]; otherwise, one becomes a partaker of faults according to the Siddhānta.
Through two hundred thousand recitations of the Aghora mantra, one is indeed purified.
In the venerable *Sahasrakālottara* as well, the introduction states:
"Alternatively, one should perform it according to the rule within three months.
And elsewhere it is also said: "When such time has passed, one should perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*)."
"When Āṣāḍha has arrived, at its end, and again at its end, there is no [other time] for it. Likewise,
during the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha, while Janārdana is asleep,
the planting of seeds is recommended, whether in the bright or the dark fortnight.
One who is afflicted by the increase of diseases and the like, a traveler, or one oppressed by the king—
by whomsoever this has been stated for a period of three months, he should perform the "sūtrarohaṇa" (the rising of the thread).

"When the sun has entered Virgo, one should give ten thousand sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and perform the rite of the sacred thread (pavitraka) for Śambhu; in Libra, however, one should by no means do so.
Likewise: "The three months beginning with Āṣāḍha are prescribed for the offering of the sacred thread."

"In the absence of that [specific time], one should recite ten thousand [mantras] when the sun has entered the sign of Virgo. Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*, it is stated: "If it is the ninth day of the bright fortnight, having prepared an *atasī* flower on the Kṛttikā [nakṣatra].
How is this heard? This is not a rule for the timing of the Pavitrārohaṇa rite during the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha.

This is because of the restrictive scriptural injunction "and indeed," and because the prescription for atonement (*prāyaścitta*) applies to performing it after the month of Bhādrapada; however, [the performance] continues until the conclusion of the *pavitra* vow.
This is the rule. It is stated in that very same work:
"O bird, one should spend the four months of the rainy season according to the observance. And in the venerable *Pauṣkara* it is also said:
"Having fixed upon a location, one should maintain the desired resolve for the four months."
By them, the undertaking of the heart-mantra, the sacred ash, and so forth must be performed as a rule.
"The breaking of the Āṣāḍha [vow] is the path to wisdom; the Guru should avoid it elsewhere.
Also, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"For four months, or three months, or two months, or even one month..."
For half a month, or seven nights, or five nights, or three days, or a single day.
Or rather, it is the conclusion of the ritual action. And it has been stated that the month of Kārttika is indeed the zodiac sign of Libra (Tulā).
In this very month, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, the awakening of Viṣṇu occurs. Thus it is said in the Jyotiḥśāstra: "One should awaken Madhusūdana."

Therefore, the commencement of the *pavitra* rite must certainly not be performed after the month of Bhādrapada. By the restrictive statement "Janārdana is indeed asleep," he prohibits the *pavitra* before Viṣṇu’s sleep.
As it is said in the venerable *Mohaśūrottara*:

"And if Hṛṣīkeśa is asleep, one would otherwise become a partaker of fault. In that same work it is said: "He who should cause the sacred thread (*pavitra*) to be made when Janārdana is not asleep, whether out of delusion or ignorance, is a sinner deluded by sin."
Having fasted for five days and recited [the mantra], one should take away the five weapons;
thus he attains purity, and never otherwise.
It is stated elsewhere as well: "It should not be performed even in Āṣāḍha, while Madhusūdana is asleep. Now, what is said to be the time of Viṣṇu’s sleep?
Generally speaking, it is his conjunction with the light fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha while he is situated in the zodiac sign of Gemini (Mithuna).
Viṣṇu’s sleep occurs on the tenth lunar day of the month of Jyeṣṭha. As it is stated in the venerable *Bṛhatkālottara*:
"The sleep of Viṣṇu, however, takes place in the month of Mithuna on the twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight. And in the science of astrology (*Jyotiḥśāstra*) as well:
"On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, Hari performs his reclining."
And in the *Dakṣiṇasrotas*:
"One should indeed perform the purificatory rite [with the mantra] 'O Couple, you are the sun. Likewise, it was stated by the venerable Jñānaśivācārya in the *Jñānaratnāvalī* as well.

From its own essential nature, Viṣṇu enters into sleep; therefore, during the months beginning with Āṣāḍha, the *pavitra* rite, which constitutes a constant limb [of worship], must be performed—this is the rule. Thus it has been stated regarding the six months and so forth, known by names such as Mādhava and others.

When there is an excess of lunar months (*cāndramasa-karavyāmāsa*) within any one of the zodiacal signs (*rāśi*), then, in that year, [the calculation applies] to that which resides in the two signs of Gemini (*mithuna*) and Cancer (*karkaṭa*).
Because two lunar months bear the name Āṣāḍha, this year becomes one with two Āṣāḍhas. And in that year, Viṣṇu’s sleep occurs in the zodiac sign of Cancer.
As it is stated in the venerable *Mohaśūrottara*:
Where two new moons occur without the transit of the sun [into a zodiacal sign], that is to be known as an intercalary month (adhimāsa); Viṣṇu sleeps during the month of Karkaṭa.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the reading "two years" (*varṣadvayam*),

if one were to accept that it constitutes an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) simply because of its conjunction with two *parva*s, it would follow as a consequence that all months would be intercalary months.

In the view that an intercalary month occurs due to the conjunction with two full-moon days (*paurṇamāsī*), there is an absence of scriptural authority; rather, it occurs solely through the conjunction with two new-moon days (*amāvāsyā*),
because it is an intercalary month within a solar month and because this is corroborated by other scriptural statements.

By the word *parvan*, the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) alone is intended. As it is stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*: "When the sun enters a zodiacal sign after having passed two new moons, that should be known as the intercalary month (*malamāsa*), excluded from all ritual acts."

"When the sun, situated in Gemini, touches two new moons, it is known as 'double Āṣāḍha'; and in Śrāvaṇa, O Acyuta, [it is likewise]. In the *Mādhavādi* and other works, the word "Mādhava" refers to the zodiac sign Aries (*meṣarāśi*), and by the word "Śrāvaṇa," [the sign Cancer is meant].

This is because it has been stated that the occurrence of an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) is possible during the six months beginning with Vaiśākha (Mādhava) when the Cancer zodiacal sign (*karkaṭarāśi*) is intended, and because an intercalary month is impossible in the Libra zodiacal sign (*tulārāśi*) due to the absence of an excess of days.
Thus, by the force of the exception stated for the year joined with an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*),
it is well said that, as a general rule (*utsargataḥ*), Viṣṇu’s sleep occurs in the zodiac sign of Gemini (*mithuna-rāśi*). It is precisely with this intention [that it was stated].

In every case, the injunction is prescribed. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "In the month of Śrāvaṇa and its conclusion, as well as in Nabhasya, having procured the purifying thread (*pavitra*) of Śambhu as it is being described, one should fulfill the annual rite."
Thus it is said;
and also in the *Śrīmanmaya*:
"In the month of Nabhasya and Nabhas, during whichever of the two fortnights—namely, the two bright fortnights—"
"On the fourteenth or the eighth [day], Āṣāḍha is the first month.
Thus it is also stated in the *Śrīmanmohaśūrottara*:
"The son of Āṣāḍha is white, or the son of Śrāvaṇa is black," and so forth.
Also in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*: "It should be performed on the fourteenth and eighth days of both the bright and dark fortnights of Āṣāḍha and the two months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada."

If it is thus, then because the statement "one should not urinate during the Āṣāḍhas" is intended to prohibit the Pavitraka rite from Śrāvaṇa until the month of Āṣāḍha, and because the lying down of Viṣṇu itself serves as the occasion for the Pavitrārohaṇa rites, [the rites should be performed] prior to that sleep.

Because an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed for performing the *pavitrārohaṇa* after the month of Bhādrapada, whereas no such expiation is prescribed if it is performed during that [lunar] fortnight; for this very reason:
In the *Śrīmanmṛgendra*, the term *tadupānta* has been explained by the commentator as follows:

that time whose proximity (*upānta*) is the month of Śrāvaṇa is called *tadupāntakāla*; this refers to the full moon day of Āṣāḍha and the fourteenth day [of the dark fortnight], because the end of that [month] of Āṣāḍha occurs subsequent to the full moon day.
The meaning is that because of its proximity, Śrāvaṇa constitutes its "border" (upānta). For this very reason, it is stated in the Vimalāvatī:
"At the beginning of Āṣāḍha, the superior, middling, or inferior [observance] should be performed for two fortnights while Acyuta is asleep."

In the *Kāmyapaddhati*, it is stated that [the rite] should be performed every year by the preceptor and others with the resolve, "May Brahmaśambhu [be attained]"; and that it may be done in the month of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, or Bhādrapada.
And in the *Bhojapaddhati*:
"There too, in any one of the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, or Bhādrapada, during either the bright or the dark fortnight. It is also stated elsewhere:
During the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha, while Janārdana is indeed asleep,
the laying of the foundation lines (sūtra) is recommended, whether in the bright or the dark fortnight.
Thus [it is asked]: if this is so, since there is no conjunction with the *āṣāḍhā* nakṣatra for this full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), how does it receive the name "Āṣāḍha"?
In expressions such as "on the twelfth day of Kārttika," since the word *āṣāḍhī*—
meaning "belonging to the month of Āṣāḍha"— is established by etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*),
and because it is possible for the moon to be in conjunction with the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) of Āṣāḍha even when it is in the zodiac sign of Gemini (*mithuna*), there is no contradiction.

Some maintain that the full moon joined with the month of Āṣāḍha occurs when the moon is situated in the zodiac sign of Cancer (Karkaṭaka), and that it is by this very statement that the fourteenth day preceding it is called the "first day of Āṣāḍha" (Āṣāḍhādicādimanī). That is incorrect; for according to this view, since the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha would be established, the month of Bhādrapada would necessarily correspond to the zodiac sign of Leo (Siṃha) alone.

Since it has been established that there is a scriptural mention of a fault regarding the performance of the *pavitraka* rite when the moon is in the sign of Virgo (*kanyārāśi*), and because an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed for this, it follows that even here, during the three months [of the rainy season] including the intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*),
the *pavitrārohaṇa* must not be performed. As it is stated in the *Śrīmanmohaśūrottara*:

O Śatakratu, one who desires his own welfare should not perform the installation of [deities] such as initiation (dīkṣā), nor the offering of the sacred thread (pavitra) and so forth, during an intercalary month.
Thus it is said; and elsewhere also it is stated:
"Excluding the intercalary month (malimluca), the ritual procedure is prescribed for the double Āṣāḍha."
"But that month which is *malimluca* is censured for all ritual acts.

Therefore, in a year devoid of an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*), one should [perform the rite] on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight associated with the zodiac sign of Gemini (*mithuna-rāśi*), extending up to the zodiac sign of Leo (*siṃha-rāśi*).
The Pavitrōtsava should be commenced [at the beginning of the month]. However, if there is an intercalary month (adhikamāsa),
it should be commenced on the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) associated with the zodiac sign of Cancer (karkaṭaka).

Even there, during an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*), the commencement [of the rite] is not to be performed. If the prescribed time has elapsed, the commencement of the *pavitrotsava* must be carried out after first performing the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) when the moon is in the sign of Virgo (*kanyārāśi*). However, it is established that in the sign of Libra (*tulā*), the rite must not be performed even by one who has performed the expiation. [This concerns] the *pavitra*.

The word "evam" (thus) is used for emphasis; it shows that this [practice] is not necessarily mandatory, nor does it indicate an expiation for its non-performance. Likewise, in the venerable *Mohaśūrottara*, after introducing the count of two hundred thousand recitations, it is said:
"Or even from the knowledge of the deities, that which is performed during the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha is indeed to be accepted;
thus the penance has been prescribed, O Purandara.
Thus it is stated in the venerable *Ṣaṭsahasrasaṃhitā* (Kālottara).

"O Purandara, if the *pavitrārohaṇa* is performed during the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha, that [penance] must indeed be accepted; such is the prescribed expiation. Thus, there is a hundred thousand repetitions of the Aghora mantra.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Somaśambhupaddhati*: 'One who is pure [should perform] the *adrāya* [rite]'."

"Having performed the *pavitraka* rite for the deities during the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha, and having recited the Aghora mantra two hundred thousand times, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
Therefore, at a later time, the offering of the *pavitra* must necessarily be performed by the preceptor and others. Thus it is said:
And in the venerable Mṛgendra-tantra (p.
"Thus is this supreme secret, the most excellent among all observances."
A person should overcome all obstacles by relying on the signs of the task at hand.
By those dwelling in forests or caves who are intent on the worship of Rudra,
as well as by householders, teachers, and others, who seek the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Since the attainment of all fruits occurs when [the ritual] is performed even if it is incomplete, this should not be performed by anyone at all, as it is very difficult to master.
