In the venerable *Kiraṇatantra* it is also stated: "Thus the *pavitraka* should be made by men who are endowed with the conduct of Śiva.
Regarding the phrase "arising from cotton and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes silk cloth, bark, and other materials.

As it is stated in the Śrīmanmaya: "The thread— whether made of linen, cotton, or muñja grass, in the absence of these— should be praised as being unfrayed, even, and smooth, [woven] by a brahmin girl."
Also in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*: "A thread produced from silk, bark, lotus fiber, linen, darbha grass, hemp, muñja grass, and so forth, is recommended for the *pavitra*."
Regarding "bindubāṇam": by the word *bindu*, a single place is indicated; by the word *bāṇa*, which refers to ten places, the number fifty is indicated. Regarding "nāgacandrakam":
by the word *nāga*, which refers to a single place, the number eight is indicated. Therefore...
By the term *nāgacandra* (elephant-moon), the number eighteen is expressed.
Therefore, starting from fifty and decreasing by four at each yoke (*yuga*), there are four reductions.

In the nine [types of] *liṅgas* beginning with the largest (*jyeṣṭha*), knots should be made. In the largest of the large (*jyeṣṭhajyeṣṭha*) *liṅga*, which is nine cubits in height, there are fifty knots. In the medium of the large (*jyeṣṭhamadhya*) *liṅga*, which is eight cubits in height, there are six knots. In the smallest of the large (*jyeṣṭhādhamā*) *liṅga*, which is seven cubits in height, there are forty-two knots.

In a liṅga of six cubits of the middle-superior type, there are thirty-eight knots; in a liṅga of five cubits of the middle-middle type, there are thirty-four knots; in a liṅga of four cubits of the middle-inferior type, there are thirty knots;
and in a liṅga of three cubits of the inferior-superior type, there are twenty-six knots.
Regarding the knots (*granthi*): in a *liṅga* of two cubits of the lowest-middle type, there are twenty-two knots;

in a *liṅga* of one cubit of the lowest-lowest type, there are eighteen knots. Thus, the knots should be made with equal intervals. [This is established] by the passage beginning with "The *praṇava*, the moon, fire," and so forth.
In that regard, those [deities] have been mentioned; the deities of the knots (*granthi*) are also stated in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*:
"O Hero, [the first is] Prakṛti, the second Pauruṣī, and the fourth is Aparājitā."
Jayā is the fifth, Vijayā the sixth, then Ajitā and Sadāśivā.

Then the tenth, Sarvatomukhī, is declared as Manonmanī. "Anointed with all medicinal herbs" refers to the characteristics of the *sarvauṣadhi* (all-herb) mixture. Thus it is stated in the *Śrīmanmohaśūrottara* (p.

"Murā, māṃsī, vacā, kuṣṭha, śaileya, the two types of rajanī, cavya, and mustā—these are remembered as the group of all medicinal herbs. Thus [it is said]. Then, regarding the limbs, even by Brahmā the characteristics of the limbs were stated: "ghanāhṛta" [and so forth], in the context of being covered by armor (kavaca).

Regarding the statement "the offerings made during the *saṃpāta* are protected by the mantras," the *saṃpāta* should be performed just once with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), as previously described.

As for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other items that are prohibited by such statements as "there is no destruction [of the *pañcagavya*]," these *pañcagavya* and other substances must be employed at the conclusion of the offering of the purifiers (*pavitra*).
"Having prepared the sacrificial porridge (caru) according to the rules"— this means that at the time of cooking the caru on the day the purificatory rite (pavitra) is performed,
one should take it out and cook the caru with the Śiva-fire (śivāgni) preserved beforehand in another pit, prior to the invocation of Śiva into the fire,
because that fire is already consecrated by Śiva’s contemplation. Alternatively, [one may proceed as follows]...

The commentary on this aphorism is: "By you, who are Time itself, in the manner described by Līlāvatī—whether through a Sanskrit [form] or by means of another [method]—that which was done, though difficult, was seen in its entirety, yet it was abandoned, not observed, and not performed.
O Lord, that which was done by you, who abide within me and possess a manifold nature as Time, was indeed arduous;
it was fully perceived, yet it was relinquished, not scrutinized, and not carried out.

Whether it was done by disregarding one's own heart or one's own pleasure, whether it was done secretly or with stinginess regarding wealth, or even if not done out of a desire for preservation— that which was previously afflicted or unafflicted, and even that which was conditioned— has now been made pure by what has been performed through your will.
In the passage "Self-knowledge through the auspicious principles," there is the utterance of the root mantra; [it begins] with "ātmatattve" and ends with "pratyante palite pa...
a ni neti" (p.
According to the words of the illustrious Somaśambhu, at the time of the first offering of the purifying thread (*pavitra*),
within the *ātmatattva*— which is of the nature of the transformation of the *bindu*, protected by Brahmā, and pervading as far as the end of the *prakṛtitattva*—
there is the *rudra-vācaka* (the designator of Rudra), which manifests at the palate and pervades as far as the end of the *māyātattva*.
Following the utterance of the root [mantra] of the letter *ma*, during the bestowal of the purifying [initiation],

at the time of the transformation of the *bindu*, within the *vidyātattva*— which is protected by Viṣṇu as its cause and pervades up to the end of the pure principles (*śuddhatattva*)— there is the utterance of the root mantra; [one perceives] Īśvara, the pervader of that [tattva], between the eyebrows.
The effect is at the end of the Bindu, which is manifest and denotes Īśvara;

at the time of the third bestowal of the sacred thread (pavitraka), [it is] at the end of the Brahma-randhra, pervading up to the end of the Śiva-tattva, which is the form of the Bindu as the Prathamara.
The utterance of the end of the *nāda*— which is manifest and accompanied by the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and the stopper (*nirodhin*)— should be performed. At the time of the descent of the Gaṅgā,
[it is performed] below the pervasive one among all the principles (*tattva*), which are protected by the five causes beginning with Brahmā.
Beginning from Kuṇḍalinī, the recitation of the mantra— which denotes the partless (niṣkala) reality starting from the letter *ha* up to *unmanā*— must be performed from this fourfold purity;
thus, whether for four months, three months, one day, three days, two days, or even for a long period.
Since it has been stated by the venerable Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha in his commentary on the *Śrīmṛgendra*, [the ritual] must be performed;
thus, the commentary reaches its conclusion with the action, at whatever time that action [is completed].
It is completed in two days, four days, or six days;

this is the distinction from [the rites lasting] five nights, seven nights, or seven days. One should offer the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścittāhuti*) with the *mūla*, *aghora*, and *asit* mantras. At the conclusion of the vow, having performed the ritual up to the end of the expiatory homa:

Just as in the daily worship, one should offer the *pavitra* with special *arghya* water while reciting the root mantra, saying: "O Lord, let there be no bondage for me. Having thus made this request, one should dismiss [the deity].
One should make the formal announcement beginning with: "Whatever has been done during the year... and so forth.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the purifier (pavitra).

Now, initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the purification of one who is impure; for the self is impure due to its state as a bound soul (*paśu*), by virtue of its connection with the fetters (*pāśa*) such as the intercalary month (*malamāsa*).

Initiation (*dīkṣā*) is that which consists of the removal of impurity and the bestowal of one's own nature as pure luminosity upon this [soul] which has been purified by the digging prescribed in the scriptures. As it is said in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "That which is desired as the two syllables and two meanings for the sake of liberation through the perfection of the cause is given (*dīyate*)."
The latent impressions of karma are destroyed through the presence of gnosis.
And through the application of giving and austerity, purification by initiation is attained by one who has disciplined the self.

And so it is said; likewise in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "Now, initiation (*dīkṣā*), which issues from the mouth of the Supreme Lord as the means for accomplishing the desired goal, is described in brief; because its purpose is twofold, it is of two kinds."

In the statement "the true nature of knowledge is given," the manifestation of one's own knowledge and action—which are [otherwise] obscured by impurity (mala) and the state of being bound (siddhi)—is precisely what is meant for the self who has been designated as the recipient of the initiation that bestows knowledge. As it is said in the venerable *Mataṅgaparameśvara*: "Now, for the sake of removing the series of steps of bondage for the individual soul..."
"He eats for the sake of manifestation and for the sake of enjoyment," as stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
"Now, for the sake of liberation from the bonds of karma known as the impurity of the self and māyā,
and for the sake of manifesting the state of Śiva, the knowledge of Śiva proceeds."

"A Brahmin born in a holy land (*puṇyadeśa*). Here, by the term "holy land," a region is meant that is fully endowed with the purity prescribed in all the scriptures, such as the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. Now, one might object: is it not simply the exclusion of lands beginning with the letter *ka* that constitutes the "holy land"? For it is said: [text follows]
Smṛti: "The Sindhus, Sauvīras, Saurāṣṭras, as well as those dwelling in the border regions,
the Koṅkas, Vaṅgas, and Kaliṅgas— having gone [to them], one deserves the purificatory rite."

The mention of Krauñcī, Kautsa, Kāśmīra, and so forth is not for the purpose of prohibition; for it is stated in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts that "O subduer of enemies, the region of Kāśmīra is meritorious, being among all sacred fords (*tīrtha*). (p. 187)

This is because regions such as Kaśmīra are renowned for their great merit (*mahāpuṇyatva*). A region endowed with an abundance of conduct prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* is indeed meritorious; furthermore, even the statement that regions beginning with the letter 'Ka' are impure is prohibited by the *Smṛti*.

Regions such as Koṅkaṇa and Kaliṅga are [considered] territories (*viṣaya*). Therefore, this verse—which prohibits [initiation] in regions such as Kārā—must be observed with the utmost respect by those who abide by the scriptures of the Siddhānta, because it establishes a distinction between the three [types of] bathing. [This applies to one who is] a devotee of Śiva.
The ripening of the impurities is known through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), which is characterized by an excellence of devotion to Śiva. As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"For those embodied beings whose power [is directed] toward the cessation of bondage, their indicative sign is a longing for that [liberation]."
Aversion toward liberation arises in those who remain [in worldly life], while devotion toward the devotees of Śiva and faith in the prescribed rites flourish in them.

Thus, this refers to one endowed with the conduct of the good (sadācāra) as defined by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* according to their respective caste (*varṇa*) and stage of life (*āśrama*); there is no qualification here for those devoid of such appearance. As it is stated in the venerable *Raurava*:
In a Brāhmaṇa endowed with vows, in a Kṣatriya who has mastered the Vedas,
in a Vaiśya engaged in his duties, and in a Śūdra devoted to service.
"The Guru should perform the initiation. This has also been stated by the commentators, the venerable Sadyojyotiḥ: "Only those who possess the qualification for the Vedas are eligible here.

Regarding those who are entitled [to Vedic study], since it has been stated that the entitlement consists of "service by the Śūdra for the other castes," even he (the Śūdra) is indeed entitled to the Vedas. This is also stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and likewise women,
as well as the blind, the mute, and the deaf, are eligible for initiation when prompted by their spiritual capacity.
Thus it is said;
and also in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"And those practitioners (*sādhaka*) in the Tantra who are to be initiated, whose minds are dedicated to Śiva."
Śūdras who are devoted to the company of the virtuous and who turn their backs on the company of the wicked.
They are devoted to service, tranquil, and praised as being at the proper times;
they are patient, always attached to their guru with their whole being.

Externally, these noble women are highly accomplished and protectors of their own duties; internally, having discerned the movements of the inner organ (the mind), they are touched by the hands of Śiva and Śakti, humble, and lovely to behold.
Those who are free from anger, not fickle, full of faith, and have conquered their senses—such people are always to be favored; whereas the cruel who merely observe their own conduct [are not].
Thus it is said;
and also in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*: "Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, Śūdras, and eunuchs..."
At the time of initiation, one should not engage in critical inquiry; at the time of realization, one should investigate.

In this [passage], by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the *anuloma* castes such as the Ambaṣṭhas and others are intended. But what about the *pratiloma* castes such as the Kaivartas? As it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
Those born here in the natural order who are indeed joined with the twice-born—
for them, one should perform the purification of the six paths and so forth, as is appropriate for their mother’s lineage.

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might ask: does this initiation, as described by Mānava and others, effect a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the body, or of the genus (*jāti*), or perhaps of the self (*ātman*)? It is of the self alone. We state this accordingly in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*:
That formative force (*saṃskāra*) which, through auspicious Śiva-consciousness, is ignited by consciousness within the body—
without that [consciousness], there is no such presiding over the birth resulting from that formative force.
In one [reality], the refinement of all castes becomes refined;
that which is without support cannot be refined, whereas that which has a support is presided over by consciousness.
"The other [the soul] is that which is to be refined; therefore, it is he who is declared to be the enjoyer of the fruit.
Also in the venerable *Raurava*:
"There is no refinement of the body, nor of its conjunctions or separations."
Nor is it established by way of arising and destruction, nor even by way of birth.
"Even for the conscious, pure knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), the embodied one, who is the knower, the self, and the agent— that [purification] is desired as a refinement (*saṃskāra*).
Thus, because it has been stated that the self, as qualified by the body, is the object to be refined—

The sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) prescribed for embodied beings such as Brāhmaṇas and others applies only to them as those to be consecrated, and not to others, namely those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*).

Because it has been stated that [the state of] being unfit for social interaction arises from physical contact; and because "the rainy season" (*varṣā*) is defined as being without the months of Pauṣa and Caitra—the word *pauṣa* refers to the zodiac sign Sagittarius (*dhanūrāśi*), and the word *caitra* refers to the zodiac sign Pisces (*mīnarāśi*). Thus, it has been established previously in the section on the purification rite (*pavitravidhi*) according to how it appropriately applies to the location.

"The ground following the colors" refers to the characteristics of the site as described by the venerable Brahmaśambhu in the passage beginning with "the kulācala mountains and so forth"; the characteristics of the ground following the colors will be explained further below. Regarding the phrase "one's own place on the left," the word *savya* denotes the southern part of the altar (*vedī*).

In the context of "in *kalā* there are *rāga* and *vidyā*," the term "the Person" (*pumān*) refers to the male principle (*puṃstva*). In that same region, together with the *śakti*, the *bindu*—which is the transformation of what is to be presided over by Īśvara and the others—is called the *īśvaratattva*, the *sadāśivatattva*, and the *śivatattva*. Having presided over these, [there are] Īśvara and the others; their transformation...
Because there is no possibility of dissolution due to its non-transformative nature, [it is characterized] by the "arising of qualities through concentrations" (*dhāraṇā*);
in this context, by the word *dhāraṇā*, the *kalās* such as *nivṛtti* and the rest are meant. This was stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu:

The meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) here consist of the very digits (*kalā*), namely those of Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, and the Navel, which are placed upon the object of purification and colored by it.
The definition of *udghāta* (the upward stroke) is stated in the venerable *Catuḥśatikā*:
"There are five *udghātas*, four, three, two, and even one.
This is the commentary on this aphorism: preceded by inhalation (*pūraka*) and retention (*kumbhaka*), the *udghāta* of the breath occurs through the function of sound (*nāda*).

*Udghāta* is the impulsion [of the breath] as far as the *dvādaśānta*. The *guṇas* are the elemental qualities known as smell, taste, form, touch, and sound. Through *prāṇāyāmas* corresponding to the qualities of *prāṇāyāma*, such is the process for each individual *prāṇāyāma*.

The removal of [the notion of] qualities (*guṇa*) has been accomplished. Because it is stated that the Supreme Lord— who is characterized by omniscience and omnipotence— is "above" the moon-faced [nature], and because it is impossible for Him to be the creator of all without an instrument, [the term *nāmantām*] functions as the designator of Power (*śakti*), which exists as the instrument of action.
The thirty-eightfold division of the Brahmās— such as Īśāna, Sarvavidyā, and the rest— as taught in the venerable Svāyambhuva and other scriptures,
is now described; these are designated by such phrases as "Śānti in the east," and so forth.
The powers of pacification (*śānti*) and so forth are not the *bindu*-kalās; rather, they are the Śiva-powers (*śiva-śaktis*) that preside over the kalās. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"That by which [the Lord] causes beings to cease [from worldly activity] is his power called Nivṛtti."
"Nivṛtti" is its locus; therein even Īśa is possessed of cessation.
And so on. Likewise, there is also a scriptural passage on this point:
"Therefore, his power alone [is the cause], not some other entity produced by the activity of that [power].
Regarding the phrase "internal sacrifice and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes the fire-oblation in the navel-pit and meditation upon the space between the eyebrows.

By the statement "the weapon of Śiva in the *vardhanī*," the exclusion of the *Pāśupata-astra*— which consists of a collection of syllables— is intended for the sake of attaining [the true weapon] through its place and time.
The perfection of place (*deśasaṃpatti*) consists in the conceptualization of being among one of the five groups of eight sacred fields (*pañcāṣṭaka-kṣetra*).
As for the perfection of time (*kālasaṃpatti*), it is the accomplishment of the internal time (*ādhyātmika-kāla*) in accordance with initiation; [this is twofold:

the "material" (*bhautika*) and the "final" (*naiṣṭhika*). The material (*bhautika*) is one who is fit for the initiation of a practitioner (*sādhaka*), while the final (*naiṣṭhika*) is one who is fit for the initiation of a lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*).
He is fit for initiation as one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). Regarding the phrase "beginning with inspection" (*nirīkṣaṇādi*): here, by the word "etc.

(*ādi*), there are included sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), striking (*tāḍana*), sprinkling with water (*abhyukṣaṇa*), the closing of the lotus of the disciple's heart (*śiṣyahṛdayapadmāṃ*), the suppression of the self (*ātmanirodha*), burning (*dahana*), flooding (*āplāvana*), the installation of the Self within the body (*purātmanyāsa*), and the flooding with nectar (*amṛtāplāvana*).

Having performed the rites of *śivīkaraṇa* and *sakalīkaraṇa*, one should perform the union (*saṃdhāna*) of the fire situated in the pitcher and on the sacrificial ground; in this regard, after the union of the channels (*nāḍīsaṃdhāna*), three oblations must also be offered for each [deity]. One may perform the libation with the root [mantra]; thus, there is a hundred oblations of the root mantra and [oblations] for the limbs (*aṅga*).

Since it has been stated by the illustrious Bhojadeva that "by a tenth part," one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) one hundred times with the root mantra and ten times with the Brahma-limbs (*brahmāṅga*).

By the verse beginning with "of those arisen from the destruction of the devourer of seeds" (*bījāśanāśayotthānām*), the specific consecration (*saṃskāra*) is described. [This refers to] the defect of the seed-mantra (*bījadoṣa*).
While this [embryo] resides in the womb, the good and evil deeds committed by the parents [affect it]; there is a Vedic scripture on this point.
193) Thus, "the fault of eating" refers to the consumption of forbidden food; "āśaya" refers to the fault. [The rite involves] three oblations.

"One should give"—thus, three oblations for each [deity] must be performed with the root mantra. Regarding "with the cord": according to some, this refers to the womb of Vāgīśvarī by means of the *aṅkuśa* (hook) mudrā; this pertains to the specific consecration (*viśeṣasaṃskāra*) following the sequence stated in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*.
Having given the extended application (*atideśa*) of the [rules] pertaining to the fortnight, [the text says] "and the sacrificial thread" (*yajñopavītam*);
thus, the sacrificial thread should be given to the Brāhmaṇas and others according to the scriptures. As it has been stated in the *Śrīmad-Brahmaśambhu-paddhati*:
The sacred thread (upavīta) is prescribed for Śūdras, Vaiśyas, and Kṣatriyas respectively as having three strands, being threefold in its twist, and being white with one, two, or three threads.
"For a Brahmin, however, it should be with an upper garment and double the length of three strands.

Thus, "consecrated by the lords of one's own caste" refers to the lords of the castes—Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jyeṣṭha—in the order stated for Brahmins and the others; this is because there is a scriptural authority regarding the sequence of recitation, worship, meditation, and fire-offering.
Listening to the Siddhānta scriptures. Regarding the phrase "for the ascetic there" (*tapasvine tatra*), it refers to specific consecrated items, namely matted hair (*jaṭā*) and ashes (*bhasma*).
By the word *jaṭā*, the rudrākṣa beads to be tied in the matted hair are intended.
Having placed the rudrākṣa beads, ashes, staff (*daṇḍa*), loincloth (*kaupīna*), and sacred thread (*upavīta*) each into separate vessels—

Having placed [the remnants] in another vessel and performed the *saṃpāta-homa* oblation, one should bind the matted locks (*jaṭā*) from the mass of hair on the head, and having fastened the crest-jewel (*śiromaṇi*) within them, [one should proceed].

Afterwards, one should offer the ashes and other substances. Regarding "the powers of the *kalās*": the *kalās* are the thirty-eight *kalās*, which are the powers (*śaktis*). The nine purifiers beginning with Vāmā, the five Brahmans, and likewise the mantras together with them, the eleven *tattvas*, the thirty-six lords of mantras (*mantreśas*), and the eight Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvaras*).

"Completion through the intellect regarding the existent" means that completion is liberation (*apavarga*). "Uttering the name for the sake of separation" refers to names such as Devadatta and others. "The *suṣumnā* is the heart-casket" means that because the *suṣumnā* is the vehicle of Śiva, one should join [the deity] to the thread with one's own name—which is conjoined with the root [mantra] encased within the heart and ends with a salutation (*namaḥ*).

It should be performed. Regarding the phrase "the bonds beginning with Śāntyatītā," the word "beginning" (ādi) refers to Śānti, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Nivṛtti. Regarding the phrase "containing the principles (tattva), worlds (loka), and so forth":
the principles are the thirty-six, beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth; the worlds are those beginning with Anāśrita and ending with Kālāgni.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), syllables, words, and mantras are meant: the syllables (*varṇa*) are the fifty from *a* to *kṣa*;
the words (*pada*) are the eighty-one of the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra, beginning from the initial *praṇava* up to the final *praṇava*.

The "mantras" refer to the root-mantras (*mūlamantra*), the Brahma-mantras (*brahmamantra*), and the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*); by the word "etcetera," the impurity (*mala*), karma, and the power of obstruction (*rodhaśakti*) are included.
Among these, that which is called *mala* is, from the very beginning, a veiler of the powers of knowledge and action belonging to the selves;
it possesses infinite powers, is eternal, all-pervasive, and has a form. It is immutablely eternal and consists of the nature of a substance (*dravyasvarūpa*).
And karma (p.

195) consists of the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) of merit and demerit, which are enjoined or prohibited; as for the power of obstruction (*rodhaśakti*), it refers to those [powers] already mentioned.
Since all fetters (*pāśas*) are insentient by nature, they lack the capacity for autonomous engagement or withdrawal;
therefore, it is the Supreme Goddess Śakti alone, acting as their auxiliary power, who is metaphorically called a "fetter. As stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
Among them, the power of Maheśvara is Śivā, who bestows grace upon all;
it is only because she conforms to dharma that she is metaphorically designated as "bond" (pāśa).
Thus, it has been stated that all these, beginning with *kalā*, are indeed bonds (*pāśas*).
In the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"The covering (*prāvṛti*), the power of the Lord (*īśabala*), and *karma*—the fourfold effect of *māyā*."

"In brief, the snares (*pāśa*) are proclaimed by their very names as *dharmas*. Thus, even for the *bindu*, its status as a snare is stated on account of its being the primary constituent of the *bindu*-grantha and so forth. The justification for the status of the three previously mentioned [categories], beginning with *kalā*, as snares is set forth in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:

The *kalās* are established in the *tattvas*, and the multitude of worlds (*bhuvanavraja*) is established in the *tattvas*. In the *nivṛtti*-kalā and the others, the *tattvas* such as *kalā* reside within the *tattvas* that constitute their state of existence;
as for the worlds, they possess the quality of being a bond even by virtue of being the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*). Thus, the *kalās* and so forth, which consist of objects, [function as bonds].
The state of being a binder has been established. But how can the state of being a binder be predicated of phonemes, words, and mantras, which consist of sound? [Regarding] objects (p.

Without the interpenetration of sound (*śabdānuvedha*), the state of being an object of experience (*bhogyatva*) is untenable. It is established that even those things whose nature is sound possess the quality of bondage. As it is stated in the *Ratnatrayaparibhāṣā*:
"There is no cognition of the atoms which does not involve the apprehension of sound."
In this world, knowledge arises as permeated by every word.
Furthermore, in that very context,
those who know the Self call that same speech by the name of *sūkta*;
for these mental fluctuations, when directed toward the individual self, are of the nature of bondage.

Thus, because it is the cause for the arising of cognitions that serve as the means for enjoyment, [the mind] is always deluded by the permeation of sound when discernment is absent. In this way, the binding nature of sound in its general sense has been stated. How, then, is it so for specific sounds—namely, words and mantras?

The state of being a "bond" (bandhakatva) is now explained. First, regarding the eighty-one words known as the "Pervaders of Space" (vyomavyāpin), each one of these serves as a bond for the infinite other words that accomplish the attraction of objects.

Because it is impossible for them to be purified, and because the Supreme Lord has declared in the scriptures that they denote the power of Śiva who presides over them, they possess the quality of being binders.
This has been stated in the *Ratnatraya* regarding the power (*śakti*) on the path of limited agency (*kalādhvan*):
The Goddess consists of eighty-one words according to the sequence of the words of re-creation;
here, she is established by means of twenty-eight words.
Because, as stated by such passages, the relationship between word and meaning is dependent upon the volition of Īśvara.
This has been said in the *Tattvatrayasaṃgraha*: "Of the Vidyās and Vidyeśas..."

Since it is observed that the denotative power of words is seen to imitate the expansion of general and specific properties as well as mantras, the binding nature of these nine elements— beginning with *kalā*—
has been described. Among these...

In the venerable *Svāyambhuva*, it is stated that the nature of the paths (*adhvan*)— consisting of Kalā, Tattva, Bhuvana, Varṇa, Pada, and Mantra— is the means for the purification of existing selves and for their attainment of Śiva.
Now, [this path serves] for the cessation of the continuity of bondage of the self and for the manifestation of its Śiva-nature.
The path here is proclaimed to be sixfold:

the path of time (adhvā), the path of words (padādhvā), the path of phonemes (varṇādhvā), the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvā), the path of mantras (mantrādhvā), and the path of kalās (kalādhvā); [beyond these] is the single, auspicious state (śiva-pada).
Thus,
even regarding the Three Jewels:
having abandoned one by one [the lower levels] and attained the state free from old age and death among the Kalās and so forth.
"Therefore, the goal is reached by men; hence, our path consists of *kalā* and the other [categories]."

Regarding the statement "by the heart" (*hṛdayena*) and so forth, which describes how the purifying nature ceases for the *pada* and *mantra* that were previously stated to be the objects of purification: it is because these possess a dual nature consisting of the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*),
and [the purification occurs] by means of the signifier-nature arising from the *bindu*.

(198) The state of being the object of purification belongs to the nature of the denotable [word], while the state of being the purifier, in the form of Śiva and Śakti, constitutes primarily the mantra-nature of Śiva. As it has been said:
"Because of the scriptural statement, 'Śiva is the mantra for the sake of favoring the worlds,' that power which is the bestower of grace has attained the state of being mantra here;
and as long as there is a presiding deity, it is considered to consist of both the signified (vācya) and the signifier (mantra)."

"Having taken them from the body of the disciple. How are these fetters situated in the disciple? For the body of the disciple is well known to be composed of the five elements; how then could there be the existence of these other entities within that body? It is said in response: with respect to the grasping of the principles (*tattva*), [the earth is... the foundation.

Because of the statement, "This [soul], having reached the end of the portion fixed for males, wanders by the power of karma through all bodies born in the worlds," it is said that the thirty principles beginning with earth and ending with *kāla* abide by means of the *puryaṣṭaka*. As the cause of these [bodies]...

And thus, through the nourishment of that [energy], there arises the manifestation of the five pure elements and so forth within the mantra-body; it is heard in the scriptures that the primordial Kuṇḍalinī is conjoined with the moon, fire, and sun.
"She should be known as situated in the region of the heart in the form of a sprout.

In the commentary (*vṛtti*) on this *sūtra*, it is stated that prior to the connection with the *puryaṣṭaka* consisting of *māyā*, there is first a connection with the *puryaṣṭaka* whose nature is *nāda*, just as it was said: "And she is primordial..."

At the first break of day, it is conjoined with the Puruṣa; immediately thereafter, the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city) and so forth arise from the *bindu* as its effect, since they originate from it as their cause.

And there is the emergence of the *kalās*, the pure principles (*tattvas*), the worlds (*bhuvanas*), and so forth; and the emergence of *karmas* by virtue of being the cause of the gross and subtle bodies. Of this body—which is dense due to its obscuration of knowledge and action—there is the power of concealment (*tiraskāra-śakti*).
Its establishment is through its being the cause of all active manifestation (*pravṛtti*). Therefore, the abiding of all [entities] within the body is possible;

thus, the previously mentioned group of nine *pāśas* is joined with their respective names in the Sūtra, preceded by salutations and followed by *svāhā*. We [perform this] with these names ending in *svāhā*.

One should satisfy each [deity] with three oblations. Regarding the previously mentioned conjunction of the heart-syllable (*hṛt*), the *puṭa* syllable, and the *ātma*-seed (*auṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ*), the disjunction is performed with:
*oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ śāntyatītakalāpāśāya hā hūṃ phaṭ*. Then, one grasps the bond of the *śāntyatīta* kalā with: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ śāntyatītakalāpāśaṃ gṛhṇāti*.

The vessel: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ śāntyatītakalāpāśāya svāhā*—this is the libation (*tarpaṇa*). *oṃ hāṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ śāntyatītakalāpāśāya hāṃ huṃ phaṭ*—this is the disjunction (*viśleṣaṇa*). *oṃ hāṃ heṃ hāṃ śāntyatītakalāpāśaṃ gṛhṇāmi*—thus [one says] "I seize."
Seizing: *oṃ hāṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ śāntikalāpāśāya namaḥ*. Joining: *oṃ hāṃ hyaiṃ hāṃ śāntikalāpāśāya svāhā*.
Satisfying: *oṃ hāṃ hūṃ vidyākalāpāśāya haṃ huṃ phaṭ*.
Disjunction: *Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ*, "I seize the noose of the *vidyā*-kalā"—this is the seizing (*grahaṇa*).

Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the noose of the *vidyā-kalā*; this is the conjunction (*saṃyojana*). Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the noose of the *vidyā-kalā*; this is the satiation (*saṃtarpaṇa*). Oṃ hāṃ hlīṃ hāṃ, haḥ huṃ phaṭ to the noose of the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*; this is the separation (*viśleṣaṇa*). Oṃ...

"Hāṃ hlīṃ hāṃ, I grasp the noose of the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā"—thus is the grasping (*grahaṇa*). "Oṃ hāṃ hlīṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the noose of the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā"—thus is the conjunction (*saṃyojana*). "Oṃ hāṃ hlīṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the noose of the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā"—thus is the satiation (*saṃtarpaṇa*). Oṃ hāṃ...

*Hlāṃ hāṃ nivṛttikalāpāśāya haḥ huṃ phaṭ*—this is the disjunction (*viśleṣaṇa*). *Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ nivṛttikalāpāśaṃ gṛhṇāmi*—this is the grasping (*grahaṇa*). *Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ nivṛttikalāpāśāya namaḥ*—this is the conjunction (*saṃyojana*). *Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ hāṃ*...
The satiation is performed with: *nivṛttikalāpāśāya svāhā*. The separation is performed with: *oṃ karmapāśāya haḥ huṃ phaṭ*. The grasping is performed with: *oṃ hāṃ karmapāśaṃ gṛhṇāmi*.
The conjunction is performed with: *oṃ hāṃ karmapāśāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ karmapāśāya*... [continues].
*Oṃ svāhā* is the libation (*tarpaṇa*). *Oṃ hāṃ malaśaktaye haḥ huṃ phaṭ* is the separation (*viśleṣaṇa*).
*Oṃ hāṃ malaṃ gṛhṇāmi* is the grasping (*grahaṇa*). *Oṃ hāṃ malaśaktaye namaḥ* is the conjunction (*saṃyojana*). *Oṃ hāṃ malaśaktaye svāhā* is the libation (*tarpaṇa*). *Oṃ hāṃ*...
The disjunction is performed with "haḥ huṃ phaṭ" for the power of obstruction (rodhaśakti); [then one says] "Oṃ hāṃ, I take up the power of obstruction."
The grasping: *oṃ hāṃ rodhaśaktaye namaḥ*—this is the conjunction. *oṃ hāṃ rodhaśaktaye svāhā*—this is the libation. *oṃ hūṃ hoṃ hrūṃ śāntyatītakalāpāśaṃ huṃ phaṭ oṃ hāṃ hūṃ hyaiṃ hūṃ*.
Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ! For the noose of the *śānti* aspect, hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ hūṃ hrūṃ hūṃ! For the noose of the *vidyā* aspect, hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ hūṃ hlīṃ! For the noose of the *pratiṣṭhā* aspect, hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ hūṃ hlāṃ hūṃ! For the noose of the *nivṛtti* aspect, hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ haḥ hlīṃ! [For] *pratiṣṭhā*...

*Kalāpāśāya huṃ phaṭ | Oṃ haḥ hūṃ vidyākalāpāśāya huṃ phaṭ | Oṃ haṃ hyaiṃ*— having entered with these very mantras ending in *namaḥ* as internal threads, one should bind them with these same [mantras] ending in *badhnāmi*. The seizing of the nooses is their seizing by means of binding.

Subjugation (*vaśīkāra*) is the binding of a person through the complete prohibition of [their] boundless [desires], by means of a row of arrows; here, the word "row" (*paṅkti*) signifies the number twelve.
The meaning is "by twenty more."
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the preliminary consecration.

Regarding the phrase "the channels, the junctions, and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the performance of three oblations at each respective station is included. Regarding the phrase "then the pervasion by means of withdrawal": here, the pervasion of the *nivṛtti*-kalā is shown through its worlds (*bhuvana*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and mantra-words (*mantrapada*).

The seed-syllables (*bīja*) proclaimed in the *Śrīmat Kālottara* and other scriptures, the channels (*nāḍī*), the winds (*vāyu*), the objects of the senses (*viṣaya*), the qualities (*guṇa*), the states (*avasthā*), the causes (*kāraṇa*), and the presiding lords (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) are to be explained. Among these, within the seed-syllable, by means of the forms *ā* and *la*, there are the two channels named *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, as well as the two winds, *prāṇa* and *apāna*.

In the manifestation of the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇopasthiti*), the qualities (*guṇa*)—namely smell, taste, form, touch, and sound—are the states (*avasthā*). Brahmā, the Lord who is the cause of the waking state, is the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātā*) over Sadyojāta in the form of the mantra to be recited; he [is the one] who should purify that which is other than the tree of karma-initiated [existence] for the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*). Thus it is said here.
It must be accepted that even the rites of *samaya*, conduct, sacrifices, and works of public utility (*iṣṭāpūrta*) are incapable of purification.
As it was stated by Somaśambhu:
"In the case of initiation with seed (*sabījā dīkṣā*), [there is release] from the fetters of *samaya* and conduct..."

"By means of separation from the karma that initiates the body," and so forth; thus it should be performed with the *jyeṣṭhā* [power]. One should contemplate that the *jyeṣṭhā*, *vāmā*, and *raudrī* powers, as prescribed by the rule regarding their source (*yoni*), function as the instruments (*karaṇatva*) in the rites known as meditation. "Having informed Śiva regarding the embryos"—herein lies the act of generation (*janana*).
In which of those wombs does the manifestation of the gross body occur? Its function therein, however, is the capacity for being an enjoyer; that which is to be enjoyed— (p.

Because it is stated in the *Pañcikā* that "the emergence of self-awareness through the agent is the purification by means of that single essence; this is the purification of the principles (*tattvaśuddhi*)," there is an absence of even a sprout of this [impurity] for one who has realized the principle (*tattva*)— which is not differentiated from the causal self of the principle of cessation (*nivṛtti-tattva*)— and for whom the births, additional enjoyments, and dissolutions belonging to those [principles] have ceased.
In that regard, these purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) prescribed by the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) are not to be performed in the world of *bhūr*.
Why are these rites, for which the purifications have already been accomplished previously, enjoined as things to be done?
They are performed for the sake of the embodied soul through rites prescribed for the present time. However—

In the *Śrīmanmataṅgapārameśvaravṛtti*, it is stated that for women and Śūdras who have been graced by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), [the rites] are performed even in their current bodies, without regard for the body of a twice-born (*dvija*). It is not the case that those who have been initiated must perform only those practices specifically prescribed by the specialized scriptures after their initiation.
Furthermore, the performance of the specific injunction must indeed be preceded by the performance of what is enjoined by the general scripture. On this point it is said:
the definition of the general and the specific is stated in the venerable *Mohaśūrottara* as follows:
The *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Purāṇas*, as well as the general scriptures such as the venerable *Kāmika* and others, constitute the specific scriptures (*viśeṣa-śāstra*).
The generality of the Vedas and so forth arises from the fact that they grant authority merely through [birth in] castes such as the Brāhmaṇa;
whereas the specificity of the *Kāmika* and other [Tantras] lies in their [granting authority] to those very Brāhmaṇas and others [who have been initiated].

Since authority [to practice] begins only after initiation, preceded by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) which ripens impurities (*malaparipāka*), it must therefore be preceded by the common conduct (*sāmānyācāra*).
The performance of what is prescribed by the specific scriptures must be carried out. As it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva* [Tantra], in the chapter on the *saṃdhyā*:
"Having first performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), one who belongs to two stages of life (*āśrama*) should perform the *brāhmī saṃdhyā* twice. This is the meaning of this aphorism (*sūtra*).

The commentary states: Having sipped water and facing either northward or eastward, the twice-born student (*brahmacārin*) should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*), which is the rite of sprinkling (*mārjana*) as prescribed in the Veda by the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and so forth.
He should perform this service twice. Thus ends the section on the student.

Abiding in any one of the four stages of life known as householder, forest-dweller, or wandering mendicant, and performing both the Vedic rites and the authorized rites dedicated to the Supreme Lord, he should remain in that state for "dvirit," meaning for two times.

The meaning is that after performing the practice of the sūtras established by the Vedas, the Śaiva practitioner should perform the *saṃdhyā* worship. In the venerable *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*: "Having performed the vessel of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should then commence the *saṃdhyā*; however, the Vedic [saṃdhyā] comes first."
Having performed that, one should then practice the Śaiva [rite]. In that regard, the three Vidyās should be performed, especially with two or four [repetitions];
likewise, having recited the Vaiśvadeva and the Sandhyā prayers, for indeed, [these] are for the three [castes], excluding the Śūdra.
In the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*:
"Having bathed and emerged [from the water], one who belongs to two stages of life (*dvirāśramī*) should first perform the Brāhmī twilight devotion (*saṃdhyā*). Thus it is said.

"Having presided over the twilight [ritual] regarding embryos," it is said; here, that which is stated concerning the duties of birth applies also to other ritual matters. As it is said in the venerable *Mataṅgapārameśvara*:
"The conduct of one who walks the path with a purified soul is of two kinds."
The attainment of both visible and invisible fruits proceeds unfailingly.
This [conduct] is well-established in the world; it is not contradicted by scriptural evidence, and it must be protected for the sake of the highest good by those who are esteemed and blameless.
The Śaiva [tradition] should be understood with effort by those whose souls are practitioners elsewhere;
and within this Śaiva authority, the worldly [tradition] attains the status of an auxiliary limb.
Nevertheless, this [conduct] must be observed, because no fault arises when it is observed; whereas if it is abandoned, some merit [is lost]. For this reason, it is called "common" (sāmānya).
Its practice is well-known in the world, and so forth. This is the point.
Conduct (*ācāra*) consists of the specific duties of the Brāhmaṇas and other classes.

This is well known to be rooted in the scriptures of the Vedas (*śruti*) and the law-books (*smṛti*), which are distinguished by their origin. For instance, social transactions such as marriage must be performed exclusively by the twice-born who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*); furthermore, that [initiation] itself must be observed as its cause.

Nor even by this [objection]. For although, in this case where specific rules have been prescribed, the worldly conduct regarding the self—such as the obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth—is not a constituent part (*aṅga*), nevertheless...
They must indeed be maintained for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). Therefore, the word "no" (*na*) here negates the notion that there is a fault (*doṣa*) [in not maintaining them].
This is connected to the idea that when that which consists of the conventional agreement (*samaya*) is not maintained, no merit (*guṇa*) whatsoever exists; rather, there is only a fault.
Since it is permitted here as something to be maintained, its non-existence [as a fault] is established by this very negation.

Precisely because of this equality of action, this conduct is called "general" (*sāmānya*). In this context as well, because it is permitted as something to be protected, the aphorism states: "one who is endowed with general conduct. Its commentary is: that which exists within the general injunctions of the Vedas and so forth is "general," and it is also [the conduct] itself.

The meaning is that he is endowed with that conventional conduct which is expressed by both general and specific [characteristics], and thus performs the rites of both the general and the specific. As it is said in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*:

In the Śaiva tradition, only two stages of life—the householder and the student—are capable of bestowing grace upon the world; neither the wandering mendicant nor the forest-dweller possesses this power.
The states of being a householder and a student of sacred knowledge are merely designations;
in the ultimate sense, for them there is neither a stage of life nor any ritual activity belonging to those stages.

For whose sake those who have performed their duties are appointed to the supreme state, and for whose sake the stages of life (āśramas) are proclaimed as based upon the Śiva-scriptures; [for that purpose].

Commentary: For the sake of that fruit which is liberation by nature— for which purpose these disciples, having performed the rite of initiation, have been joined to the supreme state and have properly resorted to the Śiva-scripture— they are called "those who have resorted to the Śiva-scripture" (śivaśāstrasamāśritāḥ).
p.

207) For them, for that purpose—that is, for the sake of attaining it—there is the attainment of the stages of life (*āśrama*). Furthermore, the performance of the rituals belonging to those stages of life is heard of in the scriptures; however, this is so by virtue of their being prescribed.

It is heard in scripture that one must practice that [duty] solely for the purpose of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*): "Because of violating the command, the state of being a flesh-eater (*kravyāda*) is declared for a hundred years"; and it is also said that one whose self is defined by the conduct of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*) should not transgress even that.
Even if one were to be a knower of the three times and capable of attracting the three worlds,
nevertheless, one should not transgress even the slightest bit of worldly conduct.
And again in that same place:

"One who is constantly devoted to the mantra should perform some portion of the morning twilight recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and whatever ritual sequence has been inherited, for the sake of stability."

The commentary on this is as follows: that which is prescribed by the scriptures and so forth regarding the connection with a previous stage of life (āśrama), such as the twilight prayers (saṃdhyāvandana) and fire-oblations (homa), as well as other duties inherited through tradition, is also impermanent.
The meaning is that [the practice of] Śiva-worship and the like, when performed with a view toward fruits and the like, remains within the sphere of worldly activity.
One should perform [the rites] for the sake of avoiding the transgression that arises from the non-performance of prescribed duties. As it is heard in scripture:
"In whichever stage of life (āśrama) one stands, having attained initiation whose essence is Śiva, remaining steadfast in that very stage, one should also protect the Dharma of Śiva."
"One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites with the desire to avoid transgression;
one who seeks liberation should engage in those [rites], but not in optional or prohibited ones. (p. 208)
O Dehin, one who has received initiation while remaining within their own social class (varṇa) [attains the goal].
Remaining constantly established in that very state, one should protect the Dharma of Śiva,
as well as the conduct of the social classes and stages of life, and the worldly rites of expiation.
He should cause the local customs and established practices of the region to be observed,
beginning from the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) up until the marriage ceremony itself.
One may indeed perform Vedic rites first, but thereafter one should follow the Śaiva path and not anything else.
Its commentary states: by the word "and" (ca), it is meant that householders established on the worldly path (*lokamārga*) should not transgress [the rules], nor should they... [laṅghayeyur na lau].
"Those who have been initiated through the [proper] conduct should perform that [rite] for the sake of worldly convention"— this is the statement of Svāyambhuva.

Thus, in all the scriptures, such as the venerable *Kiraṇa*, *Mṛgendra*, *Mataṅga*, *Svāyambhuva*, *Sūkṣma*, *Svāyambhuva*, and *Raurava*, the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*), which are prescribed in the Vedas, are established.
During initiation (*dīkṣā*), the Śiva-mantras are prescribed for the purpose of withdrawing the karma that would otherwise result in birth in the Brāhmaṇa caste.
This has been stated by Bhūtikaṇṭhācārya, the author of the commentary on the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*, regarding initiation.
The forty-eight sacraments (*saṃskāra*), beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception), are to be performed individually;
even those pertaining to this body, being included therein, somehow [arise] from a non-human source through your power.
"And those [topics] that are to be performed should be connected [to this]," as stated in the *Śrīmatkiraṇavṛtti*. It was said by the venerable Sadyojyotiḥpāda in the *Mokṣakārikā*:
And since its object— the pillar— is not sublated by any other means of valid cognition,
even those learned in the Vedas (śrotriyas) must accept it as the means for attaining its results and so forth.

However, it has been stated that there is no sublation of this [scriptural statement] by either perception or inference. As previously discussed in the section on experience (*bhoga*), the authority of such statements as "one should sprinkle with fire" and so forth would be established; thus, everything is consistent. This [scripture] should be accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by those who know the Veda—the cause of the supreme good—as well as by others.

And in the *Śrīmadrauravavṛtti*, the Teacher has stated: "Even for one who has been consecrated by the complete initiation in the Śaiva [tradition], it is said: 'One should not transgress the conduct of the castes and stages of life even in thought. Thus, by the venerable Somaśambhu, [the passage beginning with] "of the path" and so forth refers to unworthiness.

This very point— that one is unfit for liberation— is stated by the words "by the Śaiva [initiation]," and so forth. Precisely because of this capacity to remove obstacles, even after initiation, the Vedic rites must be performed simply because they are prescribed, without regard for their fruits or other such considerations.
Success! It has been said: "One should not transgress, even in thought, the conduct prescribed for one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramācāra*).

By such statements, it is established that ritual action consisting of both Vedic (*śrauta*) and Smārta duties must indeed be performed by initiated Brahmins and others, even after the time of initiation.

(210) Now, it has been stated that the Vedic and Smārta rites, which are prescribed as things to be performed, are impure because they are means for the slaughter of animals and seeds, and because they involve decay and excess.

Since the revealed (ānuśravika) [dharma] is, according to the Sāṃkhyas and others, seen to be possessed of impurity, destruction, and excess— just like that which is perceived in this world— how can these two types of action be said to be to be performed by those seeking liberation?
Three reasons have been stated for their being to be performed.
Because it is preceded by the slaughter of animals and seeds, and because it possesses impurity, decay, and excess,
the Śrauta rite such as the Agnihotra— which was previously described as pure due to its being accomplished through animals and seeds—
is, on the contrary, declared to be impure by the Supreme Lord. Thus it has been said:
In the venerable *Mataṅgapārameśvara*, it is stated:

"By means of sacrificial offerings such as the *agnihotra* and likewise by [penances] such as the *cāndrāyaṇa*. However, because [the fruits of these acts] are subject to decay and excellence, success for uninitiated practitioners occurs through the pursuit of those fruits. For this very reason...
For those who perform [rites] solely because they are enjoined, without seeking their fruits, those two [defects] do not occur.
As it has been said:
"One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites with the desire to ward off transgression; one who seeks liberation should engage [in them] for that purpose."

Regarding the phrase "therein, of the optional and the prohibited": therefore, by not pursuing their fruits, these two must indeed be performed as a means of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*). Now, it was stated that even those actions prescribed in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* are to be practiced just like the obligatory daily conduct (*nityācāra*). From that [context], of that...

(211) Since ritual action (*karman*) has as its means clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, and so forth, it is possible for it to consist of non-violence and prior merit; therefore, it is appropriate that it be performed. This applies to that which is based on the Veda (*śrauta*).

In the case of the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices, such acts as the immolation of the Agniṣṭomīya animal and the drinking of Soma—which involve contact with remnants (ucchiṣṭa) and so forth—there might arise a suspicion that they possess the nature of dharma; thus, their status as "to be performed" (karaṇīyatva) is established.
However, this is not the definition of dharma and adharma in terms of their means (sādhana), nor is it their definition in terms of their essential nature (svarūpa).
It is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva* that [the knowledge of Dharma] arises solely from the *Āmnāya* (revelation) and the *Smṛti* (tradition):

"The cognition of the means of Dharma arises from the *Āmnāya* alone; because the *Smṛti* is rooted in that, [Dharma] arises from those two alone, or from the Supreme. This refers to the quality of being Dharma (*dharmatva*) in the case of actions prescribed by *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.
Because it is perceived that unrighteousness (*adharma*) results from the two prohibited actions,
and because the Veda declares that the immolation of animals— which is an auxiliary part of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*— is a means for accomplishing righteousness (*dharma*),
even initiated Brahmins and others must indeed perform the *Agniṣṭoma* and other such sacrifices.

It should be understood that even the fear of contact with remnants (ucchiṣṭa) is dispelled by the very words of the sūtra concerning the immolation of animals, which state that one does not become defiled by remnants through the Soma. Furthermore,
in the great Aśvamedha sacrifice, many evildoers are liberated merely by the sight [of it].

Likewise, according to the Śrīmadraurava scripture, "in the form of Maheśvara," there is the scriptural teaching that even the sight of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) liberates one from sin upon seeing the maṇḍala of Śiva; thus it applies to the horse-sacrifice and so forth.
The merit (*puṇyatva*) of that action is indeed not prevented by punishment.

Therefore, for the sake of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*), the *agniṣṭoma* and other sacrifices must be performed. However, they are not to be regarded as a means for attaining supreme liberation (*paramokṣa*)—as is the case with the worship of the Śiva-liṅga after initiation—as has been stated.

According to the *Śrī-sarvajñānottara*, one should practice the worldly duties of Skanda as the primary mode of conduct. Now, it may be asked: in the *Śrī-mṛgendra* it is said—“In the earthly [state], prior to the field (*kṣetra*) and prior to the eightfold group of immortals (*amarāṣṭaka*) which is gross...”*
One should remove the obstruction to the purificatory rites prescribed in the sacred tradition.
By this Sūtra, it is stated that the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) prescribed by traditional authority (āmnāya) constitute an obstacle [to initiation].
Since the Vedic (śrauta) and Smārta rituals are similar in this regard, this prohibition would also apply to the Aṣṭakā, Parvan, Pitṛmedha, Ekoddiṣṭa, and other such rites.
Therefore, since there is no distinction [between them], those [other rules] should not be observed here either; if this is argued, it is not so.
A householder should never transgress Vedic conduct.
The ritual duties consisting of Śrauta and Smārta rites are for the Brāhmaṇas and others respectively.

By such statements as these, it is understood that even after initiation (*dīkṣā*), these purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) must necessarily be performed. Since there is no prohibition in the specific scripture stating that "only those prescribed by the Smṛtis should be performed, not those prescribed by the Śruti," all of them should be carried out without distinction for the purpose of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*).

And thus, even the cessation of that obstruction is accomplished precisely through initiation (dīkṣā). This was stated by Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, the author of the commentary (*vṛtti*) on this sūtra: [p. 213]

It is stated in the *Dīpikā* as well that when the collection of Śaiva purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)— to be described below— is performed, the multitude of latent impressions (*saṃskāra-vrāta*) residing in the hearing of obstructing causes becomes an obstacle to the fruit of Śaiva initiation; this is precisely because of its power to remove such obstructions.

It is established that even for those following the Vedic tradition, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) subsequent to initiation (*dīkṣā*) are to be performed merely because they are prescribed, without aiming for their specific fruits. However, in the *Mataṅgapārameśvara*, it is stated in the aphorism: "The action contained within the altar (*vedi*), whether white or black, is called 'devotion' (*bhakti*)," regarding that which pertains to the altar.

The black-and-white nature of action has been stated. Therefore, how can such action be said to lead to liberation? [This is addressed] in the commentary on the Mataṅgapārameśvara by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭhācārya, in his commentary on the sūtra beginning with "That which is internal within the object of knowledge" (vedyāmantargatam).

There is no such scriptural authority. By stating that "the Agnihotra and Vaiśvadeva rites, consisting of white and black [elements], which are being performed at the end of the Vedas," you have asserted that the Agnihotra is white.
Therefore, because the Agnihotra and other such rites are white, they must be performed even after initiation.

Without seeking fruits such as [worldly rewards], for the sake of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*), the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)— beginning with birth and extending up to the *pavitra* and *medha*, according to one's caste and stage of life (*āśrama*)—
are prescribed by the venerable *Svāyambhuva*, *Mṛgendra*, *Raurava*, *Kiraṇa*, *Sarvajñānottara*, and other scriptures.
According to the Siddhānta scripture, with the mantra *oṃ hauṃ haḥ śivāya huṃ phaṭ*,
one should perform the worship of the Abiding Power (*ādhāraśakti*) in the fire by means of its own name.
Having taken up the three oblations from the thread while first contemplating the penetration of the other paths and the subsequent contemplation of the *kalās*,
one performs the application of the *kalā* into the fire, worships it with its own name, offers three oblations,
and— having worshipped— the invocation of the Lord who is the cause of the simultaneous contemplation of the ritual action performed therein.
The satiation with three oblations using one's own name, the petitioning of that [deity], the invocation of Vāgīśvarī,

her worship, three oblations, and the satiation; the prayer to the Supreme Lord for the sake of uniting the disciple, and the sprinkling and striking of the disciple with the Astra-mantra while exhaling.
The entry into the body of the disciple is performed with the Astra-mantra; the separation [of the soul] is performed with one's own mantra joined with the Śiva-mantra;

or rather, the entry into one's own body is the casting into the womb of Vāgīśvarī, the mental conjunction with those respective wombs, and three oblations with the Hṛdaya-mantra for the accomplishment of the union.
The invocation of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-vijñāpana*) and the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*); three oblations with the left [hand];

the invocation of the Supreme Lord; the severing of the bonds (*pāśacchedana*) with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) alone, recited seven times, ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; by that same [mantra], the crushing (*vimardana*) and the rounding (*vartulīkaraṇa*).

One should not offer oblations with that very mantra; rather, one should generally perform the casting of the *bindu* with the heart-mantra of Vāgīśvarī, and at every watch (*kala*), one should offer three oblations with the root-mantra.
In the case of seedless initiation (*nirbījadīkṣā*), however, one should invoke a Brahmin, worship him, satisfy him with three oblations,

inform him of the intent for restraint (*nirodha*), and perform the offering of the fee (*śulka*) by means of an oblation with the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*). This should be understood as applying to each individual [deity] in turn.
Now, regarding the *pratiṣṭhā*-kalā,
other activities not mentioned in this manual, as described in the venerable *Kālottara*,
are written here: the *gajārī* and *hastijihvā* channels, which are called the "equal-abdomen" (*samānodara*) and the "wind" (*vāyu*), and the tongue.
The organ is the anus; the object is taste; the qualities are taste, form, touch, and sound;
the seed-syllables are *ma* and *va*; the state is dreaming;
the cause is Viṣṇu-Vāmadeva as the presiding deity.
Now follows the section on knowledge.

In the *puṃs* (the individual soul), the world known as all the sense organs (*sarvendriya*) and the Lord of the World (*bhuvaneśvara*) are to be understood as residing within the principle of *rāga* (attachment) by virtue of being the presiding deities over the impurity of *puṃstvamala*. Since there is no such principle called *puṃs* that is insentient in nature, [these two] reside in the Self which has not been previously mentioned, like the first digit of the moon (*pūrvakalā*). [The eight worlds] are the Vasus.

They are written as follows: Pūṣan and Hastijihvā are the channels (nāḍīs); the hands are the two *repha*s of the seed-syllable; the mountain is the measure (*māna*). Wind is the object; form is its nature. The feet and eyes are the sense organs; their qualities are form, touch, and sound. (p. 216)
The state is deep sleep; the cause is Rudra; the presiding deity is Ghoras.

At the conclusion of the purification of Vidyā and Kalā, two hundred oblations must be offered with the Mūla-mantra for the sake of purifying the impurity of personhood (puṃstvamala) and for the purification of the subtle body (sūkṣmadeha). As it has been said:
The teachers [state]: "For the sake of purifying the impurity of masculinity and for the purification of the subtle body,
one should offer two hundred oblations with the root mantra, concluding with the purification of the Vidyā."
Now follows the rite of pacification (śāntikalā).
As before, here too other functions are described as entities:
the two channels are Alambuṣā and Yaśā; the two winds are Krakara and Kūrma;
the sense organ is the skin; the object is the quality of touch; the seed-syllables are *biṃ* and *ya*; the causal deity is Īśvara; and the state is the fourth (*turyā*).
The Tatpuruṣa is the presiding deity. "The complete discharge of Vidyā"—here, by the word *vidyā*, Vāgīśvarī is denoted.
Now, in the *Śāntyatīta-kalā*, the subjects not previously mentioned are stated as follows: the two channels (*nāḍī*) are Kuha and Śaṅkhinī;
the two winds (*vāyu*) are Devadatta and Dhanañjaya; the two organs are speech and hearing; and the object (*viṣaya*) is sound.
Sound is also a quality (*guṇa*). The state is that which transcends the fourth (*turyātītā*). Nāda and *ahaṃkāra* are the seed-syllables (*bīja*).
The causal state of authority is Sadāśivajña, [who is] Sadāśiva.

Īśāna is the presiding deity over the pentad of *kalās*, because it has been stated that [the functions there] consist of the enjoyment of experiences (*bhoga-bhojana*) and initiation at the time of death (*maraṇodīkṣā*). Since experience is caused by *karman*, and *karman* exists in a threefold form beginning with *bhūtādi*,

[the purpose here is] the exhaustion through experience of that *karman* whose effects have already begun among those [three types], as well as [the removal] of the remaining latent impressions (*āśaya*).

Since karma is not [itself] to be purified, it is stated in the Sūtra that those karmas residing within the latent disposition (*āśaya*) are to be purified by being joined with the body of the disciple through ritual action. At the time of purifying future karmas, one should keep in mind their pervasion, including both their means and their fruits. As it has been said:
In the *Śrīmanmṛgendra*:
"The intentions of the individual soul (aṇu), which consist of Śiva, transcend the paths of worldly tradition;
its karmas, however, extend from the *kṣetrajña* up to the *īśvara*, the *gaṇas*, and the *aṅgas*."
"O Sage, those actions which produce difficult dispassion regarding the three abodes arise from yoga and knowledge, each becoming progressively more subtle."
In this context, the construction of wells, tanks, and the like is called *pūrta*. That which consists of the *soma* sacrifices and so forth is called *iṣṭa* by the word *kṛcchra*.

By the word "vairāgya" (detachment), the internal actions consisting of the intention [to renounce] are expressed; by the name "yoga," the actions to be accomplished through the Śrī Pāśupata and other systems are expressed.
(218) The term *yoga* refers to the rites to be accomplished through the Śrīpāśupata and other systems;
by the word *vijñāna*, those [rites] produced [by such means] are meant, which consist of the nature of Śiva and lead to the attainment of the world of Sadāśiva.

The rites pertaining to the practitioner are now described. The ground to be attained by these [practitioners] extends from Kālāgnirudra up to the limit of the five groups of eight (pañcāṣṭaka); starting from that same five-group-of-eight, it continues upward from the Guṇatattva to the end of the Puruṣatattva, and further beyond that to the end of Māyā.

Beyond that, extending as far as the world of Sadāśiva, there is pervasion; [this process] culminates in the dissolution of the connection with karma and so forth within the fire of the *upasthāpana*.

If it is asked: "How is the possibility of the implantation (*ādhāna*) and birth of this individual soul (*aṇu*) explained in the case of the Power (*śakti*), which is of the nature of consciousness, just as it is in the case of the *sakala* souls who are of the nature of insentience?"

By stating that "conception, entry, birth, and the arising of vision and action" occur within the Supreme Lord, whose nature is partless (*niṣkala*), the process of ritual action—from conception to dissolution—is established; likewise, here too, birth is said to occur within Śakti. [Objection: When the two have been joined, why was purification not performed at the time of their purification? [Reply: No.
The expiation has indeed been performed; that which must be done is stated in the *Śrī Mṛgendra*:
"The root of this universe is the two powers of the Lord, which are impurity (*mala*);
they are removed precisely through expiation, as will be explained along with the [other] associated [topics]."
Thus, as previously stated, even for that which is to be experienced, supreme purification arises in this very [state], by virtue of which the body is said to exist within another creation (p.

"Of the solitary Self alone. Its commentary is as follows: by the phrase "the producer, the sustainer, the non-object," and by the word "object" (*bhogya*) itself, it is taught that even for the *karman* (action) spoken of in the context of the instrument of action, the supreme and most excellent purification is achieved only through atonement (*niṣkṛti*), according to the path instructed by the Guru.

The recitation of mantras, preceded by the application and contemplation of the *viṣuva*, follows the path taught by the Guru. There are seven kinds of *viṣuva*: first, the *prāṇaviṣuva*, which is the union of the disciple’s mind and self with the internal vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) of the Teacher, occurring within the resonance (*nāda*) of one's own self.

Having meditated upon dissolution in the locations such as the heart, the second equinox (*viṣuva*)— known as the "mantra"— consists of the contemplation of the mantra characterized by the sequential pronunciation of the conjunctions and disjunctions of the measures (*mātrā*) of *ahaṃ*, *au*, and so forth, within the locations such as the heart and the *bindu*.

By piercing the knots known as the genitals, navel, heart, throat, uvula, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmabila) at the twelve-finger limit (dvādaśānta), one attains the third equinox (viṣuva), which is the practice of contemplating the primordial sound (nāda) within the Suṣumnā, the root mantra.

This should be understood by means of the trident (*triśūla*). Among the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, there is the abandonment of the six locations—namely the letter *ha*, the vowel *au*, the vowel *ū*, the bindu, the *nāda*, and the end of the *nāda*—at the seventh location, which is the station of Śakti;
at that seventh station of Śakti, through the abandonment of the six locations, there is the dissolution of the *nāda*.
The fourth is the tranquil equinox (viṣuva), which is the power (śakti).
As long as the upward movement of the nāda situated in the center continues, that is the power-equinox (śaktiviṣuva).

The fifth is the *kālaviṣuva*, so called because the powers— namely Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā— are measured as being devoid of any objective reality (*prameya*) that could be grasped by the power of the limbs of the entire wind of breath (*prāṇa*), even down to its ten-millionth part. The sixth is likewise [measured] by the sixth.

At the conclusion of that [rite], which is devoid of the form of the Sage (the Guru), the dissolution of the disciple’s consciousness into the Supreme Śiva occurs by means of the Prāsāda mantra; this is the seventh equinox (*viṣuva*), and the method of reciting the mantra is now described.
Among the twelve mantras contained within the Prāsāda mantra, it is that which is accompanied by the syllable *Hauṃ*.
The pervasion of the letter *ha* extends from the *mūlādhāra* up to the lotus of the heart;

the pervasion of Brahmā also extends as far as that point. Above that, up to the throat, is the pervasion of the sixth [letter], Viṣṇu, whose pervasion ends there. Above that, together with Rudra, it extends to the middle of the palate.
Renunciation. Beyond that, the pervasion of the Lord’s *bindu* extends to the midpoint between the eyebrows;

above that, the pervasion of the *ardhacandra* extends for one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*); above that, the pervasion of the *nirodhin* extends for one finger-breadth; and above that, the pervasion of the *nāda* extends to the end of the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*).

The pervasion of that which denotes Sadāśiva [extends] from the *brahmabila* for a measure of one *aṅgula*. Above that, the pervasion of the end of *nāda* (*nādānta*) extends for one *aṅgula*. Above that, the pervasion of *śakti* extends for three *aṅgulas*.

Two finger-breadths above that is the pervasion of Vyāpinī; two finger-breadths above that is the pervasion of Samanā. Beginning from Nāda and ending with Unmanā is the station of Śakti; above that is the station of Śiva, which consists of one's own established, dense, and purely conscious nature—this is indeed that very [state].

The station of union, distinguished by omniscience and other qualities, is [attained] through oblations of clarified butter from the *sruva* ladle: *oṃ hāṃ ātman sarvajño bhava svāhā*; *oṃ hīṃ ātman aluptaśaktibhir vasu svāhā*;
*oṃ haṃ ātman anantaśaktibhir vasu svāhā*.
Thus, the ritual procedure for initiation is completed.
Now follows the procedure for consecration.

"A Brahmin who has mastered the *Saṃhitā*, who is tranquil, and possesses the characteristics described in the scriptures"—here, among those other than Brahmins, one who is worthy of the preceptor's consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*) is intended. As it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "Now, the excellent preceptor should be a venerable Brahmin, highly skilled and well-disposed."
Śiva is the knower of the truth regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, devoted to his own teaching,
a knower of the truth of the aforementioned triad, one who performs sacrifices, and one who has conquered his senses.
He is patient yet free from pride, causing all beings to tremble;
he is faithful, pure, skillful, consecrated by the glorious initiation, and wise.
He is one who suppresses the fear of horses among gods, asuras, and humans;
for he is neither deficient in stature nor possessed of redundant limbs, but is endowed with auspicious marks.
He who knows the principles of place, time, omens, location, the earth, and colors,
as well as the constellations, and who is skilled in the rite of seizing land;
One who knows the reality of acceptance, who has constructed the auspicious pavilion,
who understands the rites pertaining to the authority of the scriptures, and who knows the subsequent procedures;
He is skilled in the ritual of the six paths and preeminent in the procedure for the Caṇḍayāga;
he knows the rite of consecration and understands the primary practices of bathing and worship.
He is a master of yoga, one who has transcended vows, and a knower of the scriptures on the method of transmigration;
he understands all procedures for the departure [of the soul] and is skillful in the rites of Śiva.
"Likewise in the mental [discipline], in yoga, and in the rules for the water-pot.
Also, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Now, one who is endowed with generosity, compassion, dexterity, self-restraint, and faith..."
There, those whose doubts have been consumed by the fire of knowledge [attain] the collection of the essential.
The wise one, whose essence is the initiation of Śiva, is dear to the Āpāśakins and Miśas;
therein resides the reality that protects the great treasury and worships Śiva.
If one possesses conduct inherited from the tradition of the scriptures, is born in a meritorious land,

has excellent limbs of the body, and a deep voice like that of a peacock— if he is not afflicted by disease and is pleasing to the eye through right knowledge— then for that very reason it is said in the *Mokṣakārikā*:

223) Regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*), [it is said] "as if for the sake of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) among the four castes"; thus, while there is eligibility (*adhikāra*) for the status of a teacher (*guru*), it is proclaimed that this applies only to a Brāhmaṇa. Even in such cases, [the duties include] study, discipline, sacrifice, and so forth.

It is heard that [the status of] a Brāhmaṇa alone [is prescribed]; however, in his absence, the status of being a teacher (ācārya) for Kṣatriyas and others is also heard. As it is said in the venerable Parākhyatantra: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya are teachers for all three classes."
One who knows the purpose of vision and action should initiate both Vaiśyas and Śūdras as well.
In the venerable *Kiraṇa* as well, it is stated:
"The status of being an *ācārya* here is declared for all four castes;
among the group of four beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, the twice-born is not considered the one who performs the initiation (*grāhakṛt*)."
A Kṣatriya preceptor should initiate those belonging to the three classes beginning with the Kṣatriya;
a Vaiśya should initiate those belonging to the two classes beginning with the Vaiśya, as well as a Śūdra.
Thus [it is said].

Also in the illustrious *Sarvajñānottara*: "Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are pure practitioners (*sādhaka*s), according to their respective castes in order; and the six-faced one (*Ṣaḍānana*) is the teacher (*ācārya*)."
Those who are faithful and free from malice, who understand ritual action, are devoted to it, have been authorized,
and have been consecrated— they are remembered as the benefactors.
One should know that region to be fit for sacrifice where the black antelope roams, O Six-faced One,
and which is inhabited by Brahmins.
Where there are Brahmins of virtuous conduct, ascetics whose wealth is their austerity,
and likewise gods, one should designate that as a holy land.
