The teachers born in that region and family, who are esteemed by the scriptures,
are constantly devoted to the Śiva-scriptures and are more intent on Śiva than upon the sacrificial fire.

Thus, when the preceptor, despite seeking one, does not find a Brahmin who is his own equal, and he himself becomes desirous of transmitting his authority, then, for the sake of ensuring the non-interruption of his own lineage and for the purpose of transmitting his authority,
he may consecrate even a distinguished Kṣatriya as his guru.

He, however, should perform the initiation for only three [castes]. Likewise, in the absence of a Kṣatriya, [the Brāhmaṇa and Vaiśya] should perform the initiation for a Śūdra; those two [the Brāhmaṇa and Vaiśya] should also perform the initiation for one or the other [of the remaining castes]. Similarly, disciples too, in the absence of Brāhmaṇas and so forth, should take recourse to Kṣatriyas and so forth. A Brāhmaṇa...

In the absence of Brāhmaṇas, having obtained the authority even for Kṣatriyas and others to ensure the attainment of their own human goals and the non-interruption of their own lineage, he himself should once again establish that authority for all. Nevertheless, it is said that in former times, due to the absence of teachers, students were on the verge of interrupting [the tradition].
It is heard in the scriptures that a Brāhmaṇa, having studied the Vedas from a Vaiśya, taught the Brāhmaṇas. In this way, the meaningfulness of all such statements [is established].

Otherwise, statements such as "the foremost of the twice-born" (*dvijāgryam*) would be rendered meaningless. Now, one might argue that by the word *dvi* ("two"), those who have received initiation (*dīkṣita*) are not meant here; rather, the meaning is "the foremost among them," referring to one appointed to superior knowledge. But what is being postulated [by this interpretation]? That is incorrect, because when the state of being initiated is purified by the word *dvi*, [it refers to] those initiated into Śiva.

Because this would lead to the contingency of rendering the term "one whose bonds are severed" (vicchinnapāśa) redundant; and because if one were to admit that the capacity [for initiation] exists even for those called "elder-born" (agraja), it would result in the redundancy of the phrase "the uninitiated becomes initiated. Furthermore, forest-dwellers (vānaprastha) and renunciants (saṃnyāsin) are not eligible [for this initiation].

As stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*: "In the Śaiva [tradition], there are only two stages of life (*āśrama*), namely the householder and the student; they are the ones who perform grace for the world, for the wandering mendicant and the ascetic are not [so]. Such is the definition of the teacher (*ācārya*) in the *Siddhāntārthasamuccaya*.

Having observed what was taught by the Guru, one proceeds along the path of one's own Lord—consisting of the *kalās*, *tattvas*, worlds (*bhuvanas*), phonemes (*varṇas*), words (*padas*), and mantras, together with their presiding deities; such is the procedure for consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
The meaning of "one should place" (nyaset) is that one should place [the mantra] upon Śiva precisely before the rite of dismissal (visarjana).

226) Now, the extraction of the vow (*vratoddhāra*), [intended] for those seeking to grasp [the essence]. This is also indicative of [the case of] one who is incapable. Now, the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*).

"Devoid of the neuter (*ṣaṇḍa*)" means devoid of the neuter vowels beginning with *ṛ*. "Joined with the fifth long [vowel]" means joined with the fourteenth vowel; after that, it is joined with the sixth vowel. "Crowned by the half-moon, the resonance (*nāda*), and so forth"—by the word "half-moon," the *nirodhaka* is also implied.

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of *nāda*, *nādānta*, *śakti*, *vyāpinī*, *samana*, and *unmanā*. By the word "bindu," there is also the inclusion of the *nakāra* and the *mātrā*. Thus, the utterance of the Śiva-mantra joined with these twelve *mātrās* constitutes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the Śiva- and Praṇava-syllables.

There is a pervasion of the aforementioned Śiva-mantra as well as the Praṇava of that same nature throughout the adhyātma (the internal self), adhidaivata (the presiding deities), and adhibhūta (the physical elements). This occurs through the mouth of the Guru in the following manner: within the adhyātma, [it resides] in the mūlādhāra and other centers; within the adhidaivata, in Brahmā and others, as well as Sadyojāta and the rest; and within the adhibhūta, in the earth and other elements.
"It is obtained" means "from the mouth of the Guru. The mouth of the Guru refers to the Guru who is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara).

Since He alone is the Guru even for the Vidyeśvaras and others, the word "mouth" (*vaktra*) denotes the power (*śakti*) whose nature is both speech (*vacana*) and protection (*trāṇa*). By [the phrase] "by that which is the locus of its manifestation,"...
It is understood through the *Kuṇḍalīpariṇati-siddhānta-śāstra* by means of the mouth of one's own nature (*svarūpa-vaktra*), which is Brahman, because its form is light (*prakāśa*). (p.
Regarding the term "conjoined" (*saṃyukta*): among the vowels beginning with *madhya* (the middle vowel), [it refers to] the short form of *e* and *o*.
This was established there by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha in his commentary on the *Śrīmat Kālottara*.
As for the phrase "conjoined with the long vowels of the limbs" (*aṅganādīrghasaṃyukta*), it refers to the four [mantras] beginning with the Heart and ending with the Armor.

Regarding the phrase "with the anusvāra for the eye," this means that the letter *ha* joined with the *anusvāra* constitutes "Netravant. Furthermore, the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha has stated therein that the distinction between this mantra of the eye and Sadyojāta-Brahman is to be understood through the syllable *li*. The [mantra] of the weapon (*astra*) would be joined with the *visarga*, that is, accompanied by the *visarjanīya*.

The syllable *ha* is the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*). Regarding "of all the seat-mantras": for all the mantras beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with Śivāsana, one should employ their respective names preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ) and the Heart-mantra (Namaḥ), followed by the fourth case-ending and joined with the word of salutation (*namas*).

Regarding the mantra of Caṇḍeśvara, the Lord of the Gaṇas: one should perform the conceptualization of Brahman for the syllables of his own name, beginning with the letter *ā* and so forth, according to the proper method. As for the primary limb (*mūlāṅga*), however, that [should be done] according to the very *Paddhati* of the venerable Somaśambhu, concerning those meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇās*).

"Lavarayā" refers to the group beginning with Nivṛtti and others, as well as the other [energies] distinct from Muktā, such as Avajñā and so forth; for these, the application of the generic form is "na svāhā," using the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) and the others ending with "svāhā. In rites for specific desires (*kāmya*) and the like, such as worship and fire-offerings (*homa*), the formula "na svāhā" applies to all of them.
The practice should be performed. Regarding the phrase "with the fifth vowel and the bindu":
the fifth vowel is *u*, and it is joined with that *bindu* [to form *ū*].

The third [syllable] of the third group is the letter *ya*; following the initial *praṇava*, it is the conjunct syllable beginning with *ha* accompanied by the *visarga*. This is the *mṛtyuñjaya-mantra*; such is the extraction of the mantra.
Now follows the funeral rite.

"Of the gurus, sādhakas, and sons. Now, it may be asked: by means of the initiation into liberation (nirvāṇadīkṣā), the purification of all bonds (pāśas) has been accomplished through the enjoyment of worldly experiences and so forth;
as for the *prārabdha* [karma], its exhaustion occurs through experience; and as for the portion of impurity (*mala*) that acts as its auxiliary—
Daily bathing leads to auspiciousness; the destruction [of past karma] occurs through rituals such as worship, recitation (*japa*), and fire-oblations (*homa*).

The destruction of intentional omissions of prescribed duties and the performance of prohibited acts occurs through expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Therefore, for what purpose is this funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*)? True.

For those who, after initiation, unintentionally fail to perform prescribed duties and engage in prohibited conduct, the *antyeṣṭi* (funeral rite) is performed. Regarding the sequence beginning with "unborn" (*ajātādi*) and so forth: one should place the Brahmins associated with the *sadyojāta* mantra and the others upon the branches starting from the little finger and ending at the thumb; [likewise] upon the limbs.

The placement of Brahmā, Sadyojāta, and the others must indeed be performed; having done so in the form of the earth and the other elements, [one should visualize them] with yellow and other colors, such as sovereignty and the rest.

"In due order" means that by means of their respective nourishment, one should worship [the powers] ending with sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and virtue (*dharma*)— as opposed to non-sovereignty, non-dispassion, ignorance, and vice— in the directions starting from the west and proceeding to the north, east, and south. "And likewise Manonmanī and the others" refers to Manonmanī, who subdues all beings.

One should worship Balapramathinī, Balavikaraṇī, Kalavikaraṇī, Kālī, Raudrī, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Karṇikā, Īśānā, and the others, starting from the northeast (Īśāna) and ending with the east. Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa [of the deity] by means of Sadyojāta and the others— namely Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna— one should worship them from the feet to the top of the head.

One should perform worship. One should worship the weapon (*astra*), armor (*kavaca*), crest (*śikhā*), head (*śiras*), and heart (*hṛdaya*) mantras, from the weapon up to the heart. One should also worship the weapon, armor, and so forth upon the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*). Having invoked Śiva, one should worship him; thus, one should perform worship ending with the offering of the recitation (*japa*). One should sacrifice to Śiva there in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

There too, one should worship precisely in reverse order. Regarding the phrase "resorting to the *ātivāhika*": merit and demerit, which are self-created, are carried beyond through experience; thus, by means of the application of the great net (*mahājāla*) of the subtle body that carries [the soul], it is called the mudrā known as the Great Net (*mahājālamudrā*).

The specific arrangement of the hands is manifested here. Having purified the self— situated anywhere according to the influence of merit and demerit obtained through the opening [of the channels] by the power of Śiva—
by means of the self-conjoined with the self, encapsulated within the heart, and united with the seed-syllable of the self, under the name of initiation (dīkṣā).
"One should place the corpse's body within the heart-lotus; one should perform everything according to the procedure for initiation.
Having said this, [it is taught that] beginning with the bestowal of the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta), everything must be performed.
Alternatively, having established [the fire] in the fire-pit according to the requirements of place, time, and substance, this other option is as follows:

"O Agni, you have reached the end of your time"—thus addressing the fire presided over by Śiva as "O Agni," you, being capable, should perform the concluding rite; therefore, [I say], "you have been brought forth by Time itself."

Because of the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma, this sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) is prescribed for one who has died by hanging or other such means as a result of the sequential attainment [of death]; according to their view, when the other [prescribed] time has passed, this sacrifice must be performed after first offering the *rudrabali* and other oblations, with a representative image [of the deceased].

According to the Smṛti statement, "for them [the period is] a year by way of the path of sin," this [rite] must be performed at that very time for those who have died an untimely death through lack of prior awareness; however,
before the offering of the Śrāddha, the Rudra-bali must be performed using Darbha grass and an image.
This must be done. The number of those *darbha* grasses is to be understood from the statement of Āpastamba:
"If one who has gone abroad has died and is not known [to have perished], then the number of *palāśa* wood pieces is prescribed;
in that case, the number of *darbha* grasses is also to be adopted."

There are one hundred and sixty-three blades of darbha grass. With forty of these, the head is fashioned; ten for the neck; twenty for the two arms; thirty for the belly; fifty for each of the two thighs;
five for each of the fingers; and seventy for each of the two shanks.

On those [bricks], one should fashion a human figure upon a black antelope skin, with five fingers for each foot, eight for the penis, and twelve for the testicles; thus, with three hundred and sixty-three [bricks], one should construct the image. Thus is the representation.

Having performed that [preparation], one should carry out the deposition (*nyāsa*) upon the pedestal (*talanyāsa*), according to the procedure taught by the venerable Sarvajña, like the consecration of a clay image.
As it is said in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*: "And these principles (*tattva*) [should be worshipped] with *kalikā* and *karavīra* flowers."
Having recited it, the practitioner of mantra should perform the placement (vinyāsa) with the [five] embryos once the *puṃnālīka* has been formed.
Having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow and auspicious water using the seed-syllable of the weapon-mantra,
and having consecrated it with water endowed with qualities, one should place its name in the heart.
Having meditated upon his form in that manner, one should contemplate three channels;
one should place Śuddhavidyā in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus,
and having visualized Śakti in the partless (niṣkala) station, [one should visualize] all [the channels] facing downwards.
One should place the god Sadāśiva above the uvula at the crown of the head;
there, one should place the circle of Śakti, which is conjoined and dissolved therein.
One should apply the Vidyā there, in the middle of the tongue;
the practitioner of mantra should place the eight Vidyeśvaras on the tongue and at the joints of the arms.
One should indeed place Māyā on the left side and Kāla on the right;
having established Kalā upon the chest, one should place Nīlalohita in the heart.
In that regard, moreover, another form of knowledge is traditionally taught concerning that very person:
passion is its coloring agent, while its characteristic is the awakening of knowledge.
Having meditated upon the Unmanifest within the belly, one should place the subtle elements at the navel:
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth.
Having placed the qualities upon the spinal column, and likewise the three persons there;
[he places them] between the navel and the penis, and at the joints of the intellect and the ego.
One should place the god Vyomeśvara in the womb within the center of the void;
right there one should join Vāyu, the secret [element], and the extracted eightfold secret.
When the fire residing in the seat of bile moves from within the womb toward the region of Varuṇa below, that is the time when the circle of birth occurs.
One should place [the syllables] beneath the circle of his feet down to the very edge of the soles;
outside of that, one hundred Rudras.
The interior space of that very [structure] extends as far as the pegs at the ankles;
one should install the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara at the beginning of the world-space.
And those hells in Pātāla that are devoid of praise.
With the big toe, O Lord of Gods, [he should touch] Kālā...
having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) starting from the first day until the end of the tenth, joined with that mantra.
Having worshipped [the deceased] with their respective mantras and having given clothing, food, sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and so forth to a Brāhmaṇa,
when the fire of the funeral pyre has been extinguished, one should perform the purification rites (*ku-saṃskāra*) and the cremation (*agni-saṃskāra*), and then... [the remainder of the sentence].
Having offered three oblations for the principles (tattvas) beginning with Earth— that is, for those starting from Earth and ending with Śiva—
one should never transgress the non-Vedic practice. Now, it may be objected that it is said that Brāhmaṇas and others must perform the observance of Vedic rites.
How should the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*) for one who has performed the *agnihotra* and possesses latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth be performed?

Is it not the case that, as with the *saṃdhyāvandana* and other rituals, he is first cremated by the Vedic fire and afterwards by the Śaiva fire? How could this [latter] be considered improper? Thus, previously...

Since [the deceased] has been reduced to a mere residue burnt by the Vedic fire, the final rite (*antyeṣṭi*) must be performed when all [impurities] have become auspicious (*śiva*). By that statement, the final rite pertains precisely to the absence of [remaining] objects. According to others, having first performed the Vedic rites prior to the cremation, the final rite is performed afterwards.

234) [Some] maintain that, having performed [the rite] without the casting into the fire (*agniprakṣepa*), one should subsequently perform the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) after performing the cremation with both fires. Others [hold that this applies] by virtue of being the performers of those [acts] that are not prohibited.

They consider that the *pitṛmedha* rite, being contrary to the *Śruti*, must be abandoned. Others maintain that after performing the cremation up to the *dahara* stage by means of the recitation of mantras, the final funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*) should then be performed. Still others, however, hold that after performing the *pitṛmedha* consecration, one should wait for twelve days.

And having established that the final funeral rites (*paramantyeṣṭi*) must be performed, [it is concluded that] in the first case, when the specialized fire (*viśeṣāgni*) has been consecrated by the general fire (*sāmānyāgni*), a penance (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed by Bhojadeva; for there are scriptural statements such as: "While dwelling and remaining in a place where a fault exists due to the breaking [of the fire], one should protect the *Śivadharma*," and so forth.
Because it is stated as something to be performed by one who desires Vedic results, there is no contradiction with the Vedic injunctions;
since it is not in conflict with the third and fourth [stages of life],
the Vedic consecration (*saṃskāra*) is like the final consecration established in the Siddhānta.

This is indeed in accordance with the established scriptures (*siddhāntaśāstra*). As it is said: "Whosoever, while remaining in whichever stage of life (*āśrama*), receives initiation whose essence is Śiva, he should dwell at the end [of his life], remain steadfast, and protect [the teachings] as if they were himself.
Householders established on the worldly path should not overstep the worldly conduct;
likewise, those who have been initiated should act in accordance with what is well-known among the people.
Even if one were a knower of the three worlds and capable of attracting the three realms,
one should not transgress even slightly the worldly conduct; for this is well-established in the world, as seen from the observation of its own internal consistency.
He must be protected by blameless men for the sake of ultimate liberation, and he must also be properly supported by them.

A householder should never transgress Vedic conduct; this has been stated even by the venerable Sadyojyoti in the *Mokṣakārikā*: "Thus, the conducts of the castes and stages of life are authorized. And since that [conduct] is to be accepted even by those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), therefore...
Regarding those who have renounced even the means superior to the fruits [of worldly life] and are devoted to true austerity— such as those who carry clods of earth on their heads—
it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅgapārameśvara* that the performance of Vedic rites is optional (*pākṣikatva*).
Furthermore, there is no fixed rule regarding beginning or end for ascetics who are free from attachment.

This has been stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva* [Tantra] concerning the transcendence of worldly conventions: "But the other [type of ascetic] is characterized by dispassion and is averse to worldly objects."
One may perform the Brāhmī initiation or not; for my [initiation] is that which belongs to Śiva.
Therefore, the Vedic and Śaiva consecrations must necessarily be performed,
especially according to the venerable Svāyambhuva-śāstra.

Furthermore, because this has been demonstrated at the conclusion of the section on funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*) in both the *Śrīmadbrahmaśambhupaddhati* and the *Vimalaśivapaddhati*. [The phrase] "at the end of the eleventh year" refers to the fact that the intermediate-period (*antardaśā*) ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*), the single-ancestral offering (*ekoddiṣṭa*), the annual increase (*vṛddhi*), and so forth, function as the initiators of the physical body.
Because it is so heard [in scripture], the ritual procedure prescribed here for the Śiva-śrāddha is established as being the same;
thus, at the Ekādaśāha-śrāddha, the inclusion of the Viśvedevas and the fire-oblation (agnihoma) are not to be performed. [The rule is:
"First the ancestors, afterwards the Viśvedevas, facing east and facing north."
Having offered oblations to Rudra and Ananta in the order of south and north respectively,

and to Īśāna and the others starting from the east and ending with the west, one should offer three times with their names ending in *svadhā*, *namaḥ*, and *svāhā*; and to Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta, one should offer each time with the word *namaḥ* following their respective names.

Three oblations are to be performed with the mantras ending in *svadhā*, *namaḥ*, and *svāhā*. Regarding the householder, while kneeling on the ground, one should prepare two *kūrca* grass mats for the paternal ancestors who have not yet descended into the earth, and the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) should be performed using their names ending in *svadhā*.
The rites performed with the water-offering (arghya) following the general one, using that same portion, are for the sake of the prosperity of the performer;
however, they are not for the sake of the deceased, because their purpose has already been fulfilled.
Thus ends the rule for the final sacrifice (antyēṣṭi).
Now follows the ritual procedure for consecration.

Regarding "on an auspicious day": during the period of the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa), in the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), on a day endowed with an auspicious lunar date (tithi), asterism (nakṣatra), weekday (vāra), planetary hour (gahorā), decan (drekkāṇa), division (aṃśaka), and the rising of benefic planets, the consecration—meaning the taking of the stone and so forth—should be performed. Regarding "in the taking of the stone and so forth," by the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi), wood is also intended.
It is stated: "Speckled with black spots" (*abinduśabalām*). Here, the term *kārabindu* (black spot) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (metaphorical indicator) for other defects of stone as well.
As it says in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
One should abandon the bark of trees that is split, scorched by forest fires, or stripped of its sound,
yet variegated with waves of ash and stainless drops.
Even if it possesses one flaw or lacks lines,
the commentary on this sūtra states that, having entered the field situated in the intended direction,
the artisan should examine it there for softness by means of blows from a chisel with an even touch, according to the words spoken by the Teacher.

One should abandon [a site] that is divided, burnt by fire, devoid of sound, or similarly characterized by *puṭas* shaped like the *śakti*, by *kīlas*, by sprouts, by waves resembling surging billows,
by those resembling crystal, by those causing the destruction of many metal vessels, and by impure *kāṇikās*.
[It is] threefold: by subtle [particles], by drops like lightning on a separate stone while still in the womb, and likewise at the time of formation by the frog and the fish.

One should also discard that [leaf] which has fragments resembling snakes upon its own surface— white, jewel-like, and yellow— and upon which there exist rows of lines consisting of white, black, red, and yellow, arranged in the order "hitā nā" (beneficial for the white, deficient for the black, red for the red, and yellow for the yellow). As it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga-piṅgalāmata*:

As stated by Mahīnakha and Mahīnārekhokta, [the mantra] beginning with "āśubhe" is known; "raḥ" signifies the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*). By the word "mūrdhan," the upper portion is intended—whether that be the back portion, the head portion, or the Īśāna portion—for the sake of the *mūrti* and for the purpose of offering the *brahmāhuti*.
One who desires non-play (or liberation) should perform [the rite] starting from the portion of Brahmā; one who desires enjoyment should perform it starting from the portion of Rudra.

One should have the artisan fashion the desired *liṅga* itself, whether it be made of stone or other materials. Among these nine types, ranging from one cubit (*hasta*) up to nine cubits, there are three categories based on the distinction of inferior, middling, and superior: namely, those divided into three cubits, six cubits, and nine cubits.

Regarding the lingas, starting from the lowest of the low at one cubit, one should fashion thirty-three lingas along with the others up to the highest; "purification by the Aghora-weapon" means purification of the ground. By "by the power and so forth," the word "and so forth" refers to the shadow of the power (śakticchāyā).
The constellations Puṣya, Pūṣan, Maghā, and others are included. Having recited [the mantra], one should touch [the object] with kuśa grass;
the recitation should be performed according to the number of oblations.

"Having meditated upon the site according to the scriptures"—this refers to the characteristics of the Vāstupuruṣa as stated in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*: "One should visualize the Vāstu as having an unbent armor, being naked, and possessing a divine form; for the purposes of worship, he is situated within the walls and so forth, with his face turned downwards."
His knees are joined to his elbows; he faces the wind (northwest) and fire (southeast);
his feet are in the direction of the ancestors (south), his head in the direction of Rudra (east), and his heart is in the *añjali* gesture.
"The auspicious deities are worshipped as being mounted upon his body"— thus,

from two cubits (*vasu*) up to twenty-one fingers (the end of the lunar days), the construction of the bathing pavilion for the eight other types of *liṅgas* proceeds by an increase of one finger per cubit.
"Twice that of the sun and so forth" means that the consecration pavilion for the other eight lingas should be constructed starting from two cubits and increasing by one and a half cubits each.
In the center of those two, a sacrificial altar (vedi) should be marked out with a width of one and a half [cubits].
Between those two— the bathing pavilion and the consecration pavilion— one should construct a hall (dhāma) marked out [therein],
measuring half the width of the pavilion, with its dimensions designated from eight finger-breadths up to one cubit; that is, starting from two cubits down to a single finger-breadth.
The height of the altar (vedi) should be made such that it does not exceed two finger-breadths, up to one cubit.

Having placed the general offering-vessel (arghyakara) in the directions starting from the east in sequence, this is called the worship of the pavilion (maṇḍapapūjā). In that regard, concerning the worship of the doors of the installation pavilion (pratiṣṭhāmaṇḍapa):
The statements beginning with "the two, the two" regarding those who dwell in the eight great continents, as found in other [texts], are due to the grasping of worldly conventions. (p. 240)

Other deities are also to be worshipped. Namely: at the eastern gate, there is the archway of Peace (Śāntitoraṇa), the *Ṛgveda*, the Kṛtayuga, and on the archway’s trident, the Suns known as Pūṣan, Dhātṛ, and Vidhātṛ; and in the two jars situated near its branches, the two deities Praśānta and Śiras.
The two planets Soma and Bhauma, along with Bhūrloka and Bhuvarloka, are the dawn and light upon the upper udumbara cloth; Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, and Mahālakṣmī are upon the two jars;
Nandin and Mahākāla, as well as the rivers Gaṅgā and Yamunā, are upon the jar of Indra.

Īśvara is the presiding deity (adhidaivata); the *ava* and *ka* groups of consonants are the two syllabic classes; Tatpuruṣa is the Brahman; and the Astra-mantra is on the Udumbara post. In the south-eastern direction, Agni is in the pitcher. Thus is the worship of the eastern door. Now, at the southern door: Bhūti is at the corner, the Yajurveda, the Tretā Yuga, and the trident at the archway (*toraṇa*).
The triad of suns known as Bhaga, Parjanya, and Indra [is located] in the two jars situated at the base of the branches;

the two deities Parjanya and Ākāśa [preside over] the heavenly world (svarga) and the Mahāloka. Then Bṛhaspati is the object that is neither inferior nor superior among those planets. Gaṇapati and Sarasvatī are in the *udumbara* tree above.
The Mahālakṣmīs; the door of the Vidyā-kalā; Bhṛṅgin and Vināyaka as the two door-keepers; the rivers Narmadā and Sarasvatī; in the pitcher (kumbha), Yama and Rudra as the presiding deities;
the group of letters from *va* to *da*, known as Aghora-Brahman; and below the door-post (dumbara), the Astra-mantra in the pitcher located in the southwest (nairṛta).
In the Nirṛti-pitcher (p.
241), Brahmā is the lord of the site (vāstvadhipati) in the pitcher; Viṣṇu is the guardian of the lower world (adholokapāla). Thus.

Worship of the Southern Door. Now, the worship of the Western Door: the Sāma Veda, the Dvāpara Yuga, and the triple-pronged arch (toraṇa). Upon the trident of the arch are the three suns known as Aryaman, Mitra, and Tvaṣṭṛ. In the two jars situated on the branches of the arch are the two deities Bhūtasaṃjīvana and Amṛta.

The two planets Śukra and Śanaiścara, known as Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, [preside over] Janoloka and Tapoloka; the door to the kalās of Vastu and Nivṛtti is at the upper *udumbara* [beam]; Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, and Mahālakṣmī are at the two jars (*kumbha*);
the two door-keepers are Vṛṣabha and Skanda; and the two rivers are Buddhā and Godāvarī, located at the jar.

Varuṇa and Mahālakṣmī, with Brahmā as the presiding deity, [are worshipped] in the water-pitcher; the *tavarga* and *pavarga* consonant groups, and the *Sadyojāta* mantra of Brahman [are worshipped]. Then, on the Udumbara pillar in the northwest corner, the *Astra* (Weapon) mantra, and in the two pitchers, Vāyu and Gaṇapati—this is the worship of the western door. Now, for the northern door: the Ārogya archway and the Atharvaveda.

The Kali Yuga is at the trident of the archway; the three suns named Viṣṇu, Savitṛ, and Śubhada are at the base of the branches; the two deities Dhanada and Śrīprada are in the two jars situated at the base of the branches; Satyaloka and Dhruvaloka are the planets Rāhu and Ketu; the Kalā door is established in the jar and the upper udumbara post.
Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, and Mahālakṣmī [are worshipped] on the two jars; the goddess Caṇḍī and the two door-keepers [are worshipped] on the jar and the northeast [corner];

and likewise the preceptors (gurus) [are worshipped]. Thus is the worship of the pavilion (maṇḍapa). [This is performed] with their respective names, joined with the Praṇava (Oṃ), the Heart-mantra (Namaḥ), the dative case ending, and ending in the word of salutation (namaskāra).
242) Afterwards, the ritual action should be performed, and worship should be conducted as usual through the western gate.
Furthermore, [one should perform it] in other wheels, as well as among the grasses, the bindings, the bamboos, and the stalks.
One should worship the principles (tattvas) beginning with the five elements (pañcabhūta) and earth (kṣiti) with the [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta.
[The attendants are] Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Śaṅkukarṇa, and likewise Śarva; [these are located] in the Triṇetra and Sumukha [faces].
And the presiding deities of the banners are named Saṃjñika and Supratiṣṭhita;
they are surrounded by the limits of existence (bhūtakoṭi) in the cardinal directions beginning with the east.
Hetu, Hantri, and Puraghna; Vajra, Dharma, and Nijjihva; Kālī and Karālī as the sixth; Ekāṅghri and Mahimā, which bestows the eightfold [attainments].
In the same manner, one should worship the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas) in the directions in due order;
one should also worship these [other deities] as desired.
Regarding the bed: "One should place [the image] with its head toward the northeast and its face level"—this is the general rule here.

The state of having Īśāna as the head has been mentioned. Specifically, however, the arrangement of the bed according to the division between the western and eastern doors is described in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*.
One should place [the deities] upon an auspicious seat, beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti.
In the Prasāda temple, one should place Śiva, who faces west, in the center facing east;
then, one should install his pedestal (piṇḍikā) and the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā) in the western part.
In that case, it would belong to the former [deity] first, because of the reversal;
having raised the *liṅga* onto the seat previously described, with its head facing east, from the *dvādaśānta*.
Regarding the manner of reciting the mantra at the time of the deposition of life (jīvanyāsa), it has been stated by Ācārya Somaśambhu:
"Having brought [the breath] from the bulb of the navel, there is a spreading forth like the resonance of a bell."
By abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, it is established at the limit of the twelve finger-breadths (dvādaśānta).
And having brought forth the mantra, which is non-different from the mind and from which the surge of the essence of bliss arises,
one should draw it from the *dvādaśānta* along with the spreading resonance of a bell.
Having brought down from the *dvādaśānta* the partless, all-pervading Śiva,
who is endowed with thirty-eight *kalās* and resplendent with a thousand rays;

"Having meditated upon [the deity] as consisting of all powers (sarvaśaktimaya) and complete with all limbs (sāṅga), one should install [him] in the liṅga. Thus, the installation of the life-force (jīvanyāsa) in the liṅga becomes the accomplisher of all goals.

This refers to the system of five sacrificial pits (pañcakuṇḍa-pakṣa), where the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) are the lords of the forms (mūrtīśās) corresponding to their respective [five] axes (kuṇṭhas).

The Mūrtipās (image-priests) and Upahotṛs, having performed the installation of their respective Mūrtīśvaras in the east, south, north, and west— up to the Puruṣa [mantra]— and having worshipped the mantras of Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta, should offer oblations with them. In the case of nine sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*), [they should offer] in these eastern and other pits, as well as in the southeast, northeast, and...

In the eight pits (kuṇḍas) located in the directions of the Ṛtus and Vāyavya, one should worship the four Brahmans— the Heart, Head, Crest, and Armor— and perform oblations in both cases; furthermore, in the northeast corner is the pit of the Preceptor (ācārya), which is associated with Īśāna.

At the time of the installation of the *brahmaśilā*, as stated in the passage beginning with "one should install the *brahmaśilā* resting upon the Śakti," it is said that the Guru, having contemplated the entire path and that which is mounted upon it, [performs the rite].

For it has been stated that even the sixfold path (*adhvan*), consisting of time (*kāla*), reality (*tattva*), world-sphere (*bhuvana*), word (*pada*), and mantra, resides within the Brahma-stone (*brahmaśilā*). Furthermore, the powers (*śakti*) which bear witness to the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the liṅga situated above this [stone] make known nothing other than the Śiva-reality (*śivatattva*). And in the world, by means of expressive mantras...

One should perform the deposition of the *cicchakti* (consciousness-power) upon the *liṅga*, accompanied by the seed-syllables beginning with *la* and the names of Indra and the other [guardians], while offering oblations (*varāhuti*) as prescribed.
This is because it is stated that the *cicchakti* is to be deposited in the *liṅga*; thus, the *liṅga* is the *jñānaśakti* (knowledge-power).
However, the *bindu* and so forth, which constitute the *kriyāśakti* (action-power), are to be placed upon the *pīṭha* (the seat). Thus, it is said: "upon the *pīṭha*."

Because the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is that which is to be projected, it is called the "power of action of the seat" (*pīṭha-kriyā-śakti*); furthermore, this too does not consist of *mahāmāyā*.
As it is said in the *Śrīmanmaya*:
"Now, the seat consisting of action is that which is to be presided over by the Lord, whose nature is the power of consciousness."

In the venerable *Mṛgendra* as well, regarding the sūtra "The pedestal (*pīṭha*) of the Lord is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*)," the commentary states: "That which is the nature of the pedestal, the support for the *liṅga* consisting of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), is this power of action belonging to the Supreme Lord."

The substratum of this power, which is free from the reproaches regarding its relation [to the object] and is characterized by its own nature, is Śiva, who consists of consciousness and is established in himself. As it is said in the *Ratnatraya*:
The instruments (*karaṇa*) are synonymous with *śakti* and *vāsanā*; the mantras do not exist there [independently].

Worship is performed upon the foundation-stone (*ādhāraśilā*) of both the Foundation Power (*ādhāraśakti*) and the Seat of Ananta (*anantāsana*). However, for Ananta and the others, worship is on the pedestal (*pīṭha*) itself; therein, Ananta is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).

It is logical that [the first element] abides there as its primary object. Since the four [elements], beginning with *dharma*, consist of its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), they abide therein. Furthermore, the [other elements], beginning with *māṃsa* (flesh), likewise abide in that same manner, by virtue of being the lower covering, the upper covering, and the enclosure.

Because the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is all-pervasive, it resides within the bulb (*kanda*), the seed, the sprout, the stalk, the lotus petals, the filaments, and the pericarp; for these constitute the domain of the manifestation of the power of action, which is itself the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*). As for the powers such as Vāmā and the rest—
Śiva’s power itself, which is differentiated by its presiding over [the worlds] beginning with Ananta and so forth, is indeed the Unmanifest Mind (Manonmanī) when not yet conditioned;
the three Śakti-maṇḍalas are the Bindu-spheres, and their presiding deities are specific divine beings who dwell in both the pure and impure realms. However, the Śivāsana belongs to the Supreme Lord.

The nature of this Kuṇḍalinī is that which is eternally presided over by an inherent power, the sphere of the manifestation of the creative energy (*kriyā-śakti*) that serves as the support for the entire universe; she who extends from the infinite *nada* up to the seat of Śiva (*śivāsana*), encompassing all of these.
In this seat (*pīṭha*), which is the very nature of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) of the mantras, there is the non-entry of the cause of the power of action;
here, [it is called] the *śivaliṅga* by virtue of the calculation of the three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*). (p. 246) [It consists of] four and eight-sided [forms].
Circularity is observed; therein, the designation of the portions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra is heard.
Among those, the squareness of the portion of Brahmā and the designation of the portion of Brahmā are heard.
Therein, the squareness of the portion of Brahmā and the designation of the portion of Brahmā [are heard].
Due to the proximity of Brahman— which sustains the pure phenomenal world that constitutes the object of knowledge— to the Śivaliṅga whose nature is the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti),
it possesses the designation "the portion of Brahman" (brahmabhāga) and the quality of being four-cornered (caturaśratva); and Brahman [itself] has four faces.
Above that, because Viṣṇu is denoted [by the term], and because he serves as the sustainer of the mixed state which constitutes the object of knowledge,
he is described in the scriptures as being above Viṣṇu; and since he is the support for the selves associated with the Paryaṅka [seat], his eight-cornered nature is established by that very means.
As it is stated in the venerable *Varuṇapaddhati*:
"Resembling a blue lotus, brilliant white, endowed with eight faces and eight arms,
and possessing a single face with a gentle countenance— this is proclaimed as the *vidyātattva*."

Above that, regarding the fact that this portion is designated as the portion of Rudra (*rudrabhāga*), one should understand that the pure phenomenal world (*śuddhaprapañca*) which constitutes its manifestation, along with Rudra—who possesses limbs marked by the figure of Rudra-Bhaṭṭāraka—is expressed by the point (*bindu*).
Since the point is circular, it is circular; thus, Śiva in the form of the point is the object of meditation.

Because of the scriptural statement; because the Cause, who is the Lord of the Śiva-tattva, is denoted by the word Rudra, there is indeed no other internal distinction here between those known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. [The power] presiding over that consists of knowledge.

Śiva-Śakti alone is the *liṅga*. Here, upon this *liṅga-pīṭha* made of stone and other materials, at the time of consecration (*adhivāsa*), there are the eight forms beginning with Earth (*pṛthivī*), the five forms beginning with Space (*ākāśa*), the [five] beginning with Sound (*śabda*), the [four] beginning with Brahmā, and their presiding deities; all these are installed within it as belonging to the Supreme Lord.

The word "mūrti" (form) serves to exclude the notion that the entity being grasped is the subject under discussion [the individual soul]. Furthermore, since all entities depend upon the Supreme Lord as their presiding authority, there is no inherent portion of existence whatsoever; rather, there is the pervasive Śiva-portion which brings about the cessation of the two-fold continuum.

"In which no presiding deity is found. Thus, although this [Śiva] is also pervaded by Śakti— which, though designated as "Earth" and so forth through conventional usage, is designated by all the names of the directions— and by Śiva, who is designated by all those names, yet those various forms of Śakti belong to him.

The power of installation (*pratiṣṭhā-śakti*), according to the stated method, consists of bathing, fire-oblation (*homa*), recitation (*japa*), meditative absorption (*samādhi*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and so forth;

it is not destroyed by conjunction with that which impairs the seed’s power to produce a sprout, for that is the subject at hand. However, their ritual placement (*nyāsa*) does not [impair it]; therefore, through this bestowal of action upon the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*pīṭha*), the power of knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā-śakti*) [is established].

It is made manifest; just as fire residing in the fire-drill is made manifest by friction, so too is consciousness within that common sign (liṅga). Because it is not worshipped by initiates, yet is common to the world, it is "common" (sādhāraṇya).
248) Regarding that *liṅga*, at the time of the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the conscious life-force (*caitanyajīva*), the deposition of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*) must be performed.
Having set aside the doctrine of consciousness (*caitanyamata*) and having established that [life-force], one should dismiss the *sthāṇu*. "The *sthāṇu*" means...

The meaning is that one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*) in the same manner as before— just as it was done previously for the sake of purification— even for that [mantra] which has been established through the lineage of one's own succession and perfected by the collection of ascetic practices (*tapas*), and which was deposited at the time of the mantra-installation (*nyāsa*); this dismissal must be performed as a constant rite (*nityavat*), even though it depends on [the prior performance of the installation].
"Having first performed the meditation on Caṇḍeśa, one should worship the image of the Liṅga. Now, an objection is raised:

previously, the Liṅga was established as belonging to the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara). Yet now it is heard that worship of Caṇḍeśvara must also be performed upon that same Liṅga. How is this consistent? This [is explained as follows]:...
Whether Caṇḍeśvara is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) distinct from this [deity], or whether he is within the self (ātman), in the case of his being the Supreme Lord,

it is proper— even in another ritual context— to first perform worship with a similar visualization and then offer what has been presented. However, if he is within the self, [the offering is made] in the *liṅga*.

The worship of the *liṅga* is said to be improper. Among those various portions of specialized knowledge (*vijñānakalā*), Caṇḍeśvara is the very inner self (*antarātman*) of that moving being (*cara-bhūta*) in the third enclosure (*tṛtīyāvaraṇa*) consisting of Nandin and others, who have been graced by the Supreme Lord; [this is so] because of the fact that he is presided over by the power of obstruction (*rodhaśakti*).

And Śambhu himself, whose own nature is to be presided over by the power of obstruction (*rodhaśakti*), [binds those] who have fallen from their commitment (*samaya*), according to the scripture: "I bind [those who have fallen from their commitment].
It has not been stated [in the scriptures] that one should perform the hearing of the *samaya* after having established the disciples before oneself;
rather, having established the disciples before him, one should say, "Listen to the *samaya*," and then,
according to the capacity of the power of the obstruction (*rodhaśakti*), [provide] the pure bath, the offering of oblations, the vessels, and so forth.

"The offering of what has already been offered belongs to Caṇḍeśvara, the Supreme Lord; it consists of food to be licked, sucked, and drunk, as well as betel, garlands, and ointments. By the command of Śiva, this remains of the offering (nirmālya) is given to you. Thus it is established.
One should bestow the authority over even the mobile [deities] beginning with the *pīṭhas* upon the devoted practitioners. What need is there to speak of others?

This is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of these manifest signs (*liṅgas*), which is well-established and has been stated in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*: [The text continues with the Sanskrit verse: *sthāvarāṇāṃ tu sarveṣāṃ pīṭhapūrvāṇi yāni ca / teṣāṃ vyāptiṃ pravakṣyāmi yathoktaṃ somabhūbhujā // ... [omitted] ... iti śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhatyām uktam.* Thus it is stated in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*.
Just as other deities and so forth are established by means of mantras arising from their own respective spheres,
or through the differentiation of the first letter, they are meditated upon as pervading their own essential nature.
The gods headed by Sārdha, the rivers, the sages,
the guardians of the fields, the kinnaras, and others— all those who have taken refuge in the earth element.
In some places, Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī abide in the waters of rivers;
and the station of the lords of the worlds is the arrangement of the mechanical contrivances.
The triad of principles ending with the bestowal of the intellect (buddhi) is the station of Brahmā;
the triad beginning with the subtle elements (tanmātra) and ending with primordial matter (pradhāna) is the state of the individual soul (puṃstva), O Hari.
O Gaṇapati, may the station of Nādeśa, the Gaṇas, the Mothers, Yakṣeśa, and the one born of Śaraja (Kārttikeya)—
who are unborn, lords, and pure knowledge— be yours forever.
"Śivā [is] from Māyā up to the limit of Sadāśiva-śakti; Śiva [is] from the Sun (Uṣṇarociḥ) up to Īśvara; and the Unmanifest (Avyakta) is well-proclaimed [to extend] up to that. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Varuṇapaddhati*:
"The pervasion of the linga, the pedestal, and the stone proceeds in order from the principles (tattvas);
furthermore, there is the conceptualization of the three sections extending as far as the seat of Śakti."
Like the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti), that Māyā reaches the limit of the power of space (deśa-śakti);
it extends sequentially through the stone linga-pīṭha, reaching the end of the region where sound is contemplated.
The pervasion of the jar is proclaimed to extend as far as the principle of Māyā;
or alternatively, it extends from the three sections up to the end of the Māyā that consists of a fraction of the mind.
The path of the person (puruṣa) consists of three sections, extending up to the Śabdapuruṣa;
its pervasion is said to be like that of the door, the temple, and the pinnacle of the liṅga.
There, one should sequentially place the triad of Self, Knowledge, and Śiva within the teaching of Knowledge (vidyāśāsana), up to the limit of one's own essential nature (svatattva).
Let there be either eight or five image-protectors; this is the rule.
In the case of a *liṅga*, they are indeed the hands of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, presiding over the ritual of the principles (*tattva*).
Thus it was said: "This entire sequence applies to the images of the deities as well;
however, the installation of the three principles (tattvas) extends up to the knees, the throat, and the head.
Regarding the door, the door-lintel (udumbara), and the door-posts (śākhā), the pervasion (vyāpti) therein consists of the [specific] sections."
One should also contemplate [the goddesses] from the calves up to the neck and crest within the temple;
for Gaurī and the others, one should install the Śakti, whose nature is action (kriyātmikā), upon the pedestal as the object of worship.
The knower should install the Jñānī [deity] within the body; the remainder should be performed as in the case of a pedestal (pīṭha).
Now the procedure for the installation of a face-liṅga (mukhaliṅga) is described.
One should place the principle of Sadāśiva in the center and Īśvara in the east;
one should place Vidyā in the southeast, and Māyā in the south and southwest.
When the wind has reached its fixed course at the proper time, it enters the interior of the arena;
the Pradhāna is in the direction of the Lord (Īśa), and the five Brahmans are in their own respective quarters.

The conceptualization of the three principles (*tritattva*) is as before; however, within the *vṛtta* (circle), one should place Sadāśiva, and likewise the Mūrtis and Tvaras as before. Now, these principles beginning with Earth (*pṛthivī*) [are to be placed] even in the images (*pratimā*) of the Mūrtis, Mūrtīśvaras, and so forth.

Having understood the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the name, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) everywhere according to its nature and as it exists. Earth is established within the water-element, and [the other elements] such as air are each situated in their own respective domain.
Above the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), the Moon and the Sun are situated;
above those two is the one called Dharma, and in the subtle element of smell resides Śarva.
Established in form and existing as a bound soul (paśu), the fierce one resides within the sphere of ego;
therein, taste is to be understood as having the sphere of the subtle element of taste.
Mahādeva, whose abode is the mind, resides in the subtle element of touch belonging to Īśvara;
and Bhīma resides in the subtle element of sound; such is the established arrangement of the forms of the Īśānas.

The Vidyeśvaras are to be known as established within the principle of Vidyā (Vidyātattva). From the earth up to the limit of Pradhāna, that which begins with Brahmā and ends with Māyā is designated as [the sphere of] Āṇava.
Rudra consists of the principles from Earth (kṣmā) up to Knowledge (vidyā); Īśvara consists of those from Earth up to the Bindu;
Sāṃkhya consists of those from Earth up to Nāda; and Śakti consists of those from Earth up to Parā.
The pervasion of others as well should be considered in that very context. Regarding the manifest [form] such as the Bāṇa-liṅga and so forth— that is,
concerning the manifest linga-form— one should worship Caṇḍa and then take [the deity] via the path of the vital breath (prāṇapatha).

The meaning is that one should not perform the installation of Caṇḍa at all; however, this is not a prohibition against the installation of Caṇḍeśvara. Therefore, having placed the disciples in his presence, one should cause them to hear the rules (samaya) equally; thus, the proclamation of the rules takes place in the vicinity of Caṇḍeśvara.

In the phrase "on the sacrificial mound, on the unmanifest, or on a stone, a jewel, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) is intended to include self-manifested (*svayambhū*) and perfected (*siddha*) lingas and the like. This has been stated in the *Śrīmat-somaśambhu-paddhati*:
In the case of a Bāṇaliṅga, a mobile liṅga, a rohaliṅga, a siddhaliṅga, or on the ground,
as well as in all images, Caṇḍa is not authorized;
this applies even when performing the rite of mending a crack while endowed with the realization of non-duality (advaitabhāvanā).
"Having thus established Caṇḍeśa for the cessation of fierce defects," and so forth;

by the passage beginning with "for those who know the images and liṅgas," it is shown that the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) is a means to worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) specifically for those desiring enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), while excluding those desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*).
253) It is to be performed after initiation (*dīkṣā*); by means of the cutting of the hand, it is also a means for achieving liberation (*mokṣa*).
The extraction (*uddhāra*) of the *liṅga* that has become defiled by defects such as decay is taught; this is what is being stated by the words beginning with "it is said."

The primary object of the *liṅgoddhāra* (the rite of extracting the linga) is the human-made (*mānuṣa*) linga; however, self-manifested (*svayaṃbhū*), divine (*daiva*), or sage-established (*ārṣa*) lingas are not its objects. As it has been said:
"That which was established by asuras, sages, gods, or those who know reality..."
One should not move it, even according to the prescribed rite, if it is decayed or excessively broken.
Thus ends the ritual for consecration (*pratiṣṭhāvidhi*).
The commentary composed by the venerable Naṭeśvara, the Guru, who is Śambhu through his [divine] mouths and so forth, and the son of the illustrious Śaṅkara, is completed.
Of this work, titled *Śrīmacchrīmṛgendrarājapaddhati*, which has attained renown as a hatchet for cutting down the forest of the bonds of the bound (pāśa), composed by [the author].
Thus ends the commentary on the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*.
